articles.title_orig: ICE shooting of New York man in car with five-year-old sparks protests
articles.title_zh: ICE shooting of New York man in car with five-year-old sparks protests
articles.content_orig:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent has shot a man in New York City as he sat in a car with a child.
Citing an “unconscionable and incredibly serious situation”, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said early reports indicated that agents surrounded the man and a five-year-old in his car on Thursday in the Marble Hill neighbourhood before firing multiple rounds.
The child was believed to be physically unharmed, the mayor added as he said he has called United States President Donald Trump and would demand that he end all ICE enforcement actions in the city.
“I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorise our communities,” Mamdani said.
Protests followed on Thursday evening with demonstrators saying the shooting illustrated the dangers of Trump’s immigration crackdown, and some scuffles with police broke out.
“We are heartbroken and enraged,” said City Council member Carmen De La Rosa, who represents the area.
Speaking at the scene in the evening, Mamdani said: “Today’s shooting is only further devastating confirmation of what we have long known, which is that ICE operates with impunity, that they sow chaos and terror across our country, that they have killed far more of our neighbours than they could ever have claimed to save.”
He demanded the agency “must be abolished”.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul said she spoke with Trump and US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Thursday night.
“I expressed outrage on behalf of New Yorkers and urged them to halt ICE enforcement operations in New York,” she said in a statement.
“I also asked that any body camera footage of the shooting be released to the public, so we can establish the facts and get to the truth.”
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, said its officers were conducting a “targeted enforcement operation” in the Bronx about 4pm to arrest a 28-year-old Dominican national with a criminal conviction identified as Oscar Belgal by city police.
It said an officer “discharged his weapon” and “the criminal illegal alien” was injured. The DHS added that the incident remains under investigation.
Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said Belgal was pulling into a parking space when a federal officer in plain clothes approached with a gun drawn, followed by another federal officer who also wasn’t in uniform.
Belgal started to pull the car forward, and then at least one of the officers fired seven rounds, hitting the man below his left ear, Tisch said, confirming that the child was unharmed and was with a relative.
According to a statement by the New York Police Department, the man remained conscious and was receiving medical treatment at a nearby hospital.
The shooting took place after months of mounting criticism of the agency.
In January, federal immigration agents shot dead two US citizens in Minneapolis: Renee Nicole Good, a 37-year-old mother of three, killed by an ICE agent on January 7, and Alex Pretti, a 37-year-old intensive care nurse, shot by a US border agent.
After Good’s killing, Trump officials labelled her a “domestic terrorist” even as video of the shooting cast doubt on their claims she had tried to run over an agent.
The federal government removed local authorities from the investigation, rejected calls for a civil rights probe and sent hundreds more agents to Minnesota, bringing the total to 3,000, as protests against the killings and the immigration crackdown spread to hundreds of US cities.
Trump blamed the shift in US opinion about the immigration agency on unfair media coverage, urging DHS and ICE to publicise the “violent criminals” they arrest.
ICE has been tasked with deporting one million people a year.
The agency doubled in size in the first year of the second Trump administration to more than 22,000 agents by January and is now the highest-funded federal law enforcement agency with about $75bn allocated to it over four years under a tax bill Trump signed last year.

articles.title_orig: World Mental Health Day 2026: How losing my father and surviving illness led me to mental health advocacy
articles.title_zh: World Mental Health Day 2026: How losing my father and surviving illness led me to mental health advocacy
articles.content_orig:
By MARTIN ROBINSON, CHIEF REPORTER
Published: 10:43 EDT, 8 October 2026 | Updated: 20:50 EDT, 8 October 2026
Prince Harry has revealed he felt depressed and 'useless' immediately after Megxit, and now refuses to spend more than ten days away from Meghan and their children.
In a new video released today, the Duke of Sussex claims life in the Royal Family left him unable to properly grieve the death of Princess Diana , adding that his official duties triggered panic attacks.
Harry, 42, said getting dressed for royal engagements in a shirt and tie frequently left him feeling as though he was being strangled or suffocated.
'You would think I had the best help in the world. I'm a prince, for God's sake, but I was still grieving and didn't have any place to put those feelings,' he said, describing emotions he carried for '15 or 20 years'.
He revealed therapy eventually helped him and described the extraordinary moment when spraying himself with Diana's perfume prompted his hidden memories and emotions to come flooding back.
Speaking about grief in a video for the American education platform MasterClass, Harry said despite finding happiness with Meghan, he 'slipped into depression ' after they quit royal life and left Britain.
'We moved to Canada to get some space away from everything and simply think,' he said. 'Within two or three days of leaving that stressful environment, I experienced an adrenaline crash unlike anything I'd ever felt before.
'It was as though I needed stress for my brain to function. I became useless around the house. I slipped into depression for about two weeks and felt like I couldn't function without adrenaline.'
His frank comments about mental health and PTSD came as Meghan Markle stepped back into the spotlight yesterday for the first time in years, wearing a £28,000 outfit to take afternoon tea with Malala Yousafzai in London.
Prince Harry has described the mental health problems he suffered after Megxit and the grief of losing his mother
Meghan Markle made her first public appearance in the UK for four years, meeting Malala Yousafzai for afternoon tea at Claridge's yesterday
Meghan and Malala enjoyed smiled as they said farewell following their tea yesterday
Six years on from Megxit, the Sussexes are parents to two children, Archie and Lilibet, and are back in the UK again. The children have started school in the Cotswolds.
And Harry now says that he follows a strict 'ten-day' rule to protect his happiness.
He said: 'The biggest factor for me is the energy, joy and happiness I get from being with my family, especially our children, and from being on the ground doing my work.
'The key to maintaining that balance is spending no more than ten days away from my wife and kids.
'It's about balancing my work and sense of purpose with being a dad and a husband.'
Harry revealed he did not cry for almost 20 years after his mother's death and thinks of her 'pretty much every night and then most mornings'.
A therapist encouraged him to find Diana's perfume in an effort to unlock his grief after he had forgotten what her voice and laugh sounded like.
The Duke said doing this had a remarkable effect on him and his grief, claiming the scent brought back memories and emotions that had long been suppressed.
'It was like being transported to another time,' Harry said. 'It unlocked everything that had been locked away.
'Spraying my mother's scent was almost like knocking certain bricks through so that I could see through and certain memories and experiences could start seeping back.'
In the very personal MasterClass episode – entitled Redefining Grief: Building Resilience Through Loss – Harry also said: 'Everything I do, everything I put my energy towards, I hope that my mother will be proud of.
'Trying to continue and protect her legacy, what I didn't realise was that the work I was drawn to was so similar to the work she was doing.'
Speaking to neuroscientist Dr Mary-Frances O'Connor ahead of World Mental Health Day on Saturday, Harry added that after marrying Meghan and becoming a father, he often felt guilty about allowing himself to be happy.
The interview comes weeks after the publication of his uncle's memoir about Diana, which reignited debate about her legacy and included claims that angered the King.
Earl Spencer claimed in one angry phone call Charles told him Diana would soon be forgotten after she died in Paris in 1997.
Reflecting on his mother's death, Harry said: 'I didn't cry when I was told my mum died, only at her burial, and then not again for nearly two decades.
'I was convinced that was strength, but it wasn't. It was a 12-year-old boy with no permission to fall apart and no roadmap for how to heal.
'I'd spent so long emotionally numb because I felt disloyal and guilty at the possibility of being happy without her. I felt I had to stay sad and emotionally shut down to prove I missed her.'
Harry has explained how therapy transformed his outlook, saying: 'The reality is that what I discovered was that she just wanted me to be happy.
'That was a huge mental shift for me. It freed me and gave me a completely different outlook on life.'
Harry also said that joining the Army gave him a sense of purpose.
'For 15 or 20 years, when people asked, "Are you okay?" my answer was always, "I'm fine". It was numbness. It was emotional shutdown.
'Without realising it, adrenaline was driving me. It was the force that led me to join the military at 20. It was the perfect distraction.'
The Duke said he increasingly withdrew from his friends and social life during those years, explaining how he 'was much more comfortable sitting at home'.
Meghan smiles as she and Malala walk outside the restaurant after their catch-up
Meghan puts her hand on Malala's back as they speak after exiting the restaurant
The pair first joined forces in 2020 for a virtual discussion to mark International Day of the Girl
The Duke of Sussex spoke to neuroscientist Dr Mary-Frances O'Connor ahead of World Mental Health Day on Saturday
Harry posed for a trailer promoting the new interview where he discusses his history of grief and mental health
Harry said a therapist encouraged him to spray himself with Diana's perfume, which he said brought memories and emotions flooding back
Harry added that he struggled to find help at first.
'Unfortunately, a number of general practitioners weren't equipped to help me. It was a case of receiving advice or being offered a pill.
'I was completely against taking medication. I followed the advice but it wasn't making any difference, so I kept searching for something that would work.'
He described his deployment to Afghanistan as life-changing.
'The things I saw and experienced appeared to trigger other traumas that had been stored within me,' he said.
Harry said therapy eventually gave him the 'permission to grieve'.
'Sitting in a room with a complete stranger and having the confidence and trust to open myself up,' he said.
The Duke, who in his book Spare admitted taking a number of illegal drugs in his life, praised psychedelic-assisted therapy – a type of treatment that has split doctors.
Magic mushrooms, MDMA and ketamine are used to change the brain rather than treat symptoms of depression and PTSD with common anti-depressants.
He said: 'To combine conventional therapy with modern day medicines breaks down those walls and those barriers to be able to open yourself up and go deeper than you would ever dare to go.
'Psychedelic assisted therapy is no longer a fringe idea or thought. It's really becoming, I think, mainstream.'
Harry's revelations follow Meghan's return to the spotlight yesterday as the Duchess of Sussex , 45, and the Nobel Peace laureate Malala, 29, were photographed leaving the luxury hotel together in Mayfair before sharing a warm hug outside the foyer.
Meghan was wearing a camel Tove Studio coat worth £1,695, a £630 cashmere sweater in wheat by LA-based label CO and Ralph Lauren's £1,700 white satin Charmaine trousers.

articles.title_orig: One of the world’s wealthiest cities is enduring the world’s most polluted air. Here’s why
articles.title_zh: One of the world’s wealthiest cities is enduring the world’s most polluted air. Here’s why
articles.content_orig:
Singapore, one of the wealthiest cities in the world, has become the most polluted on the planet as it chokes under a blanket of thick, toxic smog caused by fires in neighboring Indonesia.
Pollution has cast a pall on the city-state as it gets ready to host a packed weekend of marquee events ranging from international conferences to the glitzy Formula One Grand Prix night race.
Air quality in the city-state was at the “very unhealthy” range with an air quality index (AQI) of 216 Friday mid-morning, according to Swiss air quality monitor IQAir.
The financial hub topped the list of most polluted cities by IQAir this week and was still at the top spot Friday morning. Kuala Lumpur, also deeply affected by the Indonesian fires, was at number two.
Singapore’s skyline, including Marina Bay Sands and other skyscrapers were reduced to faint silhouettes amid the pollution.
The key Asian financial hub – with a population of 6.21 million and annual GDP of more than $650 billion – and neighboring Malaysia have had to endure the haze almost annually.
Fires in Indonesia are an annual event during the country’s dry season when huge stretches of peatland are cleared and drained for commercial plantations, including those that produce palm oil, an ingredient used in a slew of products from noodles to toothpaste.
But this year, the arrival of what’s expected to be a “super” El Niño — a supercharged version of the natural climate pattern which tends to bring bone dry conditions to the country — has set the stage for unusually intense blazes.
In an update on its website Thursday, Singapore’s National Environment Agency said “moderate to dense smoke plumes from southern and central Sumatra and West Kalimantan were observed to drift towards Singapore,” referring to Indonesian regions.
“Under the prevailing southeasterly or southerly winds, smoke haze may continue to drift towards Singapore,” it added.
Entertainment events held outdoors at the F1 event in Singapore could potentially be affected but not the race itself, the motorsport’s governing FIA said Thursday, according to Reuters. On Friday, race organizer Singapore GP told CNN “there are currently no plans to modify our entertainment activities” at the event.
Acts to entertain F1 spectators include Janet Jackson and The Killers, among others.
This is not the first time the Singapore night race is facing air quality issues. The races in 2015 and 2019 were also enveloped in thick haze and they went ahead.
Nevertheless, the Singapore Tourism Board told CNN on Friday: “Action plans are in place based on the intensity of the haze.”
F1 drivers, however, don’t seem too bothered. Cadillac driver Valtteri Bottas, who cycled more than 400km (248 miles) from Malaysia to Singapore this week, told Reuters: “I don’t feel like it’s that extreme yet. I mean, it’s not great, but I don’t think there’s that much you can do.”
Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton told Reuters he has “much bigger issues to focus on.”
Neighboring Malaysia has also been heavily affected by the smog with the education ministry shutting schools across several states this week as the situation worsens.

articles.title_zh: October 8, 2026 — Gulf Coast evacuations underway as Hurricane Isaias strengthens
articles.content_orig:

Get the latest updates on Hurricane Isaias here .
Hurricane Isaias is expected to strengthen significantly over Thursday and Friday. Even if it weakens slightly before landfall, the storm will remain dangerous along the Gulf Coast.
Hurricane Isaias is due to make landfall late Friday night into Saturday as a strong Category two storm. A state of emergency has been declared across Florida and Alabama.
Meteorologist Ali Van Fleet explains how a weakening hurricane can still grow in size and threaten a broader region with rain, storm surge and even tornadoes.
All hurricanes are dangerous, but their impacts aren't always created equal. Meteorologist Chris Warren explains how storm size and storm strength influence the impacts communities experience before, during and after landfall.
To help people prepare for hurricanes, scientists studied 40 tropical cyclones and found storm surge hits in eight ways.
• Record-shattering Isaias is strengthening into a high-end Category 2 hurricane en route to landfall on the northern Gulf Coast by this weekend. The storm rapidly intensified into the Atlantic season’s first hurricane Wednesday night.
• Isaias is expected to strengthen further and briefly become a “major hurricane” early Friday before weakening some and making landfall late Friday night. Locations on the coast could see up to 7 feet of storm surge and up to 15 inches of rain , with short-lived tornadoes popping up with little notice.
• States of emergency have been issued in parts of Alabama, Florida and Georgia, and mandatory evacuation orders have been issued in some areas.
• Some Florida airports are scheduled to close ahead of the storm. Amtrak services in parts of Louisiana and Alabama are also disrupted.
Isaias’ sustained winds remain at 105 mph, according to the National Hurricane Center’s 2 a.m. ET update. NOAA and Air Force hurricane hunters are flying inside the storm, now about 230 miles south of the mouth of the Mississippi River.
Isaias could briefly become a Category 3 hurricane Friday before weakening somewhat and making landfall late at night. Even as Isaias is expected to lose some strength before landfall, it will still bring dangerous storm surge, damaging winds and flooding rain.
Residents across coastal Alabama and Florida spent Thursday boarding up homes, filling sandbags and stocking up on supplies as Hurricane Isaias strengthened into a Category 2 storm and barreled toward the Gulf Coast.
AP video from Lillian, Alabama, showed residents covering windows with plywood and loading supplies as they prepare to ride out the storm. “Everybody’s getting fuel. Everybody’s buying water. Everybody’s scurrying around like ants,” resident Richard Weekley said.
Reuters video from Gulf Breeze, Florida, showed residents filling and loading sandbags as they prepare for possible flooding from Hurricane Isaias.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis warned that saturated ground and heavy rainfall could cause dangerous inland flooding, urging residents to take the threat seriously.
Forecasters said Isaias is expected to make landfall late Friday, with life-threatening storm surge, flooding rain and possible tornadoes forecast across parts of Florida, Alabama and Mississippi.
An eye is beginning to take shape as lightning flashes within Isaias’ thunderstorms over the Gulf.
The emerging eye points to a better-organized hurricane, while the lightning near the center of the storm signals vigorous thunderstorm activity in the eyewall as Isaias strengthens tonight.
A remarkable sunset unfolded over Atlanta on Thursday. CNN meteorologist Derek Van Dam explains how distant Hurricane Isaias in the Gulf created the spectacle.
Isaias’ sustained winds have increased to 105 mph, and the National Hurricane Center now forecasts it will briefly become a major hurricane early Friday. “Major” refers to a Category 3 or stronger storm, with sustained winds of at least 111 mph.
Isaias should weaken some before landfall, likely coming ashore near the threshold between Category 1 and 2 late Friday night. However, its wind field is expected to expand, spreading dangerous impacts well beyond its center.
Isaias is in infamous company as an “I” named storm.
The list of names runs alphabetically, so “I” goes to the ninth named storm — which usually forms around the peak of Atlantic hurricane season in mid-September, when conditions are primed to fuel powerful storms. And since 1953, Atlantic storms with “I” names reach Category 3 strength or higher more frequently than any other letter.
Ivan in 2004, Irma in 2017, Ida in 2021 and most recently Ian in 2022 each reached at least Category 4 strength and went on to make landfall in the United States. Ian struck southwestern Florida with 150 mph winds, resulted in 150 deaths and caused over $112 billion in damage, becoming the costliest hurricane in the state’s history.
Storms that are especially deadly or damaging have their name retired from the official list. Thirteen names starting with I have been retired, more than any other letter.
Isaias formed on October 6, weeks later than usual for an “I” storm, thanks to this year’s super El Niño putting a damper on storms in the Atlantic. It’s currently forecast to make landfall on the Gulf Coast as a Category 1 or Category 2 hurricane.
Isaias is expected to strengthen overnight as it passes near a warm eddy, a rotating pocket of ocean water where warmth extends well below the surface. That deep reservoir of heat, marked by the darker reds in the image below, provides ample fuel for the hurricane.
Increasing wind shear is expected to weaken Isaias as it approaches the coast, but it is still forecast to make landfall as a dangerous hurricane.
Winds in Hurricane Isaias reached around 100 mph today, according to Captain Mark McCoy, an Air Force Reserve Weather officer who flew through the storm.
He told CNN’s Erin Burnett that his team experienced “a lot of dry air” that “was being sucked in on the south side and southwest side.”
“It was slowly gaining strength as we were in there,” McCoy said.
The journey, which he said was a “pretty standard mission,” lasted around 9.5 hours and included flying through the eye of the storm.
Isaias is still a Category 2 hurricane with 100 mph sustained winds as of the 7 p.m. CT update from the National Hurricane Center.
After intensifying earlier today, the storm’s strength has leveled off … for now. Further strengthening is expected through early Friday.
Hurricane Isaias is beginning to pick up speed, traveling at a 13 mph pace which is up from 9 mph reported about 12 hours ago. The hurricane is located just under 300 miles south of Louisiana.
It’s forecast to turn north tomorrow and approach the Gulf Coast later that night.
Before Hurricane Isaias makes landfall along the Gulf Coast, officials as far as Charleston, South Carolina, are already preparing for lingering effects from the hurricane.
On Thursday, Charleston Mayor William S. Cogswell Jr. activated the city’s active flood mitigation plan, anticipating heavy rain and as a king tide cycle brings risk of flooding over the weekend to the coastal city on the Atlantic.
The most intense rain affecting Charleston is expected on Saturday afternoon into the evening, with city officials expecting 3 to 4 inches of rain, though it could be higher in some areas, a city news release said. Tides in Charleston’s harbor are expected to peak near 7.7 feet Saturday morning and remain high into the evening.
The record-breaking Hurricane Isaias is getting stronger as it heads north to the Gulf Coast. The strong and rapidly-intensifying storm is expected to make landfall this weekend as the the season’s first Atlantic hurricane .

articles.title_orig: Pentagon says the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed
articles.title_zh: Pentagon says the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed
articles.content_orig:
FILE - This undated photo provided by the Bell County Sheriff's Department shows former Army psychiatrist Maj. Nidal Hasan. Uncredited/Bell County Sheriff's Department/via AP hide caption
WASHINGTON — The firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed, the Pentagon said Thursday, a stunning revelation about plans for the first military execution in more than 65 years after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had described it as being "public."
The Army announced this week that the execution would take place at Fort Hood on Dec. 3 after Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting at the military base in 2009.
Hegseth, speaking to the conservative TV outlet Real America's Voice on Wednesday, said, "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public." Officials in the Pentagon clarified Thursday that the execution would be livestreamed and that more details would follow.
The revelation from Hegseth about the public nature of the execution — let alone one as violent as a firing squad — has raised further questions about how the death penalty is carried out in the U.S., especially after the botched lethal injection of Christa Pike in Tennessee.
Hasan could choose to resist execution and file a habeas petition — a legal request to review the legality of a detention — in civilian court, which could significantly delay the execution, experts said.
"It frankly might outlast the current administration, and who knows if the next one will have the same penchant for executions," said Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specializing in military law.
Deborah Denno, a death penalty expert and law professor at Fordham University, said livestreaming an execution could make the process "much more transparent" and inform the public about all that capital punishment entails. Those are benefits that she said would be useful at a time when Pike's botched execution has raised fresh questions about the manner by which criminal defendants are put to death for their crimes.
"I think it could possibly be a good idea because it would be transparent and the public would be fully aware that it's happening," she said.
When many states have had difficulty carrying out lethal injections due to difficulty accessing drugs or finding medical professionals willing to participate in executions, firing squads are coming to be seen as a less inhumane alternative, said Brenner Fissell, a professor at Villanova Law and vice president of the National Institute of Military Justice.
"Firing squads can be a quicker, cleaner, more precise way to execute a prisoner," he said. "I don't think that's what's motivating this. There's a perceived masculinity and military-ness to firing squads that is part of the aura Hegseth is trying to emphasize — the 'lethality culture.'"
Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at UC Berkeley Law, said Hegseth's announcement raises a host of legal and public policy questions, including concerns for the dignity of the defendant, who will be eligible to view the execution and what the Trump administration has in mind in opting for an unusual spectacle.
Though there has been long-running discussion about the idea of televising an execution, "I don't recall a situation in which it was instigated by the government. I think that also raises serious questions about what is the motivation of the government," she said.
"This is a president who's about spectacle and that's, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver," Semel said, adding that she was skeptical that the administration had given a second thought to the legal and social questions being presented by the decision.
Trump, who approved Hasan's execution, has previously been critical of public executions in Iran, at times using the possibility of protesters being killed by the Iranian government as a possible rationale for military action that preceded his ultimate choice to attack Iran on Feb. 28.
"We've been told that the killing in Iran is stopping," Trump told reporters on Jan. 14. "It's stopping, and there's no plan for executions."
In his State of the Union address just days before launching the Iran war, Trump reiterated, "We stopped them from hanging a lot of them with the threat of serious violence."
The White House on Thursday referred questions about the plans for the livestreamed execution to the Pentagon.
Hegseth was asked Wednesday if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to the Trump administration. The Pentagon chief replied: "Don't care. We'll see him on Dec. 3."
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building on Nov. 5, 2009, where soldiers were waiting in long lines to receive immunizations and medical clearance for deployment. He shouted "Allahu akbar" — Arabic for "God is great!" — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He also shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot.
Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. A military judge barred him from presenting that as a defense during his 2013 trial. Hasan was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot in the back by law enforcement, and he now uses a wheelchair.
Hasan could seek a lengthy delay of his execution, though given his behavior at trial, he may not want to.
After firing his lawyers and representing himself, Hasan began his portion of the trial by telling jurors he was the gunman. He said little else over the next three weeks, which convinced his court-appointed standby lawyers that Hasan's only goal was to get a death sentence.
The military called nearly 90 witnesses, but Hasan rested his case without calling a single person to testify in his defense and made no closing argument. Yet he leaked documents during the trial to journalists that revealed him telling military mental health workers that he could " still be a martyr " if executed.
Attorney John Galligan, a former military judge who had represented Hasan in several civil matters following his criminal trial, spoke with Hasan on Wednesday but is barred from offering much detail about that conversation. He is not representing Hasan in his criminal case but said he's worried about his physical health under the plan laid out by officials, and that Hasan has not yet had access to legal counsel.
Galligan said that according to Hasan, the commandant of the facility brought a chaplain but no attorney from either the Trial Defense Service or from his civilian defense when he was notified that Trump had signed off on his execution. Galligan called that a breach of Army regulations.
A spokeswoman for the Army said Thursday that multiple attempts were made to contact Trial Defense Service attorneys, saying they made every reasonable effort and adhered to policy.
"The civilian counsel was not reasonably available to be physically present for the notification on the 5th," the spokeswoman said, adding that counsel was located in Virginia but did not provide a name.
The spokeswoman also said Hasan has not been kept from contacting and communicating with his counsel.
Hegseth said the military hasn't executed a service member by firing squad since World War II. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging.
Amnesty International said in its report on executions in 2025 that it knew of at least 17 public executions — 11 in Iran and 6 in Afghanistan.

articles.title_orig: Oxford Area High School closed Friday after confirmed case of measles
articles.title_zh: Oxford Area High School closed Friday after confirmed case of measles
articles.content_orig:
OXFORD, Pa. (WPVI) -- The Oxford Area High School in Chester County will be closed Friday after a confirmed case of measles was identified within the school community.
The school district announced the closure in a letter sent to families Thursday.
"We understand that news like this may be concerning for families," the district wrote. "The health and well-being of our students, staff and community are incredibly important to us, and we recognize that receiving this information can raise questions, concerns and uncertainty."
READ MORE | Measles cases surpass 1,000 in Pennsylvania amid the state's largest outbreak in decades
School officials said the Chester County Health Department will contact anyone believed to have been exposed.
The announcement comes as Pennsylvania has surpassed 1,000 measles cases , with 86 cases reported in Chester County.
Earlier this week, Jeanne Franklin, director of the Chester County Health Department, said officials had been working closely with school nurses and superintendents ahead of the school year because of concerns about measles transmission.
According to the district's letter, anyone who is not vaccinated against measles, or cannot provide proof of vaccination, must stay away from school and school-related activities for 21 days following a potential exposure.
Measles is a highly contagious virus that spreads through the air or direct contact.
Early symptoms include cough, runny nose, fever as high as 104 Fahrenheit and red, watery eyes, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
Two to three days after symptoms start, patients may develop Koplik spots, which are tiny white spots that may appear inside the mouth on the inner cheek.
Three to five days after symptoms start, patients may experience a rash, first appearing on the face at the hairline before moving downwards to the neck, chest, stomach, arms, legs and feet. Fever may spike even higher than 104 F when the rash appears, the CDC says.
The CDC currently recommends that people receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, the first at ages 12 to 15 months and the second between 4 and 6 years old. One dose is 93% effective in preventing measles infection, and two doses are 97% effective, the CDC says.

articles.title_orig: Plymouth skateboarder heading to World Skate Games aged 60
articles.title_zh: Plymouth skateboarder heading to World Skate Games aged 60
articles.content_orig:
An amateur skateboarder is set to represent his country for the first time almost 50 years after he took up the sport.
Darren Miles, 60, from Plymouth, is to represent Great Britain in the slalom event at the World Skate Games in Paraguay later this month.
Miles will take part in three disciplines as part of the team made up of a mixture of professionals and amateurs.
"When I was 10 I never thought I would be skateboarding at 60 for my country so that's the main attraction," he said.
Miles first became interested in the sport in 1977 in Essex where he "always had a skateboard and always skated around".
In 2020 he "realised he was slowly losing his tricks" and took to slalom, which involves speed skateboarding around cones.
When he heads to the World Skate Games, Miles said he could be up against competitors who are in their 20s as well as those his own age.
He said "to finish and not get disqualified" would be a successful games for him.
"There's a top 16, I don't really anticipate getting into there, but I'll be going there and supporting all the other guys that are racing, because a few of the English guys are in with a good chance," he said.
"I'll be supporting them and just enjoying being at the event."
He said he enjoyed travelling for skateboarding events and the social aspect of the sport was a "big draw" for him.
"Sometimes you get a sport that's what matches your personality and it can be a lot of fun with a shared danger," he said.
"Everybody's been really supportive and I think a little bit amazed."

articles.title_orig: Museum honours two key World War Two RAF stations
articles.title_zh: Museum honours two key World War Two RAF stations
articles.content_orig:
A museum has paid tribute to two former RAF stations that played vital roles in Bomber Command operations during World War Two.
The RAF Witchford and Mepal Museum has opened on Lancaster Way Business Park in Ely, Cambridgeshire, to show the contribution RAF Witchford and RAF Mepal made to the Lancaster bombers' offensive.
Grovemere Property bought RAF Witchford from the Ministry of Defence after the war and redeveloped the site.
"It really is just amazing that we are now home to all these wonderful items and can ensure that the experiences and sacrifices of those connected with the two airfields are remembered and understood by future generations," Thomas Brand, from the firm, said.
In 2024 the Brand family, which owns Grovemere Property, decided to create a new free purpose-built museum following the closure of the RAF Witchford Exhibition, which was located in the foyer of an office building on the business park.
The museum is an unmanned facility with the public gaining entrance via a traffic light system taken from an original Lancaster bomber aircraft [John Devine/BBC]
Brand, a joint managing director of Grovemere Property whose grandfather bought the former RAF Witchford airfield, said the origins of the new museum could be traced to an excavation of a Lancaster bomber crash site at nearby Coveney in 1995.
"The project was supported by Grovemere Property, after local historian Barry Aldridge, who spent decades documenting RAF Witchford's history, got in touch," he said.
Aldridge, who died in 2016, had connections to the airfield that stretched back to childhood, when he explored its derelict buildings.
Artefacts recovered during the Coveney dig included a Lancaster engine, which later became a key exhibit in the previous RAF Witchford Exhibition, and is now the centrepiece at the new museum.
One of the exhibition's photographs shows Princess Elizabeth visiting RAF Witchford in 1944 with King George VI and Queen Elizabeth [RAF Witchford and Mepal Museum]
Brand said that many local people had donated items for the museum, which had given him "goosebump" moments.
"Recently a man gave me an old suitcase which contained his late father's RAF uniform, his medals, flight logs, flying helmet and a personal journal that documented his time in the RAF, it was incredible to see," he said.
RAF Witchford and RAF Mepal played key roles in Bomber Command operations, which saw Lancaster bombers fly missions across occupied Europe [John Devine/BBC]
Brand also said he had witnessed some emotional visitors who had found pictures of their loved ones displayed as part of the exhibit.
He did not disclose how much the museum cost to set-up, but said it was now being run as a charity "to help ensure its long-term future".
The striking design of the building incorporates one side of a Lancaster Bomber fuselage which can be viewed from inside [John Devine/BBC]

articles.title_orig: Mamdani defends Oct. 7 message that angered Jewish leaders, unnerved some Democrats
articles.title_zh: Mamdani defends Oct. 7 message that angered Jewish leaders, unnerved some Democrats
articles.content_orig:
UNION SQUARE, Manhattan (WABC) -- Mayor Zohran Mamdani defended his Oct. 7 statement on Thursday after facing criticism from some members of the city's Jewish community over remarks that referenced both Israelis killed in the Oct. 7 attacks and Palestinians killed in Gaza.
Mamdani appeared at a news conference in Bushwick on grants to nonprofits Thursday morning, less than 12 hours after demonstrators interrupted a vigil in Union Square for the hundreds of Israelis killed on Oct. 7.
The mayor was escorted past angry pro-Palestinian demonstrators at the vigil as chants echoed through the streets, with some calling him a "traitor."
In a statement issued Wednesday, Mamdani said:
"We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss. The suffering did not begin nor end that day. It instead continued through the Israeli government's devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza. Many New Yorkers are reckoning with this unbearable grief, and we mourn alongside them - all while knowing that our tax dollars fund these war crimes."
Speaking Thursday, Mamdani said he stood by those remarks and rejected suggestions that he should apologize.
"It is critically important to be able to mourn for all of those who were killed—and have been killed since. Especially given that we know this is ongoing, as opposed to something simply that was three years ago," he said.
The mayor's reference to the Israeli military response to Oct. 7 in a statement marking the anniversary drew criticism from some in the city's Jewish community. Mamdani defended his position Thursday.
"We need not choose between which death we will mourn and which we will ignore, that we will reckon with the fact that all of it is to be opposed," he said.
City Council Speaker Julie Menin said she disagreed with the mayor's approach.
"I believe October 7th should focus on the events of October 7th, not on the aftermath, but on the events of October 7th—just as I believe on September 11th, we should focus on the events of September 11th, and that's where I put my focus," she said.
The exchange highlighted differing views among city leaders over how Oct. 7 should be commemorated and discussed.

articles.title_orig: Fiery Senate Debates in Maine, Michigan and Georgia: Five Takeaways
articles.title_zh: Fiery Senate Debates in Maine, Michigan and Georgia: Five Takeaways
articles.content_orig:
Candidates traded personal attacks and clashed over a range of issues in closely watched US Senate debates on Thursday, with control of Congress at stake
With just weeks left in the contentious midterm election campaign, candidates in a trio of highly-competitive Senate races debated Thursday night, clashing over the economy, tariffs, the Iran war and abortion rights, with control of the upper chamber at stake.
In Georgia, incumbent Democratic senator Jon Ossoff faced GOP representative Mike Collins. In Michigan, Democrat Abdul Al-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers debated over the state’s open Senate seat. And in Maine, longtime senator Susan Collins met Democratic challenger Troy Jackson. Democrats need to flip four Republican-held Senate seats to win the majority.
Here are the key takeaways from the battleground state debates.
Affordability was a major topic across all three debates on Thursday night, as voters consistently name the cost of goods, gas, housing and healthcare as their top concerns in this year’s midterms.
“Can you afford your gas? Can you afford your groceries under this guy who’s going to rubber stamp everything Donald Trump tells him to rubber stamp?” El-Sayed asked during the Michigan debate, the first of two in one of this cycle’s most fiercely contested races.
Both Rogers and El-Sayed said they support suspending a fuel tax to alleviate costs, while El-Sayed argued that the Iran war, which was driving up gas prices, needs to end. El-Sayed attacked Rogers for growing his personal wealth while in office as a US representative.
Rogers called El-Sayed “bought off” by billionaire George Soros, Hamas and Hezbollah. “We cannot afford Abdul, and we cannot risk his ideology,” Rogers said.
In Georgia, Ossoff repeatedly asked Collins to justify his support for Trump’s global tariff policies, which the senator said have “crushed Georgia families” and “strangled” economic growth.
“Let’s see if he has the courage to explain his votes,” Ossoff said, adding later: “Still have not heard an explanation for the tariffs.”
Collins, who is trying to cut into Ossoff’s lead, blamed inflation on Biden administration policies, singling out spending measures that his opponent had supported.
Later in Maine, where polls show a tight race, Jackson focused his remarks on pocketbook issues, including the sharp spike in heating oil costs and high energy prices.
Collins defended her record and argued that Maine had benefited from the $50bn rural health transformation fund that was appended to Trump’s signature tax cut and spending bill, the so-called Big Beautiful bill.
In the Georgia debate, a question about data centers erupted into a pointed, personal exchange between Ossoff and Collins.
“Mike Collins voted to take that money out of your pocket and out of your community and give it instead to data center developers,” Ossoff said.
He then accused Collins of being a “bigot” who has “hired half the Third Reich” – a reference to the congressman’s history of employing staffers who have expressed white nationalist, antisemitic, and extremist views online.
“If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery,” Ossoff said of the late civil rights icon and long-serving Georgia congressman, “Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club. His office has been in cahoots with some of the most notorious white supremacists on the country.”
Collins was asked directly about his son-in-law’s social media posts promoting white nationalist and antisemitic views.
“You know, Rick, that’s my family,” Collins replied. “That’s the craziness that Jon Ossoff has been spewing out there.” Collins noted that a New York man had recently been charged after threatening to kill him, and added: “I’ve condemned racism, antisemitism, hate; I don’t care where the source is. And I tell him that too, it’s wrong. We have no place in this world for that.”
Collins, meanwhile, sought to cast Ossoff as “radical” and an “extremist” whose record in the Senate had left the state “less safe, more expensive and worse off”.
Tariffs were also a topic of heated debate in Michigan, which shares hundreds of miles of border with Canada.
This week, Rogers publicly backtracked on previous support for Trump’s tariffs on the US’s northern neighbor , saying in a campaign ad that “Canada is not our enemy” and that the “tariff war” needed to end now.
During Thursday night’s debate, Rogers said he had spoken to the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, this week to advocate for a deal between the two countries. There are tariffs in place that are “too high and not helpful for us”, Rogers said.
El-Sayed said he supports targeted, logical tariffs that protect Michigan manufacturing, but nothing like the “ham-fisted, chaotic, self-serving” tariffs Trump put in place. He called out Rogers for “flip-flopping” on the issue, saying he was only reversing his stance because of “sagging poll numbers”.
“He’s doing an ad drinking a Labatt and talking about the Red Wings, pretending like he was not for this the entire time,” El-Sayed said. “Be serious, my guy.”
In Maine, discussions about gas prices and the war in Iran raised notable tension in the second debate between Jackson and Collins, who is seeking a sixth term in her seat. “She’s the Chairman of Appropriations,” Jackson said. “Money has to come through them for these wars – she still can do something.”
Collins, who plans to continue leading the Appropriations committee if re-elected, said she had repeatedly supported war powers resolutions to halt Trump’s military action in Iran.
But Jackson pushed further, accusing the senator and her husband of profiting from the war.
She could use her leverage to stop this war, but instead they’re making money,” he said, prompting a furious response from Collins, who called the allegation “absolutely outrageous”.
“You owe me an apology,” she said.
In Maine, both candidates were also pressed to address inconsistencies in their positions on reproductive rights, a crucial issue for voters in the state.
“Our records have changed,” Jackson said. “Mine has gotten better – hers has gotten worse.”
He pointed to Collins’ vote to confirm supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh, who helped overturn Roe v Wade in 2022 . Collins, one of just two Republican senators who supports abortion rights, has said she does not regret her vote for Kavanaugh, even though she believed he had given her private assurances before his 2018 confirmation that he would not overturn the landmark ruling. Collins sought to turn the issue back on her opponent, noting his past stances on abortion that have left many voters wary. “From 2000 until he ran for the house seat in 2013 was very anti-choice,” she said, accusing Jackson of having held “extremist” views on abortion. “He was for a bill that would not allow abortion when the mother’s life was at risk.” She also pointed to legislation she helped write that sought to “codify Roe v Wade nationwide,” but the bill never made it passed the Senate.
In Michigan, Rogers repeatedly attacked El-Sayed by attempting to tie him to Muslim terrorist groups, including Hamas, and suggested government surveillance would only bother someone if he or his family had something to hide.
Rogers brought up El-Sayed’s mom and sister, prompting El-Sayed to say at one point that Rogers should just come out and say what he’s been dancing around all night, after Rogers’ repeated references to terrorist groups.
“He wants this to be about anything but his own record,” El-Sayed said.
Rogers claimed El-Sayed refused to condemn a terrorist attack in Michigan earlier this year and the 7 October Hamas terrorist attacks in Gaza, although El-Sayed said he had condemned both.
But, El-Sayed added: “I’m not somebody who tries to make political theater out of other people’s pain.”
He also retorted to Rogers: “Did you sell your yachts?” Rogers responded: “I never owned a yacht in Florida, brother.”

October 8, 2026 at 11:47 pm
The season’s winningest driver adds another to his tally with a strong performance in Ohio
Michael “Buddy” Kofoid hit the entire field with a knockout punch Thursday night.
The World of Outlaws NOS Energy Drink Sprint Car Series rolled into Findlay, OH’s Millstream Speedway to kickoff Sheldon Haudenschild ’s NOS Energy Drink Buckeye Brawl Weekend . A stout field of 39 cars checked in, and Kofoid put a beatdown on them all in the Roth Motorsports No. 83.
The Penngrove, CA native rocketed out to the early advantage after starting on the pole for the 30-lapper. David Gravel settled into second and began to regain some ground on Kofoid as lapped traffic became a factor.
But late caution flags continued to clear the path ahead for Kofoid by giving him clean air. Garet Williamson ripped by Gravel late for second, but he also couldn’t pose a threat to Kofoid as the laps faded away. Kofoid took the checkered flag with more than a second advantage to claim round one of the three-round brawl.
“That whole race I could keep the car wherever I wanted it to be,” Kofoid said. “If I needed to pull out of line, I could do something good with it. It’s just a testament to how talented Dylan (Buswell) is as well as Nate (Knotts), and Peyton (Friedrich). They do an extremely good job. I’m very thankful to have them in my corner.”
Kofoid added to his Series-leading win total in 2026 with his 15th of the campaign. That also moved he and the Roth Motorsports crew one checkered flag away from making team history. If they can pick up one more before the season is over, they’ll equal the winningest World of Outlaws campaign in the long history of Dennis and Teresa’s famed team. The 24-year-old took sole possession of 23rd on the all-time win list with his 37th career score.
Garet Williamson finishes runner-up in the Fischer Motorsports No. 23 to get back on the podium for the first time in roughly a month, his 11th top three of the year.
David Gravel posted yet another solid finish with a third-place effort aboard the Big Game Motorsports No. 2. That’s 30 podiums in 2026 for the two-time and defending champion.

articles.title_orig: Ethiopia launches drone attack against Eritrean troops who crossed into Tigray
articles.title_zh: Ethiopia launches drone attack against Eritrean troops who crossed into Tigray
articles.content_orig:
Government forces’ attack raises risk of internal conflict in Ethiopia that could trigger regional war
Eritrean troops who crossed into Ethiopia’s Tigray region have come under drone attack from government forces, raising the risk that renewed internal conflict in Ethiopia could trigger an all-out regional war between the neighbouring countries.
Military vehicles carrying soldiers drove across Eritrea’s southern border into Tigray on Wednesday, reaching the town of Adigrat 25 miles (40km) south, according to civilian witnesses, a militia commander and the conflict monitoring group Acled.
Eritrean troops were then targeted by Ethiopian government drones on Wednesday evening and Thursday morning, Acled said.
Eritrea has a historical enmity with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which launched an offensive against the Ethiopian government on 23 September, but that previous hostility has been superseded by Eritrea’s desire to head off a perceived risk of Ethiopia invading it, in order to access the Red Sea.
In the last two weeks, the TPLF and six other armed groups in Ethiopia have fought the government in Tigray and the neighbouring regions Amhara and Afar. Ethiopia’s military pushed back and an allied militia, the Tigray Peace Force, took over Tigray’s regional capital, Mekelle, on 4 October after the TPLF withdrew from the city.
Eritrea’s information minister, Yemane Ghebremeskel, said in a statement: “We are not in the business of refuting wild allegations or narratives.” He did not explicitly confirm or deny the presence of Eritrean troops in Ethiopia.
Ethiopia’s foreign ministry said in a statement on Monday: “Ethiopia stands ready to defend its sovereignty, territorial integrity, and core national interests, while urging all regional actors to address shared challenges through constructive dialogue, partnership, and adherence to the principles of good neighbourliness rather than confrontation and zero-sum approaches.”
The TPLF and Ethiopia’s government fought a brutal civil war from 2020 to 2022. Between 300,000 and 800,000 civilians died , according to British government estimates. Both sides and their allies were accused of war crimes.
Eritrea intervened on the side of Ethiopia in that conflict, after a rapprochement between the two countries in 2018, which earned Ethiopia’s prime minister, Abiy Ahmed, the 2019 Nobel peace prize .
Eritrea, which gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, has a long enmity with the TPLF, which ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018. The two countries fought a war from 1998 to 2000.
Relations between the countries have deteriorated again in recent years. Abiy has said Ethiopia needs access to the Red Sea, and state media has claimed the country has historical rights to the Eritrean port of Assab. The US-Israeli war on Iran – leading Iran to limit shipping through the strait of Hormuz – has further raised the stakes of Red Sea access.
In its statement on Monday, Ethiopia’s foreign ministry said: “Any serious discussion of regional maritime affairs and security architecture must account for Ethiopia’s legitimate interests and its enduring connection to the Red Sea.”
Yemane said in a post on X on Wednesday that Ethiopia was “incessantly beating the drums of war and openly stating … that it will launch a war of aggression against Eritrea to acquire what it calls ‘sovereign access to the sea’ … In recent weeks, it has tried to repackage this war agenda in terms of ‘self-defence’ by fabricating various allegations against Eritrea.”
Magnus Taylor, Horn of Africa deputy director at the Crisis Group thinktank, said: “The big worry is that [Abiy] might try to solve all his problems at the same time, by invading Eritrea, possibly a regime change move and also a land grab for the Red Sea port, and also solving his problem with Tigray at the same time. It’s a very ambitious military agenda, though.”
While the full impact of the fighting on Tigrayan civilians is not clear, reports have emerged of the TPLF forcibly recruiting boys as young as 15 to fight .
“The civilians in these three regions [Tigray, Amhara and Afar] didn’t get healed from the first round of violence that was halted by the peace agreement [in 2022],” said Acled Ethiopia analyst Jalale Getachew Birru. “They just started healing recently.”
Associated Press contributed to this story

articles.title_orig: Awa seeks one term in Congress: ‘I don’t care’ about world policies
articles.title_zh: Awa seeks one term in Congress: ‘I don’t care’ about world policies
articles.content_orig:
HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - Hawaii News Now interviewed U.S. Rep. Jill Tokuda and state Sen. Brenton Awa, candidates for Hawaii’s 2nd Congressional District, about the Iran war, aid to Israel and immigration enforcement.
Awa said he is seeking only one term in Congress.
“I only want to go for two years, one term, and the reason is, is because I don’t care about all of those world policies and all the votes that’ll have to be taken. I’ll have to care when I am taking it,” Awa said.
Awa said he wants money spent on the Iran war and support for Israel to instead go to American families dealing with disaster.
“But my biggest focus, if we’re going to send billions of dollars to Israel or another country, my only concern is why isn’t that money coming to Hawaii,” Awa said.
Tokuda said ending the war is the best way to reduce energy costs. She opposes aid to Israel because of its treatment of Palestinians.
“It’s a genocide,” Tokuda said.
“When you take a look at the weapons they are using, it was our weapons, which is why I voted against funding weapons sales to Israel for now, because that is blood on our hands,” Tokuda said.
On immigration enforcement, Awa does not oppose mass deportation but said he believes ICE has been too violent.
“The idea is good. The way they go and carry it out, and I don’t know,” Awa said. “I’m not there on the ground, so I don’t know, but other than what I see, through you guys, the media. But when you see people dying, there is no way that that should ever happen.”
Tokuda said there will be pressure to fix immigration laws after the election.
“We absolutely have to pass some kind of meaningful bipartisan immigration reform that protects our borders, that creates legal pathways to citizenship and doesn’t result in Americans getting executed in our streets,” Tokuda said.
Awa acknowledges the odds are stacked against him in a district that has never elected a Republican, and GOP voters have been discouraged by President Trump’s unpopularity.
Awa did not have to give up his Senate seat to run for Congress and has two years remaining on his term.

articles.title_orig: The advice immigration attorneys have for Microsoft workers worried about their green cards
articles.title_zh: The advice immigration attorneys have for Microsoft workers worried about their green cards
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration's Thursday declaration that it was suspending Microsoft and Adobe from a federal visa sponsorship program is reverberating through the tech industry.
Immigration attorneys told Business Insider that employees on H-1B visas working at Microsoft, Adobe, and the other named tech companies should seek counsel and get clarity about their status in light of the suspensions.
Individual cases may vary, and the attorneys spoke in general terms about the advice they would give without knowing a client's specific circumstances or status.
"This is a time where immigrants, high-skilled immigrants, really need to pay attention to laws," said Tahmina Watson, a business immigration attorney at Watson Immigration Law in Seattle. "Things are changing on a dime," she added.
Business Insider spoke to eight immigration attorneys on Thursday in the wake of the announcement, as part of our ongoing series, " H-1B Fallout: 1 Year Later ," which explores how foreign workers are navigating a rapidly changing US immigration landscape.
Some of the immigration attorneys said the suspensions were likely to be challenged in court. Others said they were the latest in a series of US measures targeting foreign workers. One attorney suggested they would only impact a relatively small group of workers.
"Most people will either be able to wait it out or have time to switch jobs," said Loren Locke, an attorney at Locke Immigration Law in Atlanta.
The Permanent Labor Certification, or PERM, program is an initial step that employers generally must complete before sponsoring a worker for an employment-based visa, requiring them to show that no qualified and available US workers could fill the role.
Vice President JD Vance said at a press conference on Thursday that Microsoft had "abused" this system by laying off American workers and using it to hire foreign ones, who he said were paid less. "If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants," Vance said.
Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
A Microsoft spokesperson pointed Business Insider to a blog post the company published Thursday, which said "the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans." The company said it pays its H-1B employees "the same as any other employees doing comparable work."
Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said at the press conference that the government would not accept any new PERM applications or process any pending ones for the named companies, which, in addition to Microsoft and Adobe, also include tech outsourcing firms Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL Technologies, and Capgemini.
In suspending new and pending PERM applications, the Trump administration left a very specific group of H-1B visa holders in limbo, said Matthew Maiona, an immigration attorney at Maiona Ward in Boston.
Maiona said that a hypothetical employee at Microsoft or Adobe, six years into an H-1B visa, could now, in theory, be ordered to appear in immigration court under this new suspension.
"You could be in trouble if you cannot qualify for another non-immigrant visa classification," Maiona said. "You may have to leave the United States."
But Locke said workers would only face potential removal if they exhausted their H-1B eligibility and could not secure an extension or another legal basis — of which there are several — to remain in the country.
Though H-1B visas have a statutory maximum of six years before expiring, they can be extended past that number if workers have made sufficient progress toward obtaining a green card, she said.
"If the goal is to crush H-1B workers, it's not great, but it's not really crushing them either," Locke said.
Todd Pomerleau, an immigration attorney based in Boston, said that with uncertainty around the extent and enforcement of the suspensions, "anybody who's concerned about their immigration status needs to seek competent counsel."
Some immigration attorneys who spoke with Business Insider said they expected the Trump administration's move to be challenged in a lawsuit that would argue the suspensions are outside the Labor Department's legal authority.
"I assume, by next week, we will start seeing lawsuits," said Kripa Upadhyay, the co-chair of Buchalter's Immigration & Global Mobility Practice, a Seattle firm.
Ted Chiappari, the head of immigration law at Duane Morris LLP, said federal statute only allows the Department of Labor to unilaterally suspend an employer from using the PERM program for 180 days.
"That gives the employer notice that there's an investigation going on, and at the end of that investigation, if they find something inappropriate, they have six years to decide whether to debar an employer," he said.
And even then, Chiappari said, they can only debar an employer for up to three years.
Few attorneys interviewed by Business Insider said they were surprised by the measure. Mostly, they saw it as another salvo in what they described as the Trump administration's ongoing crackdown on foreign workers.
Upadhyay said that just the day before, she had spoken with a Microsoft employee on an H-1B whose spouse also was on an H-1B.
The person's H-1B extension was running out, and they now faced the "impossible decision" of moving to their home country, leaving behind their spouse and two US citizen children.
"I have children to support," Upadhyay recalled the worker saying. "What happens now?"
Upadhyay expects to get more of these calls.

articles.title_orig: Princeton Celebrates Anne Carson, a Nobel Prize Winner Who Was Denied Tenure
articles.title_zh: Princeton Celebrates Anne Carson, a Nobel Prize Winner Who Was Denied Tenure
articles.content_orig:
Anne Carson, the Canadian writer and classicist whose work blends verse, prose and essay with influences from classical myths, has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in literature for her “bold and inventive oeuvre.”
Carson, 76, is an accomplished classicist who has taught at multiple colleges in the US and Canada while also producing works like “The Beauty of the Husband,” “An Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse,” and “Nox.” Her distinctive essays, prose and poetry, in which the ancient and modern live side-by-side, have garnered her critical acclaim.
Carson’s “playful dialogue with the classical tradition has created new forms for contemporary literature,” the Nobel committee said in a statement.
The prize, announced at the Swedish Academy in Stockholm on Thursday, carries a cash award of 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.2 million).
Carson is widely known for hybrid style where she balances multiple ideas, genres and forms. “Almost all her literary production has centered upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” said Anders Olsson, chairman of the Nobel Committee for Literature.
For example, in “Autobiography of Red,” the work that made her name, her long narrative verse is framed by an erudite, enigmatic discussion of Stesichorus, the Greek poet who inspired her. In Stesichorus’ original myth, Heracles – better known by his Latin name of Hercules – kills the winged monster Geryon and steals his red cattle as one of his 12 labors. In Carson’s 1998 retelling, she recasts Geryon as a “tender ‘hero’ devoted to his mother,” who “having earlier been subjected to sexual assaults at the hands of his brother, falls in love with the smug and boorish Heracles,” the Nobel committee said.
Such a complicated form belies the simplicity of much of the language in it. “Somehow Geryon made it to adolescence.// Then he met Herakles and the kingdoms of his life all shifted down a few notches,” Carson writes. “They were two superior eels//at the bottom of the tank and they recognized each other like italics.”
Carson was in Iceland, “listening to the wind,” when she discovered she had won the Nobel Prize, according to Ingrid Carlberg, the permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy.
“She was taken by surprise but very happy – I could hear that in her voice,” Carlberg said.
Much of Carson’s early career was dominated by her work in classics – she studied for her bachelor’s, master’s and doctorate degrees at the University of Toronto and also received a diploma in classics from the University of St. Andrews in Scotland. Although she published an essay and her Ph.D. thesis in her thirties, it wasn’t until she was 42 years old that her first book of poems “Short Talks” was published. Three more works followed before “Autobiography of Red” marked her out as a critical favorite.
“The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos,” which charts the breakdown of a marriage between two unnamed characters, came three years later. For that work, Carson became the first female winner of the prestigious T.S. Eliot Prize in 2001. She is the 19th woman of the 122 individuals who have won the Nobel Prize for literature.
Nobel Prize in medicine awarded to trio for technique that helps decode mysteries of the brain
Carson is notoriously private about her personal life, but her 2010 work “Nox” reflects on the life and death of her estranged brother, Michael. It is not a traditional book, as such, but a “box containing an accordion-fold-out of picture, letters and other written texts dedicated to her dead brother,” Olsson said.
Carson has also produced several translations of classical texts and ventured into other artforms, collaborating with visual artists, choreographers, opera and theater directors. The transition into various other artistic fields “demonstrates the freedom with which she relates to literary expectations and rule systems, which in turn lies behind the outstanding importance her work since the 1990s has had for the international art and literature scene,” Olsson added.
Last year, the prize went to László Krasznahorkai “for his compelling and visionary oeuvre that, in the midst of apocalyptic terror, reaffirms the power of art,” the committee said.
In 2024, South Korean author Han Kang was honored by the committee for her “intense poetic prose that confronts historical traumas and exposes the fragility of human life.”
Literature is the fourth prize to be handed out this week, after achievements in medicine, physics and chemistry. The Nobel Peace Prize is set to be revealed on Friday, followed by the winners in economics on October 12.
This story and its headline has been updated with additional reporting.

articles.title_orig: Michigan Senate debate goes off the rails: 4 takeaways
articles.title_zh: Michigan Senate debate goes off the rails: 4 takeaways
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navi Pillay for her efforts to promote international law
GRAND RAPIDS, Mich. — The two candidates battling for Michigan’s open Senate seat tangled here Thursday over the war in Iran, gas prices and tariffs in a debate that often veered into mean-spirited sniping.
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed sought to portray his Republican rival, former Rep. Mike Rogers, as a weak-willed loyalist to President Donald Trump who has recently changed his positions on certain issues out of political necessity.
Rogers tried to frame El-Sayed as a “con man” who is making promises he cannot pay for without raising taxes or other costs.
Each repeatedly taunted the other over real estate — a home Rogers has in Florida and property El-Sayed’s wife owns in the United Arab Emirates. The debate, hosted by NBC affiliate WOOD of Grand Rapids, became so punchy at times that moderator Rick Albin pleaded for the candidates to rein in their attacks.
“I’d like to be a part of the debate, too,” Albin interjected at one point.
Michigan’s Senate race is one of the most competitive and closely watched in the country, and the results could help determine partisan control of the chamber. Sen. Gary Peters, a Democrat, is not seeking re-election.
Backed by progressive luminaries such as Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., El-Sayed emerged from a nasty primary against Rep. Haley Stevens, who positioned herself as a more moderate Democrat. Since then, Republicans eager to win a Senate seat in the state for the first time since 1994 have tried to paint El-Sayed as an extremist.
The debate opened with Albin asking both candidates whether, at a time of high gas prices related to the war with Iran, they would support a pause on the federal gas tax. Both said they would support a pause, but the question led into a deeper discussion about the conflict. Rogers, who initially supported the war, recently said he wants it to end swiftly .
“I would support pausing the federal gas tax, but there is one thing that is actually causing this: It’s the war in Iran, a war that has been cheer-led by my opponent since the beginning,” El-Sayed said. “Called it a ‘win, win, win.’ I don’t know about you, but when I go to the gas tank, I don’t feel like I’m winning. I don’t feel like our country is winning.”
Rogers responded by pivoting to El-Sayed’s support for “Medicare for All,” a proposal that Sanders and others on the left have been championing for years. Such a policy, Rogers asserted, would force people off private insurance they might prefer while causing taxes and gas prices to rise.
“It is a disaster,” Rogers said. “We cannot afford Abdul.”
At another point, Rogers said: “Listen to this guy and what he’s trying to sell here today. You’re going to find out that this guy is not what he says he is. He is actually selling the best con I think I’ve ever seen.”
Albin then turned the discussion toward tariffs — another area in which Rogers has recently tried to distance himself from Trump.
New tariffs implemented by Trump took effect last month, placing duties of 15% to 50% on $20 billion worth of U.S. products exported to Canada. The tariffs are a major issue in Michigan, which borders and trades with Canada. Rogers, who once supported Trump’s push, released an ad this week calling for an end to the trade war .
“I have actually called the White House this week, talked to the secretary of commerce about getting the deal done,” Rogers said during the debate. “Canada still has some high tariffs for U.S. goods, and they did it before they started. Those should be eliminated. There are tariffs that I think are too high and not helpful for us. We ought to get rid of those. So this is about getting the best deal possible. I’d like to see it end.”
El-Sayed countered by noting Rogers’ initial support and a study that estimated how costly the tariffs have been for Michigan households.
“Look, you’re hearing somebody who has cheer-led, again, a Canadian tariff policy that we are paying $5,600 a year for,” El-Sayed said. “The reason he’s flip-flopping has nothing to do with policy, has nothing to do with your costs. Has everything to do with his sagging poll numbers.”
El-Sayed added, a moment later: “Weak, cowardly, won’t stand up until his poll numbers drop.”
The debate presented other contrasts between the candidates, including differences over U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which El-Sayed has called for abolishing. When Albin asked whether he believed the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement strategy had ever gone too far, Rogers said this year’s very public operation in Minneapolis, which resulted in federal agents’ shooting and killing two U.S. citizens, was “probably not appropriate.”
“I actually did fugitive raids when I was an FBI agent in Chicago,” he said. “You always want to go in quiet, get the bad guy, get out of the neighborhood for less problems. So that to me was something that they could have done differently.”
El-Sayed was pressed about his criticism of Israel and his recent refusal, in a NewsNation interview, to say whether he sees Israel or Iran as a bigger threat to the U.S. Despite Albin’s prodding, El-Sayed again declined to offer a direct answer.
“I’m just going to say that that’s a ridiculous hypothetical, because here’s what’s happening right now: Our ostensible ally in Israel has lobbied us to go to war with Iran,” he replied.
“We have watched as Iran has responded by bombing all kinds of countries in the Middle East and then choking off the world’s energy supply. So this is a situation in which I don’t think we should be a part. I don’t want to be pushed into war by Israel,” he added. “I want our money spent here to buy schools and healthcare and childcare here. I don’t understand why that is so inconceivable.”
The debate was the first of two planned between El-Sayed and Rogers, but the candidates have been circling each other for months. Both have leaned into schoolyard taunts , with Rogers mocking El-Sayed’s height and El-Sayed challenging Rogers to a “no pads” football game.
Nationally, Republicans have tried to make El-Sayed, with his progressive views and alliances, the new face of the Democratic Party. In their efforts to villainize El-Sayed, they have also emphasized his ethnicity and Muslim faith .
Vice President JD Vance, for example, has urged Republicans who are “running against a Democrat who’s not that crazy” to instead mention El-Sayed . And Trump referred to El-Sayed on Truth Social on Wednesday night as “Mohammed” and described him as someone who “goes back to the days of the Jihad.”
Earlier Thursday, at a lunch event with Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer at a Grand Rapids restaurant, El-Sayed mocked Trump’s antics, including how Trump pronounces his real name.
“Get it right,” El-Sayed said, “because we’re going to teach you how to say it properly with the word ‘senator’ in front of it.”
He added, referring to Trump and Vance: “They keep pointing to my name and my faith because they think that they can distract us from the issues that affect all of us — because my name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford a tank of gas.”
Henry J. Gomez is a senior national political reporter for NBC News
