articles.title_orig: ‘You’ve Hired Half the Third Reich’: 6 Key Moments From the Georgia Senate Debate
articles.title_zh: ‘You’ve Hired Half the Third Reich’: 6 Key Moments From the Georgia Senate Debate
articles.content_orig:
Candidates traded personal attacks and clashed over a range of issues in closely watched US Senate debates on Thursday, with control of Congress at stake
With just weeks left in the contentious midterm election campaign, candidates in a trio of highly-competitive Senate races debated Thursday night, clashing over the economy, tariffs, the Iran war and abortion rights, with control of the upper chamber at stake.
In Georgia, incumbent Democratic senator Jon Ossoff faced GOP representative Mike Collins. In Michigan, Democrat Abdul Al-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers debated over the state’s open Senate seat. And in Maine, longtime senator Susan Collins met Democratic challenger Troy Jackson. Democrats need to flip four Republican-held Senate seats to win the majority.
Here are the key takeaways from the battleground state debates.
Affordability was a major topic across all three debates on Thursday night, as voters consistently name the cost of goods, gas, housing and healthcare as their top concerns in this year’s midterms.
“Can you afford your gas? Can you afford your groceries under this guy who’s going to rubber stamp everything Donald Trump tells him to rubber stamp?” El-Sayed asked during the Michigan debate, the first of two in one of this cycle’s most fiercely contested races.
Both Rogers and El-Sayed said they support suspending a fuel tax to alleviate costs, while El-Sayed argued that the Iran war, which was driving up gas prices, needs to end. El-Sayed attacked Rogers for growing his personal wealth while in office as a US representative.
Rogers called El-Sayed “bought off” by billionaire George Soros, Hamas and Hezbollah. “We cannot afford Abdul, and we cannot risk his ideology,” Rogers said.
In Georgia, Ossoff repeatedly asked Collins to justify his support for Trump’s global tariff policies, which the senator said have “crushed Georgia families” and “strangled” economic growth.
“Let’s see if he has the courage to explain his votes,” Ossoff said, adding later: “Still have not heard an explanation for the tariffs.”
Collins, who is trying to cut into Ossoff’s lead, blamed inflation on Biden administration policies, singling out spending measures that his opponent had supported.
Later in Maine, where polls show a tight race, Jackson focused his remarks on pocketbook issues, including the sharp spike in heating oil costs and high energy prices.
Collins defended her record and argued that Maine had benefited from the $50bn rural health transformation fund that was appended to Trump’s signature tax cut and spending bill, the so-called Big Beautiful bill.
In the Georgia debate, a question about data centers erupted into a pointed, personal exchange between Ossoff and Collins.
“Mike Collins voted to take that money out of your pocket and out of your community and give it instead to data center developers,” Ossoff said.
He then accused Collins of being a “bigot” who has “hired half the Third Reich” – a reference to the congressman’s history of employing staffers who have expressed white nationalist, antisemitic, and extremist views online.
“If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery,” Ossoff said of the late civil rights icon and long-serving Georgia congressman, “Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club. His office has been in cahoots with some of the most notorious white supremacists on the country.”
Collins was asked directly about his son-in-law’s social media posts promoting white nationalist and antisemitic views.
“You know, Rick, that’s my family,” Collins replied. “That’s the craziness that Jon Ossoff has been spewing out there.” Collins noted that a New York man had recently been charged after threatening to kill him, and added: “I’ve condemned racism, antisemitism, hate; I don’t care where the source is. And I tell him that too, it’s wrong. We have no place in this world for that.”
Collins, meanwhile, sought to cast Ossoff as “radical” and an “extremist” whose record in the Senate had left the state “less safe, more expensive and worse off”.
Tariffs were also a topic of heated debate in Michigan, which shares hundreds of miles of border with Canada.
This week, Rogers publicly backtracked on previous support for Trump’s tariffs on the US’s northern neighbor , saying in a campaign ad that “Canada is not our enemy” and that the “tariff war” needed to end now.
During Thursday night’s debate, Rogers said he had spoken to the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, this week to advocate for a deal between the two countries. There are tariffs in place that are “too high and not helpful for us”, Rogers said.
El-Sayed said he supports targeted, logical tariffs that protect Michigan manufacturing, but nothing like the “ham-fisted, chaotic, self-serving” tariffs Trump put in place. He called out Rogers for “flip-flopping” on the issue, saying he was only reversing his stance because of “sagging poll numbers”.
“He’s doing an ad drinking a Labatt and talking about the Red Wings, pretending like he was not for this the entire time,” El-Sayed said. “Be serious, my guy.”
In Maine, discussions about gas prices and the war in Iran raised notable tension in the second debate between Jackson and Collins, who is seeking a sixth term in her seat. “She’s the Chairman of Appropriations,” Jackson said. “Money has to come through them for these wars – she still can do something.”
Collins, who plans to continue leading the Appropriations committee if re-elected, said she had repeatedly supported war powers resolutions to halt Trump’s military action in Iran.
But Jackson pushed further, accusing the senator and her husband of profiting from the war.
She could use her leverage to stop this war, but instead they’re making money,” he said, prompting a furious response from Collins, who called the allegation “absolutely outrageous”.
“You owe me an apology,” she said.
In Maine, both candidates were also pressed to address inconsistencies in their positions on reproductive rights, a crucial issue for voters in the state.
“Our records have changed,” Jackson said. “Mine has gotten better – hers has gotten worse.”
He pointed to Collins’ vote to confirm supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh, who helped overturn Roe v Wade in 2022 . Collins, one of just two Republican senators who supports abortion rights, has said she does not regret her vote for Kavanaugh, even though she believed he had given her private assurances before his 2018 confirmation that he would not overturn the landmark ruling. Collins sought to turn the issue back on her opponent, noting his past stances on abortion that have left many voters wary. “From 2000 until he ran for the house seat in 2013 was very anti-choice,” she said, accusing Jackson of having held “extremist” views on abortion. “He was for a bill that would not allow abortion when the mother’s life was at risk.” She also pointed to legislation she helped write that sought to “codify Roe v Wade nationwide,” but the bill never made it passed the Senate.
In Michigan, Rogers repeatedly attacked El-Sayed by attempting to tie him to Muslim terrorist groups, including Hamas, and suggested government surveillance would only bother someone if he or his family had something to hide.
Rogers brought up El-Sayed’s mom and sister, prompting El-Sayed to say at one point that Rogers should just come out and say what he’s been dancing around all night, after Rogers’ repeated references to terrorist groups.
“He wants this to be about anything but his own record,” El-Sayed said.
Rogers claimed El-Sayed refused to condemn a terrorist attack in Michigan earlier this year and the 7 October Hamas terrorist attacks in Gaza, although El-Sayed said he had condemned both.
But, El-Sayed added: “I’m not somebody who tries to make political theater out of other people’s pain.”
He also retorted to Rogers: “Did you sell your yachts?” Rogers responded: “I never owned a yacht in Florida, brother.”

articles.title_orig: World Octopus Day: new discoveries about the world’s smartest invertebrates
articles.title_zh: World Octopus Day: new discoveries about the world’s smartest invertebrates
articles.content_orig:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.
Happy World Octopus Day!  Every Oct 8, the world celebrates one of the more unusual creatures of the sea. Octopuses are well-known for their eight legs and ability to squirt ink when frightened. They’ve also been known to use tools, a sign of intelligence, and can shape-shift to mimic the colors and texture of their surroundings, an effective way to disappear from both predators and prey.
Mongabay has reported on several octopus discoveries this year, including:
Ancient octopus were apex predators
Modern colossal squid are believed to be the largest invertebrates in the sea, but Mongabay’s Shanna Hanbury recently reported on an even larger ancient octopus species whose fossils were described by Japanese researchers in April 2026.
The Japanese team found a fossilized jawbone from the now-extinct Nanaimoteuthis haggarti. Based on its jaw size, researchers suggest the octopus may have reached 6.6 to 18.6 meters (22 to 61 feet) in length. On the higher end, that’s around two-thirds the size of an adult blue whale, the largest animal to ever exist.
“It suggests that it may have been among the largest invertebrates ever known,” study co-author Yasuhiro Iba, a paleontologist at Hokkaido University in Japan, told Mongabay by email.
They were likely gigantic predators that roamed the late Cretaceous seas between 100 million to 72 million years ago.
A rare look at baby octopuses
From long dead octopus to newly born, Hanbury also reported on baby Argentine octopuses and a rare photo of them.
Patagonian octopus eggs in Puerto Lobos Protected Natural Area in Argentina. Image courtesy of Martin Brogger.
These eggs belong to a small Patagonian octopus ( Octopus tehuelchus ). It’s one of the more common octopus species in the region, but researchers still haven’t been able to determine its global conservation status, although reported catches in Patagonia have declined over the past 50 years.
The black dots inside each egg are the developing eyes of the embryos, indicating that they’re progressing toward hatching. The female octopus of this species often lays her eggs in the shell of an oyster , then guards them fiercely. She even stops eating during this period.
New octopus species are described often , including a blue octopus about the size of a golf ball recently discovered in the Galapagos.
On a deep-sea expedition in 2015, scientists used a remotely operated vehicle to find a golf-ball sized, short-armed blue octopus. In a recent study , they confirmed that it’s new to science, reported Mongabay’s David Brown.
However, questions remain about how the new species, Microeledone galapagensis , makes use of its stubby arms.
“If you gather prey by moving your arms through the sediment (as we think they do), wouldn’t it be better to have longer arms with more suckers than short little arms?” queried lead author Janet Voight.
Banner image: Big blue octopus ( Octopus cyanea ) with a diver in background. Image courtesy of David Fleetham/WWF via naturepl.com.
What does it take to turn one of the world’s richest iron deposits into a global export hub? Eastern Guinea has become a focal point in the global race for high-grade iron ore. articles.title_orig: Christa Pike is walking with help and eating after failed execution attempt, her attorneys say
articles.title_zh: Christa Pike is walking with help and eating after failed execution attempt, her attorneys say
articles.content_orig:
Two scheduled executions a week apart have highlighted the ongoing debate over the practice of lethal injection in the US, with both using the same drug but yielding dramatically different outcomes.
Texas on Wednesday executed 46-year-old Jamaal Howard, a man who fatally shot a convenience store clerk more than two decades ago.
Howard was pronounced dead at 8:03 p.m., the Associated Press reported, after receiving a lethal dose of pentobarbital, a barbiturate that can cause death, at a state prison in Huntsville.
He was the 30th person to be executed in the US this year, but the first since the botched execution attempt of Christa Pike in Tennessee, where officials administered the same drug – but she survived.
As Pike remains hospitalized and a legal battle plays out over her future, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has ordered a third-party investigation into what went wrong and halted executions in the state for the rest of the year. Pike was the second failed execution attempt the state has seen this year.
After the pentobarbital was administered Wednesday night, Howard took a couple of breaths and gasped, the AP reported, before making snoring sounds that grew quiet within 30 seconds. He was pronounced dead 19 minutes later.
After Pike was injected with the drug on September 30, she also began snoring and moaning, according to media witnesses. But she kept breathing.
An unconscious Pike was later taken to a Nashville hospital and placed on a ventilator. Her attorneys announced Tuesday she was awake and speaking in what they called a “medically unprecedented” recovery.
According to documents compiled by the Death Penalty Information Center, both Tennessee and Texas have execution protocols that require syringes to be prepared with a 100 ml solution that contains 5 grams of pentobarbital.
Pike was administered two doses of the solution, witnesses said.
It’s unknown exactly how many doses Howard received. CNN has reached out to the Texas Department of Criminal Justice for more information on his execution.
Pike, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, was to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in 200 years.
Pike’s attorneys said her executioners struggled to place IV lines to administer the lethal injection, and they previously warned the state of difficulties finding her vein access. Randy Spivey, one of Pike’s lawyers, said she talked with the execution team about where they should try to insert the IV lines.
These cases pose hard questions about the US capital punishment system
An emergency motion ordering the state to preserve evidence said those administering the lethal injection attempted to gain IV access to Pike using “at least seven needles,” with one needle “bent in a 90-degree angle when it was removed.” A judge granted the motion Wednesday.
When she arrived at the hospital, Pike’s arms were “swollen, burned and blistered,” her attorneys said. Pentobarbital “burns upon contact, including skin, tissue, and veins,” they said. The attorneys believe issues with the IV meant the drug flowed into her body instead of her bloodstream.
The Tennessee Department of Correction said it followed its lethal execution protocol, which approves a one-drug method of pentobarbital and allows a backup injection if the inmate is still alive.
There is no protocol for what happens if the second injection does not work.
Pike is “ angry and confused about everything right now,” but is “very aware that the state tried to execute her,” Spivey told reporters on the sidelines of Wednesday’s hearing on the botched execution, adding that Pike has a “long road to recovery.”
Pike has pneumonia and a blood clot in one of her arms and was not able to swallow and therefore not eating, Spivey said Wednesday.
She is walking with assistance, is now eating a regular diet and has regained some movement in her arms, her attorneys said in a Thursday statement, noting the “remarkable” nature of her physical recovery after previously receiving lifesaving care.
Pike continues to have trouble with concentration and memory as questions remain surrounding the long-term effects of the failed execution, they added.
Christa Pike’s attorneys believed she was brain-dead before she woke up ‘to the shock of everyone’
Before Howard’s planned execution, his attorneys filed motions Wednesday before the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals to block it, arguing he was intellectually disabled and faced risks similar to Pike’s case because the same drug was being used with questions raised over its quality.
The court denied his motions without comment.
Hours earlier, Pike’s attorneys were also in court as a judge ruled the state of Tennessee must preserve all evidence related to her failed execution, including 911 calls, communications between state officials, and physical evidence.
The state said it collected things like logbooks, medical waste, and electrocardiogram readouts from the execution chamber. But other evidence, such as cut IV lines transported to the hospital with Pike, may not be in the Tennessee Department of Correction’s custody.
The state’s Correction Commissioner Frank Strada is stepping down later this month amid the backlash, which has brought scrutiny to the state’s method of lethal injection and propelled the death penalty to become a main point of debate in Tennessee’s gubernatorial race.
US Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who is the Republican nominee for governor, called to bring back the electric chair and “deliver justice for these victims swiftly.”
Meanwhile, Blackburn’s Democratic opponent Jerri Green vowed to “enact a moratorium on all future executions” in the state.
“What happened on that gurney wasn’t just an administrative failure; it was torture, plain and simple,” Green said in a statement.
“The facts are clear: the death penalty has proven to be an ineffective deterrent to violent crime, it is vastly more expensive than life imprisonment, and it is riddled with bias,” her statement continues.
CNN’s Ryan Young, Isa Mudannayake and Devon Sayers contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: How quickly is China learning from the Ukraine war’s latest drone tactics?
articles.title_zh: How quickly is China learning from the Ukraine war’s latest drone tactics?
articles.content_orig:
Beijing’s effort is the most systematic of any outside power, but it faces limits learning from a war it is not fighting
But it usually took a year or more before those lessons showed up publicly in People’s Liberation Army (PLA) training, equipment or force structure, Lilly Min-Chen Lee and Kateryna Bondar wrote in a commentary published on October 7 by the Washington-based Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).
The lessons drawn by China go beyond immediate tactics. Chinese analysts have also looked at the economics of mass-produced drones, ways to shorten the kill chain, fibre-optic first-person-view (FPV) drones that are harder to jam, and multiple layers of defence against sea and aerial drones.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft Suspended From Green Card Program as Trump Officials Widen Fraud Drive
articles.title_zh: Microsoft Suspended From Green Card Program as Trump Officials Widen Fraud Drive
articles.content_orig:
Vance singled out Microsoft, accusing the company of fraud.
Vice President JD Vance on Thursday announced the suspension of tech giants, Microsoft and Adobe, from a green card program -- effectively blocking the companies from sponsoring H-1B visa workers for permanent residency green cards.
The suspension is from the PERM program -- a certification that allows employers to hire a foreign employee to work permanently in the U.S.
Vance singled out Microsoft, accusing the company of fraud.
"So if the H-1B visa is how the people get into the country, the PERM program is how they stay in the United States to begin with," Vance said. "Now there has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft."
In a statement to ABC News, Microsoft said it "succeeds as a global technology leader by developing the world’s best technology workforce. We do this by strengthening this country’s talent pipeline, hiring American workers, and attracting the best talent from around the world."
Critics of the PERM program have said it allows companies to recruit foreign workers, taking away jobs from Americans. Vance alleged Microsoft employees were laid off -- later replaced by "foreign indentured servants" who "are earning wages that are far below the average for American citizens."
"So, in the last year, Microsoft -- and I want to be clear about the data here, so let me check this -- but Microsoft laid off last year 6,000 American workers," Vance said. "At the same time, the company benefited from 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards."
"In other words, if you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants."
Microsoft said in a statement that "the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans."
It also pushed back on Vance's comments, saying it "only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category."
"We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings. We pay our H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work," the statement continued.
The criticism of Microsoft came hours before President Donald Trump awarded Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella the Medal of Technology and Innovation during an event at the Institute of Peace on Thursday.
Trump lauded Nadella at the ceremony, saying he has been "a key figure in the transformation of Microsoft, revolutionizing the company and empowering businesses, students and consumers from all over the world with some of the most capable software ever built or ever even conceived."
Vance acknowledged the contradiction of honoring Microsoft's CEO the same day as his announcement.
"Microsoft is a great American company, and we have a great relationship with them. They do a lot of important things," Vance said. "So we're going to continue to support Microsoft and have a great relationship with Microsoft, but we're also going to deny them the ability to apply for these permanent residencies until they show that they are going to get serious about putting American workers first."
ABC News has reached out to Adobe for comment.
Asked how long the suspension will be in place, Vance said it will "last as long as it needs to" and added that the administration has "a number of tools to suspend it indefinitely" if needed.
Vance, who has been asked to lead the administration’s Anti-Fraud Task Force, also criticized the H-1B visa program as a whole, saying it has become "rife with fraud" in recent years.
"The H-1B visa program is meant to allow companies to bring in really the best of the best from outside the United States of America for positions that are completely impossible to fill with American workers. Unfortunately, the program has become rife with fraud over the last several years, probably the last several decades," Vance said.
Attorney General Todd Blanche also chimed in about the issue of "foreign labor favoritism," promising that companies will be investigated if they "discriminate against an American worker in favor of someone on the other side of the world," with Blanche saying this "violate[s] the trust of the federal government and the American people."
"The Department of Justice, my department, is actively investigating companies that do this that favor foreign workers over the American people,” Blanche said.
Inspector General of Labor Anthony D'Esposito also announced that the Department of Labor is conducting a "historic investigation into the J-1 visa fraud involving nine major American universities: Pitt, Yale, Harvard, Stanford, Brown, UC Davis, CaltTech, Arizona State, and MIT," with investigations already underway, he said.
"If an American university is breaking the law to save a dollar, while exposing American research to a foreign adversary, that is not academic excellence. It's institutional betrayal," D'Esposito said.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia-Backed Firmus IPO Collapses as AI Valuation Concerns Grow
articles.title_zh: Nvidia-Backed Firmus IPO Collapses as AI Valuation Concerns Grow
articles.content_orig:
Australian AI data center operator Firmus, which is backed by Nvidia , has withdrawn its planned mega initial public offering, citing market volatility and conditions, the company said in an emailed statement to CNBC.
Firmus said its board determined that the terms of the proposed offering did not adequately reflect the strength of its business and long-term growth outlook.
"The board therefore concluded that proceeding with the offer was not in the best interests of the company and its shareholders," Firmus said in a statement. "Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options," it added.
Firmus had reportedly planned to raise $5 billion in its IPO, pricing shares at A$11 apiece, which woul have made it the second-largest new share sale in Australia's history. The IPO valued the company at around $30.6 billion.
In August, the company announced a $2 billion funding round backed by Nvidia, Coatue Management, Blackstone and Jane Street, bringing its total equity raised over the preceding year to more than $3 billion and its valuation to over $10.5 billion.
Firmus also announced agreements with Meta last month to provide GPU computing capacity at its AI data centers in Southeast Asia, built on Nvidia's DSX platform, to support Meta's AI research, model development and training.

articles.title_zh: Open Door Mission hosts 24-hour 'Conversations on a Bench' for World Homeless Day
articles.content_orig:
Rochester, N.Y. — This Saturday will mark World Homeless Day, and the Open Door Mission is raising awareness.
Thursday, it's participating in "Conversations on a Bench", a 24-hour livestream event.
Ministry CEO’s will spend 24 hours sitting on a bench engaging in conversations with anyone who stops by.
The idea is to re-humanize homelessness and amplify stories of hope and transformation.
"There are many, many reasons why homelessness comes about," said Open Door Mission CEO Robert Williams. "Here in Rochester, two of the primary drivers are addiction and mental illness."
He added, "I am celebrating 19 years of recovery. I went through a 25-year addiction. So I walked that path, and I sit here now as the CEO of the open door mission because there was something that was called hope."
The conversations continue at the corner of Plymouth Avenue and Main Street through 3 p.m. Friday.

articles.title_orig: The long-deployed USS Lincoln returns home to San Diego Bay
articles.title_zh: The long-deployed USS Lincoln returns home to San Diego Bay
articles.content_orig:
Sailors wave aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier as it returns to Naval Air Station North Island after deployment Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in Coronado, Calif. Gregory Bull/AP hide caption
CORONADO, Calif. — After more than 10 months at sea, thousands of sailors Thursday poured out of the the USS Lincoln on San Diego Bay to thunderous cheers, streaming tears and emotional hugs, marking a homecoming that included new dads who met babies born while they were away on a historic deployment supporting the Iran war.
The reunion followed an emotional rollercoaster for families who described crying and losing sleep after hearing reports of supply shortages and deteriorating mental health among the crew during the deployment that spent a record 265 days of uninterrupted time at sea. Many said they only could communicate with family via the occasional email or rare WhatsApp calls.
Abel Ramirez, 20, was glad to have that all behind him. He walked off the carrier with a big grin, overjoyed that his first deployment was over.
"It feels amazing," he said while headed out to search for his parents who traveled from Texas. "There was a certain point when I never thought I would come off."
Cassity Garduque, 14, waved as her mom in her sailor uniform frantically waved back from the top deck after the ship docked at the pier.
"It feels really overwhelming," she said about being seeing her mom again. "She missed most of my seventh grade and my birthday."
She added that she's happy her mom won't be eating ramen almost every day and can celebrate with her now.
Family and friends cheer as the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier returns to Naval Air Station North Island after deployment Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in Coronado, Calif. Gregory Bull/AP hide caption
Capt. Daniel Keeler, the ship's commander, said most of the crew was on their first deployment and that the issues they faced were normal for such a long deployment, adding everyone had access to four meals a day.
"It's a floating city as you can see and at any moment there might be a clogged toilet," he said.
The Navy initially downplayed any problems during the deployment, and President Donald Trump commented in August that the Lincoln's lengthy deployment was "not nearly long enough."
Navy leaders eventually acknowledged there were some issues aboard.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth flew out to the Lincoln on Wednesday to give the crew the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a unit can receive.
Hegseth told the crew that "what makes the U.S. military and the U.S. Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you're resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless."
Hegseth pushed back against what he said were efforts to turn the "Lincoln into some sort of a symbol, a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission."
The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier returns to the San Diego Bay after deployment Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in San Diego. Jae C. Hong/AP hide caption
The Lincoln, which set a record for uninterrupted time at sea, is the second carrier to endure an unusually long deployment during the Iran war and to receive the Presidential Unit Citation afterward, typically reserved for significant achievement in combat.
The crew of the USS Gerald R. Ford returned in May from a 326-day deployment — the longest for an aircraft carrier in the past 50 years and a record in the post-Vietnam War era. The Lincoln's deployment of 322 days was just shy of that.
Among the first to depart the carrier at the naval base in Coronado were 64 fathers meeting their babies for the first time, the Navy said. With the airwing included, there were 122 new dads, Keeler said.
Waiting for the Lincoln to bring her husband home, sailor Kathy Monterrosa held her 6-month-old daughter, Sarahi, outfitted in a tiny blue and white sailor dress.
"She's our deployment baby," said Monterrosa, of Virginia Beach, Virginia.
It was tough to hear about the ship's conditions while she was pregnant, she said. "I was crying a lot and worried. I wasn't sure if he was OK or not," she said.
When she finally heard from her husband, he told her it was "pretty bad," but now she said she feels blessed to have her family home.
Sailor Steven Rivas beamed as he held is 7-month-old daughter.
"I couldn't grasp the reality of it," he said about coming home. He became overwhelmed as they pulled into the bay, "seeing everyone and knowing my family was waiting for me," Rivas said, his voice shaking as his eyes teared up.
The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier returns to the San Diego Bay after deployment Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in San Diego. Karl Anderson/AP hide caption
Alma Solano Velez said her husband gave his family an extensive list of the foods he has been craving over the past 10 months: oxtail, barbecue chicken, broccoli and shrimp empanadas to name a few.
He had told his wife about "the lack of food and showers" on board and was looking forward to seeing their daughter, who turned 4 while he was away, she said.
The carrier left San Diego in November and arrived in the Middle East in January. U.S. and Israeli forces launched airstrikes against Iran on Feb. 28.
In August, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the Lincoln maintained adequate food supplies, but because combat operations limited resupply opportunities, meal options were reduced for a short time.
After more than 10 months at sea, the Lincoln's crew got a stop in Thailand early last month on the way back from the Middle East.
Extended naval deployments can wear on service members who are away from home for long periods and increase strain on the ship and its equipment.
The Navy told lawmakers that eight sailors attempted suicide during the record-setting deployment, though experts say that number is low in a strike group of 6,000 sailors over 10 months.
According to the citation that Hegseth read to the crew, the Lincoln and its strike group executed nearly 3,700 combat missions, launched 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles, shot down 77 one-way attack drones, sank 64 Iranian warships, and destroyed 21 anti-ship cruise missiles.
Another carrier, the usually Asia-based USS George Washington, relieved the Lincoln in the Middle East in August.

articles.title_orig: World’s largest wildlife crossing is on track to open this winter — unless El Niño intervenes
articles.title_zh: World’s largest wildlife crossing is on track to open this winter — unless El Niño intervenes
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
The world’s largest wildlife crossing over the 101 Freeway in Agoura Hills is barreling toward a Dec. 2 completion date . Perhaps the only thing that could stop it is a fierce winter storm.
Already, a concrete bridge stretches across 10 lanes of whizzing traffic. Atop that, there’s a lush landscape sewn with 6,000 native plants. Recently, crews completed another overpass over adjacent Agoura Road. A big remaining to-do is to fill in the gap between the freeway and the road — and the freeway to the land to the north — with millions of cubic feet of soil to create a seamless pathway for animals.
The idea behind the Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing is to provide a lifeline for mountain lions in the Santa Monica Mountains, locked in by traffic and suffering from the effects of inbreeding.
“We’re just hoping El Niño ‘s on our side,” said Beth Pratt, president of the Wildlife Crossing Fund and public face of the project. “I keep saying, ‘Mother Nature, we’re trying to help you. Let’s not throw any more complications our way.’” A super-sized version of the climate pattern is looming, and there’s a good chance Southern California could be doused.
Some rain is not a big deal but flooding would shut down work for safety reasons. At a final construction update held near the crossing Thursday, Robert Rock, lead landscape architect and principal designer for the crossing, explained that the soil in the area is rich in clay and silt. When wet, it gets dangerously slick and slippery.
Heavy precipitation can also derail the soil compaction process, where crews lay down the soil in layers and go over each with a construction vehicle known as a roller. In the distance, workers were busy doing just that as the fierce late morning sun beat down.
“If you’re trying to compact a mud puddle, it wouldn’t really compact, right?” he said at a trailhead off of Agoura Road. “Because if you push that down, the mud just [splats] in either direction.”
In fact, something like that happened amid historic rains in the winter of 2022-23. Construction workers were busy preparing to pour the concrete for the bottom layer of the north wall. But water collected in the trench that was dug for it as they were working to compact the soil.
That pushed back the original completion date of late 2025. Right-wing pundits and politicos in recent months have attacked the project over the delays and a high price tag that’s currently $114 million. A March post in an outlet published by a conservative think tank called it a “bridge to nowhere” and “jobs program for environmentalists.” U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy compared it with the state’s long-delayed, budget-busting high-speed train.
Around the time the outrage reached a fever pitch, however, the completion date was announced.
Pratt said “the hate” has worn on her. She’s been called a “fraud,” “retard” and worse, and she’s even afraid to post about the crossing on social media. “Of course we’re still going to celebrate” at the finish line, she said.
At stake is the survival of the Santa Monica Mountains’ isolated, beleaguered mountain lion population, which is listed as threatened. Seth Riley, wildlife branch chief for the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area, said 41% of documented matings were between close relatives since 2002, the start of an ongoing study of mountain lions in and around the Santa Monicas.
Just a few months ago, the National Park Service caught a young collared male at the western end of the mountain range who had a kinked tail — a sign of inbreeding. It’s not the first such documented deformity but shows the problems persist, Riley said. If the situation gets to the point where their reproduction is affected, modeling has shown there’s “essentially a 100% chance of extinction” within 50 years, he added.
But he doesn’t think it’s too late. The soon-to-open crossing will let the big cats seek mates in the Simi Hills and beyond — and allow fresh blood to travel into their neck of the woods, he said. Genetic diversity is expected to go up, though not overnight.
In the last three weeks, a trail camera stationed close to the south end of the crossing has captured coyotes, deer, a female lion with two big cubs — even as construction churns on next door, said Jeff Sikich, a wildlife biologist at the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area.
Recently, in the Simi Hills north of the crossing, his team marked three kittens, the first litter for the 3 ½-year-old lion known as P-113.
“These kittens might be — once they grow up and leave mom at roughly around 1½ — one of the first lions to actually use the wildlife crossing,” he said.

Lila Seidman is a reporter focused on California wildlife and the outdoors for the Los Angeles Times. Since joining The Times in 2020, she has investigated mental health policy and jumped on breaking news. A native Angeleno, Seidman holds a bachelor’s degree from Reed College and a master’s degree from Pepperdine University.
Reggie Bush was the face of USC football’s glory years — and one of the figures at the center of its collapse. But behind the saga was a group of men trying to build a sports agency around Bush, and in the process, said they provided him and his family with the benefits that would ultimately bring the NCAA down on USC.

articles.content_orig:
As leader, Bolsonaro would assume control of an economy that is heavily dependent on China – by far Brazil’s largest trading partner
Flavio Bolsonaro said he would work with the US and China if he becomes Brazil’s president, after a surprise election performance left him poised to join a wave of conservative leaders pushing Latin America closer to Washington.
Bolsonaro finished ahead of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva by about two points in Sunday’s first-round election, a result that sparked a surge in Brazilian assets due to investor views that he is more likely to pursue market-friendly financial policies.
Bolsonaro would take 52 per cent to Lula’s 48 per cent of valid votes, excluding blank and invalid ballots, in the October 25 run-off, a Datafolha poll released on Thursday evening showed. The survey has a margin of error of plus or minus two percentage points. Bolsonaro outperformed Datafolha’s final poll of the first round by about five points.

articles.title_orig: Aspen One begins work on world’s first battery-backed chairlift
articles.title_zh: Aspen One begins work on world’s first battery-backed chairlift
articles.content_orig:
Aspen One announced their plans at Wednesday’s annual Afternoon Blend event to make history with the introduction of the world’s first battery-backed chairlift on Snowmass Mountain.
The first phase of the installation happened on Wednesday.
“There are over 4,000 ski lifts in the world,” said Chris Miller, senior vice president of sustainability at Aspen One. “We are doing something for the first time here at Snowmass.”
Following a successful season with the new Elk Camp high-speed six-pack lift at Snowmass, Aspen One is now looking to replace the 1,250 kilowatt diesel generator with a 900 kilowatt battery backup, avoiding approximately 144 tons of carbon dioxide emissions each year going forward.
“We really do set the standard for resort operations in our industry, from a guest experience but also from a sustainability perspective,” Miller said. “Having an impact in the work that we do is super important.”
Every summer, fuel for lifts is pumped out of diesel tanks at the top of Snowmass, with trucks routinely making trips up and down the mountainside for fuel replacement, according to Miller.
“It’s bad from an environmental perspective, and you just don’t want to be moving that stuff up and down the mountains,” he added.
According to him, the new battery backup will be quieter and cleaner than the current generator as well as be charged with nearly 100% clean energy from Holy Cross Energy.
What’s happening in Aspen, in one click.
Sign up for our morning newsletter at AspenTimes.com/newsletter
Part of the challenge of getting the current 92% renewable energy at Holy Cross Energy to 100% is meeting peak demand periods, Miller explained, which requires supplemental non‑renewable generation to meet consumer needs.
Clean energy will back up the lift during the day, and when the lift stops running at 4 p.m., Holy Cross Energy can pull power back into the grid to support local energy demands.
“Aspen One is really at the forefront of helping Holy Cross get to 100% clean energy with the flexibility of these clean storage systems,” said Mike Steiner, key accounts specialist at Holy Cross. “We utilize these batteries to help shave peak demand and manage our renewable energy supply.”
Steiner told The Aspen Times that Holy Cross Energy and Aspen One have aspirations to expand this battery-backed system further, and continue reaching toward cleaner energy and a more sustainable environment.
“We’re going to install this and make sure it’s fully operational and run efficiently,” he said. “We’re working with them closely on a long-term planning approach.”
The project team expects to reach full completion early next month, Miller confirmed in his presentation on Wednesday.
This spooky season, bears don’t need an invitation to trick or treat.

articles.title_orig: Russia’s Plague Scare Revives COVID-Era Anxiety on Chinese Internet
articles.title_zh: Russia’s Plague Scare Revives COVID-Era Anxiety on Chinese Internet
articles.content_orig:
A mysterious death at a Russian anti-plague institute is stirring COVID-era anxiety in China, just five weeks after Chinese and Russian health officials rehearsed a response to an imported plague outbreak.
Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old laboratory worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died last week after developing severe pneumonia. Early reports suggested she may have contracted pneumonic plague after breaking a test tube containing plague bacteria, but Russia’s health watchdog said investigators had identified no accidents involving pathogens at the institute and described her illness as “pneumonia of unknown etiology.”
The death prompted authorities to quarantine about 200 people who had been in contact with her . By Thursday, the watchdog said medical observation had ended for all contacts, and nearly 5,000 laboratory tests had found no dangerous pathogens . It also denied reports of a second case.
The World Health Organization, however, says it still does not have the “full picture.”
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the agency has asked Russia for the deceased worker’s laboratory results, an explanation for what prompted the extensive public-health measures, and clarification of reports about another employee with unexplained pneumonia.
The U.S. Embassy in Moscow also issued a health alert , advising its citizens not to travel to Russia and citizens already there to “depart immediately.”
For Chinese netizens, the timing has made the story particularly combustible, reviving uncomfortable memories of the information vacuum and lockdown fears that accompanied the early days of the COVID-19 outbreak.
From August 24 to 27, just over five weeks before Shipilova’s death, China and Russia held a major cross-border infectious disease emergency exercise in Fuyuan, Heilongjiang , on the Russian border.
Chinese readout said the exercise simulated emergencies including “plague imported from abroad and a joint cross-border response,” as well as the discovery of a hypothetical emerging tick-borne “Disease X.”
Sergey Balakhonov, director of the Irkutsk anti-plague institute, was among the Russian officials who attended and spoke at the exercise. Another strand of speculation has focused on He Dahai, Fuyuan’s Communist Party secretary, who also took part in the drill. He has largely disappeared from public view since then, prompting claims that he may have been quarantined .
These coincidences have fueled speculation online. Posts circulating on Weibo, China’s equivalent of X, have invoked memories of China’s three years of Covid controls. Several related topics have surged to the platform’s trending search list, including “ COVID also began as pneumonia of unknown cause” (新冠刚开始也是不明原因肺炎) .
One Weibo user called for China to “maintain strict defense” to avoid “repeating the COVID experience.” Others compared Russia’s conflicting early messaging to the uncertainty surrounding the start of Covid.
More alarmist posts circulating on X and Chinese-language sites have urged residents of Heilongjiang, Jilin and Liaoning to stockpile masks, alcohol, medicine and food , warning that northeastern cities could soon face lockdowns.
A CGSP review of Chinese e-commerce platforms found that many doxycycline listings, an antibiotic used to treat plague, were marked out of stock. Chinese netizens also reported that the drug’s price had risen fivefold in just three days .
So far, Beijing has given little additional information about its communications with Moscow. Asked on Tuesday whether Moscow had contacted China over the suspected pneumonic-plague case, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun replied only that “China and Russia maintain close exchanges and cooperation in the prevention and control of infectious diseases, including plague.”
Public-health experts, however, say the epidemiological evidence so far gives little reason to expect another Covid-like crisis. Pneumonic plague is dangerous and can spread through respiratory droplets, but it is a bacterial disease that antibiotics can treat when detected early.
The scare comes as Russian presidential aide Nikolai Patrushev arrived in China on Thursday for a six-day visit . Patrushev, who also chairs Russia’s Maritime Board, is expected to meet Wang Yi and other Chinese officials. Beijing says their talks will cover bilateral relations and maritime cooperation, but neither side has indicated that the Irkutsk incident will be on the agenda.

articles.title_orig: Preview: ARA Australian Cycling Team ready to battle at UCI Gravel World Championships
articles.title_zh: Preview: ARA Australian Cycling Team ready to battle at UCI Gravel World Championships
articles.content_orig:
Home → ← News → Preview: ARA Australian Cycling Team ready to battle at UCI Gravel World Championships
The rainbow jerseys are up for grabs in Nannup, Western Australia this weekend, as the UCI Gravel World Championships land on Australian soil for the first time.
A deep roster for the ARA Australian Cycling Team will line up on home turf, ready to go head-to-head with the world’s best and battle for elite men’s and women’s glory.
The Australian squad includes gravel national champion Tiffany Cromwell, who will be racing for the final time before retiring.
With more than 80 per cent of the course unpaved, the stage is set for a gruelling gravel showdown, that will not only test riders' endurance, but also their handling skills on loose sections of gravel.
The elite men will battle across 144km and 3,713 metres of elevation, while the elite women face 125.6km and 3,179 metres of climbing.
Here’s everything you need to know about our athletes chasing the rainbow jerseys, and when and where you can watch.
There have been a number of changes to the Australian squad Australian squad announced earlier , with gravel national champion Cameron Scott and several age-group qualifiers now set to line up in the elite races.
Connor Sens during the 2025 UCI Gravel World Championships. Image: SWPix
Tiffany Cromwell said: "I think I'm pretty content with my decision, and I'm excited to be able to do it on my terms, and here in Australia, like Nannup, it's not Adelaide, but it's as close as I can get to a home race, on the calendar.
“I've been here, I’ve raced SEVEN a couple of times, and it’s such a fantastic event. The team is amazing who put it on. They put so much passion into it.
“The course, it's super demanding, it's super hard. Of course, I've got many good memories here, but I also know, the field that has assembled for the elite women is pretty strong.
“Of course, the dream would be to finish with the rainbows or even just a podium, but also I don't want to put that pressure on myself.
“I want to just be here, be in the moment, enjoy the race, and just give everything that I have mentally, physically left in my body one last time, and just kind of enjoy the last race.”
Australian fans will be able to watch the 2026 UCI Gravel World Championships on SBS On Demand . Coverage will begin at 9.45am AWST/12.45pm AEDT on both Saturday and Sunday.
Start lists, detailed schedules, live timing and official results are available at the competition hub .

articles.title_orig: Clinical Trial Indicates A.I. Chatbots Could Aid Urgent Care
articles.title_zh: Clinical Trial Indicates A.I. Chatbots Could Aid Urgent Care
articles.content_orig:
Can AI safely assess patients’ needs before they step into a doctor’s office? A study led by researchers at Google and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC) and published in The Lancet today, offers an encouraging first look. As Google’s first-ever publication in the main journal of The Lancet, this research marks a significant milestone.
In a real-world clinical study at BIDMC’s ambulatory primary care clinic, 98 patients consulted AMIE , our research diagnostic AI chatbot, ahead of urgent care visits. Supervising physicians monitored the interactions in real time, and not a single conversation needed to be interrupted based on predefined safety criteria. And clinicians reported that the AI summaries helped them prepare for visits in 75% of cases and influenced their approach to care in more than half. AMIE’s differential diagnoses also matched the doctors’ final diagnoses 90% of the time.
While larger clinical trials are needed to assess patient-facing AI at scale, the findings suggest the potential for AI to enhance the patient-physician relationship and ease the strain on healthcare workers. And they demonstrate meaningful progress as we push the boundaries of what’s possible for AI in science and health . Read the complete research paper in The Lancet .

articles.title_orig: At least 30 dead in Russian bus strike as Moscow closes in on Ukraine’s ‘fortress belt’
articles.title_zh: At least 30 dead in Russian bus strike as Moscow closes in on Ukraine’s ‘fortress belt’
articles.content_orig:
Russian glide bomb hits buses in Ukraine's Kramatorsk, killing at least 30
Kyiv, Ukraine – A Russian glide bomb struck two passenger buses in the eastern Ukrainian town of Kramatorsk on Thursday morning, killing at least 30 people and wounding 18, regional authorities said.
Ukrainian officials said the attack was deliberate. When dropped from planes on the Russian side of the front line, such bombs can glide to fixed coordinates on the ground, in this case, a street in the town that lies about 20 kilometres (12.4 miles) from the front line.
“The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians,” regional administration head Vadym Filashkin wrote on Telegram. “For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill the maximum number of people.”
“Russia consciously disregards all conceivable rules of warfare and norms of international humanitarian law. It selects targets where it can inflict the greatest suffering on civilians,” he wrote.
Filashkin ordered the suspension of the movement of all public transportation in Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk as Russia intensifies attacks, paralysing Ukraine’s transport infrastructure, from trains and minibuses to gas stations, bridges, seaports and freight ships.
“This is a new Russian tactic,” Volodymyr Fesenko, head of the Kyiv-based Penta think tank, told Al Jazeera. “They used to focus on depriving Ukraine of power, on switching off electricity and heating; now their task is also to immobilise the infrastructure, create a transportation collapse.”
“Unfortunately, Russia’s tactic has a certain effect with their strikes on railroads, gas stations,” he said. “They coerce to peace on their conditions.
“They also strike the public psychologically, disrupt the usual lifestyle in general.”
Throughout the war, Russia has denied it targets Ukrainian civilians, a statement that means little to Ukrainians. During the first eight months of 2026, 15,280 civilians were killed or injured, according to the United Nations – a toll that is 55 percent higher than during the same period in 2025.
With no civilian planes in the sky since Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion, trains, buses and trucks have become a lifeline for Ukrainian civilians and businesses, as well as for transporting military and humanitarian supplies.
Trains handle almost two-thirds of Ukraine’s freight volumes, including the export of steel slabs, grains and vegetable oils that keep the economy afloat.
At least 521 locomotives have been hit by drones and shelling since 2022, three-fifths this year alone, Ukrzaliznytsia, the state-run railway monopoly, said in late September.
Some locomotives were struck while in motion, and drones have occasionally hit passenger carriages, causing fires, deaths and injuries.
The largest such attack killed five passengers in January in the northeastern Kharkiv region, an act of “terrorism” that was “not militarily justified”, said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Hitting moving trains and buses has become possible because a new generation of Russian drones are no longer the slow, unmanned aircraft that can be jammed electronically or shot down with a machinegun or even an assault rifle.
Jet-powered, with bigger payloads, they are piloted by human operators who use a wireless mesh network, in which each drone serves as a relay node.
“They’re operated manually. The Russians improved their comms,” Andriy Pronin, one of the pioneers of drone warfare in Ukraine, told Al Jazeera.
Occasionally, the signal reaches the drones through a modem on the ground, on a rooftop or even inside somebody’s apartment – switched on by Ukrainians recruited by Russian intelligence, he said.
Locating the modems before attacks is “complicated, but doable”, Pronin said.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, prosecutors and officials, hundreds of recruits, including teenagers, have been offered money via Telegram. They often did not realise the consequences of their actions and have been arrested and convicted.
The video feed and geolocation are often backed by smuggled Ukrainian SIM cards or signals from mobile phone providers in neighbouring, pro-Moscow Belarus, officials believe. These drones can now get almost anywhere in Ukraine, including once-safe western regions.
A train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson crossed into Poland on September 14, just 30 minutes before a Russian drone struck another passenger train’s locomotive at Yahodyn train station in western Ukraine. Former CIA chief David Petraeus was on a nearby train and reportedly described the attack as “terrifying” and “the act of a truly barbaric leader”.
Ukrainian civilians are equally terrified.
When a daytime Russian drone attack began on September 23, Alyna realised that her workplace was in the most vulnerable place in Kyiv’s central railway station.
She works in a cafeteria located almost in the middle of a massive overpass that stretches above 14 main tracks between the station’s main buildings.
The howling air raid siren and the booms of exploding jet-powered kamikaze drones sent the 24-year-old Kyiv resident scurrying down the stairs and farther on to the subway station.
The drones hit a nearby market, sending black plumes of smoke into the sky and burning to the ground the rotund, modernist building known as the Puck.
“Everything was whistling and rattling above me,” Alyna told Al Jazeera just after another air raid alert ended and passengers began re-entering the station. She withheld her last name for security purposes.
Minutes after the conversation, one more air raid siren forced the passengers out of the railway station, and a drone hit by an interceptor turned into a black cloud in the sky a couple of kilometres east of the building.
The attacks are not limited to trains – Russian drones target petrol stations, buses and minibuses, and seaports, paralysing Ukraine’s exports of grain, vegetable oils and steel.
“You go to a minibus and can hear how [drones] buzz right next to it,” Tetiana Melikhova, a university professor in Zaporizhzhia, a southeastern city with a pre-war population of 720,000, told Al Jazeera.
Her 18-year-old student, Tetiana Bubynets , and two other civilians aged 31 and 48 were killed by an AI-driven drone that was programmed to strike a petrol station on July 6.

articles.title_orig: Democratic senator says Hegseth trying to hide costs of Iran war from US public
articles.title_zh: Democratic senator says Hegseth trying to hide costs of Iran war from US public
articles.content_orig:
Chris Murphy says Pentagon blocked him from military base in Qatar and Iran strike on US embassy in Riyadh far worse than public led to believe
Senator Chris Murphy said the Pentagon blocked him from a major US base in Qatar, yet saw enough damage on the US embassy in Saudi Arabia to conclude that an Iranian strike would have been deadly had it happened during the day.
The Connecticut Democrat, who sits on the Senate foreign relations and appropriations committees, described the destruction he witnessed in Riyadh as “extraordinary” and much more damaging than the public has been led to believe.
“Had that attack happened during the daytime, there’s no doubt that there would have been many, many Americans killed,” he told reporters on a call after returning from Qatar and Saudi Arabia. He also accused the Pentagon of trying to prevent Congress from seeing the costs of the war first-hand, saying the Pentagon secretary, Pete Hegseth , was “determined to hide the cost and the consequences of this war from the American public”.
Two drones hit the compound in the early hours of 3 March, days after the US and Israel launched the war on 28 February, setting off a fire and sending black smoke over the district. The building was reportedly empty at the time and no injuries were reported. Saudi Arabia’s defense ministry initially described the damage as minor.
But, according to Murphy, the drones caused extensive damage across several floors. The strike, he explained, hit “an area of the embassy in which there are a lot of people” and said that “part of that space is uninhabitable and will likely remain uninhabitable”. Murphy said some of it would not be repaired because the embassy is moving soon.
In Qatar, the senator visited Ras Laffan, the gas complex where Iranian drone strikes halted LNG (liquefied natural gas) production early in the war. Murphy said 17% of Qatar’s exports had been eliminated, probably for at least three years of repairs. He also said he saw just one LNG tanker in port, compared with the usual six, and about one a day leaving rather than 10.
Murphy said the Pentagon blocked him from seeing more. He said he gave notice of his visit weeks in advance and submitted a written request for access to Al Udeid air base, the largest US military installation in the region. He also said he raised it with Adm Brad Cooper, the commander of the US Central Command, who appeared surprised that military leaders had also been barred from speaking to him. On arrival, Murphy said, he was told he would not have access to the base and no contact with military leadership.
In response, a senior Pentagon official told the Guardian that Murphy’s office “was informed before his trip” that he would not receive department support to access Al Udeid air base, as per Hegseth’s 3 March directive on travel restrictions in the region.
“That decision was communicated in advance by the office of the secretary of war for legislative affairs,” the official said in a statement. “The department applies the secretary’s guidance evenly.”
Murphy said he would draft language in the coming days requiring the Pentagon to give members of Congress access to overseas bases, which he would seek to include in next year’s appropriations and defense authorization bills. If the war is still going by early next year, he said Congress should withhold defense funding unless it includes a provision to end the conflict, and vowed accountability and investigations if Democrats win one or both chambers in next month’s midterm elections.
The administration, he said, was “giving its middle finger to the Congress, pretending as if we are totally irrelevant”.
“We will potentially have power of both the House and the Senate,” Murphy said of Democrats, “and we should make the end of the war a priority.”

articles.title_orig: Trump calls for Paxton-Talarico debate as Texas Senate race heats up
articles.title_zh: Trump calls for Paxton-Talarico debate as Texas Senate race heats up
articles.content_orig:
James Talarico has been absent from the campaign trail over the past 12 days as the Texas Senate race enters a critical stretch, prompting Republicans to open a new line of attack on the Democratic nominee.
At a campaign rally in San Antonio Wednesday, Texas attorney general and GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton led the crowd in a chant about his opponent’s whereabouts.
“Where is James Talarico?” Paxton prompted the crowd to ask.
Paxton’s campaign has also drawn attention to the topic in social media posts in recent days, and President Donald Trump has jumped into the debate on Truth Social, describing Talarico as “MISSING IN ACTION.”
Talarico’s campaign said the Texas Democrat has been getting over being sick.
“James looks forward to being back out this weekend after recovering from the flu,” said JT Ennis, a spokesperson for Talarico’s campaign, on Thursday. “It’s been 83 days since James challenged Ken Paxton to come out of hiding and answer Texans’ question in a debate, which even President Trump called on him to do last night. Ball is in Paxton’s court.”
Talarico revealed his flu diagnosis September 30 when he spoke virtually with the United States Hispanic Business Council, an event he was supposed to attend in person.
“I was starting to feel kind of under the weather a few days ago and last night it got so bad that I went to the urgent care here in Dallas, and I was diagnosed with the flu,” Talarico told the crowd gathered in Edinburg, Texas, over video conference. “I’m running a fever, and I’m at my most contagious right now, and I guess I’ve been shaking too many hands on the campaign trail and so I want to keep everybody safe.”
Talarico’s last public appearance in Texas took place on September 26 when he held a press conference on suspending the federal gas and diesel tax and ending the war with Iran.
“This is the kind of immediate action we need to provide Texans some relief at the pump in the middle of this affordability crisis,” Talarico said at a gas station in Carrollton, Texas.
After publication of this story, a Talarico campaign source noted the candidate attended a private fundraiser in New York City featuring actor Robert De Niro on September 28.
During this time stretch, Paxton has made several campaign trail stops, including speaking at Trump’s rally in San Antonio on Wednesday. Paxton has spoken at four other campaign events, including a conversation with the USHBC, and was on hand at the president’s event in Denton. At that stop, Trump said he didn’t even know Paxton was there and jokingly called him a “pain in the ass.”
In a Truth Social post Wednesday night, Trump questioned Talarico’s whereabouts and called for a debate between the two Senate candidates.
“He should immediately report to a Debate Stage against Ken Paxton, who is ready, willing, and able,” Trump wrote.
The Paxton campaign did not respond to a request for comment about Trump’s proposed debate between the two candidates. Talarico has challenged Paxton to several debates, including one on Fox News, but the window for debates is narrowing with Election Day less than four weeks away.
Talarico will appear at a town hall hosted by CNN and Jubilee Media on Wednesday, October 14 in Fort Worth, Texas. The media outlets have also extended a town hall invitation to Paxton.
The two candidates are locked in a tight battle for the US Senate seat currently occupied by GOP Sen. John Cornyn, who Paxton defeated in a bruising Republican primary in May.
A recent New York Times/Siena University poll showed Talarico with a six-point lead over Paxton.
The close nature of the race in a state Trump won by double digits in 2024 is causing anxiety for Republicans, who are flooding the Texas airwaves in the final stretch. GOP ad spending in the state from September to November currently stands at more than $190 million compared to $52 million reserved by Democrats during the same time period.

articles.title_orig: Apple Music Is About To Sound Very Different On Your Apple TV
articles.title_zh: Apple Music Is About To Sound Very Different On Your Apple TV
articles.content_orig:
Apple Music is one of the major music streaming providers, competing with the likes of Spotify, Amazon Music, and Google's YouTube Music. There are differences between the giant companies, which is why some users highlight its ease of use as one of the perks of switching from Spotify to Apple Music . Some listeners also like Apple's lossless audio, which arguably makes it better than YouTube music in terms of sound quality . One popular feature all of them offer is the ability to stream music to your television, playing banger tunes while you complete household chores, get work done, or simply hang out with friends. Still, Apple TV is hoping to stand out with a new feature for its Apple TV 4K 2nd and 3rd-generation devices running tvOS 27.
In September 2026, the tech company said it would transition music streaming to high-resolution lossless audio support for the Apple TV's Apple Music app, providing even more frequencies and data in the stream. Per Apple's support page, lossless audio allows listeners to experience uncompromised tracks spared from any frequency loss. "With an Apple Music subscription, you can turn on lossless audio across all of your devices and hear every preserved detail from the original recording," it says.
Thus, if you own a newer Apple TV 4K model, but haven't yet made the switch to Apple Music, it may be worth a try to experience the sound quality, assuming your speakers are up to the task. Apple said tvOS will only compatible with Apple TV 4K devices released after 2021. Any older Apple TVs will be left behind on this update.
Apple TV's transition to high-res lossless audio for Apple Music came just five years after the service rolled it out for its entire catalog–which contains more than 100 million songs in 2026. Though some listeners may have a hard time telling the difference between hi-res and lossless audio , Mastering Engineer Piper Payne said the former produces an untouched, high quality listening sensation. "The soul and life of the mix is sitting in the extra bits of data that are stored in the lossless file," she said for a June 2021 Apple press release.
When Apple transitioned to high-res lossless, it also added spatial audio with Dolby Atmos support for the service to generate a more immersive atmosphere. "Spatial Audio gives artists the opportunity to create immersive audio experiences for their fans with true multidimensional sound and clarity," the company wrote.
Lossless audio is designed to provide 100% of an original recording despite compression, which certain listeners find more pleasant to the ear. Some reddit users likened its sound quality to that found on CDs and, to others, even vinyl records. "[Lossless audio is] literally CD quality audio," one user wrote. "Like the same sample rate every CD has, the same dumb CDs you were playing in your Chevy Cavalier back in high school."

Stanford and Brown are among schools facing scrutiny over alleged visa abuse and Chinese influence on federally funded research
The Trump administration is launching an investigation into nine US universities over alleged J-1 visa fraud, with officials raising concerns about Chinese scholars and the Chinese government.
At a Thursday press conference, Anthony D’Esposito, inspector general of the US Department of Labor, announced what he called a “historic investigation” into J-1 visa fraud at Harvard, Yale, Stanford, Brown, the University of Pittsburgh, UC Davis, Caltech, Arizona State University and MIT. Subpoenas have been issued to the universities, officials said.

articles.title_orig: Catherine Zeta-Jones shocks with sassy response for not having read husband Michael Douglas's book
articles.title_zh: Catherine Zeta-Jones shocks with sassy response for not having read husband Michael Douglas's book
articles.content_orig:
Catherine Zeta-Jones recently shared what she really thinks of her husband Michael Douglas ' new memoir titled One Helluva Ride, which was released on October 6.
The actress visited Today on October 8, where she got candid about the book.
Willie Geist inquired: "I've gotta ask you, because I was just telling you, I interviewed your husband Michael Douglas yesterday. He's got a memoir out. He told me, and I'm curious if this is true, that you have not read the book yet?"
Michael and Catherine have been married since 2000 (@ Instagram)
Catherine admitted: "It's true." She explained: "Look, I've just finished [shooting] Wednesday [for] season three. We shot in Dublin for seven months, and then I just literally got on a Ryanair plane and landed in London – did all of the Kill Jackie stuff."
The movie star continued: "Then I went to Bilbao, Spain, and now I'm here talking to you Willie on the fabulous Today show."
Aside from sharing her packed itinerary, she joked: "And as much as I love my husband, when I'm tired at night, I have no intention of reading about him…at all."
Regardless of the fact that she didn't read the book yet, she advertised: "But everyone else should. The book is called One Helluva Ride, and I think everyone should hold onto their cowboy hats, because I think it is."
Being that that memoir goes into depth about not only Michael's successful career, but his marriage with the actress, Willie teased what Michael told him in his recent Today interview.
Catherine opened up about her husband's memoir (@ Getty Images)
Willie recalled: "He told me that he came home the other night, sort of peeked around the corner, and you didn't seem upset, so he thought, 'Okay, we're in good shape.'"
Catherine charmingly replied: "He caught me in a good time," as she laughed.
The couple, who have been married since 2000, know a thing or two about longevity, and it's apparent that humor is a huge part of their personal secrets to success.
Catherine admitted that she hasn't read the memoir (@ Getty Images)
Michael shared his insight with People on what makes a marriage work long-term, confirming: "A good sense of humor doesn't hurt, number one."
He continued: "And talking things out. Never using the words 'never' or 'always' when you get angry with each other. And putting yourself in the other person's position before you make your value judgment."
Catherine added that she has "no intention" to (@ Instagram)
Overall it comes down to enjoying each other's company and sharing hobbies together as a form of bonding.
Michael continued: "But you gotta have fun. When I first met her, I said, 'Do you like golf?' She said, 'I love golf.' Well, I melted."

articles.title_orig: Canadian author Anne Carson wins literature Nobel for 'bold and inventive' works that blend genres
articles.title_zh: Canadian author Anne Carson wins literature Nobel for 'bold and inventive' works that blend genres
articles.content_orig:
Anne Carson, the Canadian writer and classicist whose work blends verse, prose and essay with influences from classical myths, has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in literature for her “bold and inventive oeuvre.”
Carson, 76, is an accomplished classicist who has taught at multiple colleges in the US and Canada while also producing works like “The Beauty of the Husband,” “An Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse,” and “Nox.” Her distinctive essays, prose and poetry, in which the ancient and modern live side-by-side, have garnered her critical acclaim.
Carson’s “playful dialogue with the classical tradition has created new forms for contemporary literature,” the Nobel committee said in a statement.
The prize, announced at the Swedish Academy in Stockholm on Thursday, carries a cash award of 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.2 million).
Carson is widely known for hybrid style where she balances multiple ideas, genres and forms. “Almost all her literary production has centered upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” said Anders Olsson, chairman of the Nobel Committee for Literature.
For example, in “Autobiography of Red,” the work that made her name, her long narrative verse is framed by an erudite, enigmatic discussion of Stesichorus, the Greek poet who inspired her. In Stesichorus’ original myth, Heracles – better known by his Latin name of Hercules – kills the winged monster Geryon and steals his red cattle as one of his 12 labors. In Carson’s 1998 retelling, she recasts Geryon as a “tender ‘hero’ devoted to his mother,” who “having earlier been subjected to sexual assaults at the hands of his brother, falls in love with the smug and boorish Heracles,” the Nobel committee said.
Such a complicated form belies the simplicity of much of the language in it. “Somehow Geryon made it to adolescence.// Then he met Herakles and the kingdoms of his life all shifted down a few notches,” Carson writes. “They were two superior eels//at the bottom of the tank and they recognized each other like italics.”
Carson was in Iceland, “listening to the wind,” when she discovered she had won the Nobel Prize, according to Ingrid Carlberg, the permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy.
“She was taken by surprise but very happy – I could hear that in her voice,” Carlberg said.
Much of Carson’s early career was dominated by her work in classics – she studied for her bachelor’s, master’s and doctorate degrees at the University of Toronto and also received a diploma in classics from the University of St. Andrews in Scotland. Although she published an essay and her Ph.D. thesis in her thirties, it wasn’t until she was 42 years old that her first book of poems “Short Talks” was published. Three more works followed before “Autobiography of Red” marked her out as a critical favorite.
“The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos,” which charts the breakdown of a marriage between two unnamed characters, came three years later. For that work, Carson became the first female winner of the prestigious T.S. Eliot Prize in 2001. She is the 19th woman of the 122 individuals who have won the Nobel Prize for literature.
Nobel Prize in medicine awarded to trio for technique that helps decode mysteries of the brain
Carson is notoriously private about her personal life, but her 2010 work “Nox” reflects on the life and death of her estranged brother, Michael. It is not a traditional book, as such, but a “box containing an accordion-fold-out of picture, letters and other written texts dedicated to her dead brother,” Olsson said.
Carson has also produced several translations of classical texts and ventured into other artforms, collaborating with visual artists, choreographers, opera and theater directors. The transition into various other artistic fields “demonstrates the freedom with which she relates to literary expectations and rule systems, which in turn lies behind the outstanding importance her work since the 1990s has had for the international art and literature scene,” Olsson added.
Last year, the prize went to László Krasznahorkai “for his compelling and visionary oeuvre that, in the midst of apocalyptic terror, reaffirms the power of art,” the committee said.
In 2024, South Korean author Han Kang was honored by the committee for her “intense poetic prose that confronts historical traumas and exposes the fragility of human life.”
Literature is the fourth prize to be handed out this week, after achievements in medicine, physics and chemistry. The Nobel Peace Prize is set to be revealed on Friday, followed by the winners in economics on October 12.
This story and its headline has been updated with additional reporting.
