articles.title_orig: John Bisset, Engineer and Educator, Has Died
articles.title_zh: John Bisset, Engineer and Educator, Has Died
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › News and Business › Headlines
John Bisset, who dedicated his career to the broadcast industry as a skilled engineer, consultant, sales executive and educator, and who authored Radio World’s popular column Workbench, has died after a period of illness. He was 73.
He spent 55 years in the industry. In his later career, Bisset served a who’s who of equipment manufacturers, including Harris Corp., Dielectric, Broadcast Electronics, Nautel, Tieline, Elenos and Telos Alliance.
[Email your thoughts about John Bisset so we can share. Send to [email protected] .]
His technical knowledge made him uniquely qualified to understand product design, but his ability to communicate, his hallmark, not only made him an asset in sales but as a teacher.
And that has been the hallmark of Workbench.
Every edition delivered hands-on, real-world engineering tips where readers learned something new. A testament to Bisset’s ability to build a vast industry network, ideas poured in from readers and contacts who wrote to him regularly.
Tips earned Society of Broadcast Engineers certification credit, again, a testament to Workbench’s standing.
“One of the fun things about this business is the long-term relationships you make, even though you may not talk to these people for years,” Bisset once wrote.
Radio World Editor in Chief Paul McLane said the column will continue, as Bisset wanted, with a new author to be announced later.
The first Workbench appeared in Radio World on Aug. 8, 1990. Bisset, who was Radio World’s technical editor at the time, began authoring the column on Nov. 7 of that year.
In his very first Workbench column, Bisset offered this piece of advice: “I’d like to encourage you to look around your plant to see what you’ve built that could help someone else. We all know of those little insignificant projects that may appear to be ‘just common sense.’ However, we’ve also all been in the position where we can’t see the forest for the trees.”
He authored approximately 920 Workbench columns over his career. Readers routinely told Radio World that Workbench was their favorite section of the publication.
Bisset told Paul McLane in 2020 that he was especially proud of the column’s popularity among programming and management readers. He understood the power of working the ladder.
“Make friends with your group’s personnel manager,” Bisset would write. “They can be an ally.”
Or, take them to your transmitter site, as Bisset once suggested in 2003. “Not only will it give them some perspective of the work you do, but you’ll earn a little more respect when they see the inside of a transmitter or phasor.”
There was, and still is, a resounding consensus among those who worked with him most of just how highly Bisset was regarded.
“He’s the same gentleman I have always known,” Marty Sacks of Telos Alliance told us in 2020. “The service he has provided to so many, including me, all these years through his Workbench columns have truly been a labor of love.”
In 2007, SBE honored Bisset with its Educator of the Year Award .
“John Bisset is an ‘engineer’s engineer,'” Frank Baptista wrote on his LinkedIn page following Bisset’s 2009 installation of an FM and HD Radio transmitter at UMass Dartmouth. “Anyone who has been a broadcast engineer for any length of time will know that he is considered one of the experts in the industry.”
He also understood his role as an advocate. A broadcast engineer, whether full-time or contract-based, is so often misunderstood. The tips and tricks included in Workbench sometimes needed the support of higher management to pull off.
“It is really important to let the people above you, the managers, the owners, know that you are taking care of their facility and are doing a good job with it,” he once told Kirk Harnack’s This Week in Radio Tech. “You’re saving the station money and you’re keeping it on the air at the same time.”
Some of the nuggets made us laugh . An almost understated simplicity was Workbench’s calling card. But every now and then, if you paid close attention, John would insert a prescient piece of wisdom that would resonate through any walk of life.
“Time. In this business, it can control us,” he wrote on May 9, 2007. “If time gets out of hand, it can destroy us.”
As a director of engineering told John early in his career : “’No radio or TV station is worth dying for.’ Your most important job is to work safely and return to your family at the end of the day.”
John often wrote in Workbench that he was fortunate to have been mentored by chief engineers as he worked his way up the ranks. Some of Bisset’s favorite memories included early AM radio improvement efforts and demonstrating Delta Electronics’ Splatter Monitor to the Federal Communications Commission with colleague Tom Wright.
Known as an accomplished chief and contract engineer, Bisset presented and moderated an all-day Radio Transmitter Workshop at the NAB Radio Show from 1997 to 2003, as well as three additional workshops at the spring NAB Show. He was also a frequent presenter at SBE Ennes Workshops around the U.S. and at chapter meetings.
Bisset co-founded Multiphase, a successful broadcast engineering service company, in 1990. He went on to serve as regional RF sales manager for Broadcast Electronics.
At Dielectric, he directed the completion of several product initiatives, including the Dielectric Pattern Viewer. During his tenure at Harris Broadcast, he earned three sales awards and sold 55 transmitters in a single year, setting a company sales record.
In a July 2018 Workbench, Bisset reflected on an early motivator of his fondness for tinkering with equipment.
“With the move by utilities to underground service distributions, you don’t see many aerial cable splicing tents anymore; but as a young boy, I watched a phone tech strap on his climbing spikes and belt and ascend the pole outside my house,” he wrote. “He assembled a platform and tent and crawled inside.
“As a little boy, I found this fascinating. I ran inside and ran a piece of string between the radiator and end table, and built a similar structure with my TinkerToys. A couple of tissues and tape completed my tent — and then I dispatched my plastic army men inside the tent to get to work.”
He was born Oct. 31, 1952 as John Paul Bisset. At age 10, he appeared on Willard Scott’s “Bozo the Clown” show in Washington, D.C. There he got his first taste of broadcasting.
John recalled going home afterward and, with the help of his father, rigging up his own version of Bozo’s TV studio, using cardboard boxes with pie tins as lights dangling from the ceiling. He used several boxes to model as television cameras, alongside empty fruit cans to serve as mock-up lenses.
As McLane detailed in a 2020 feature celebrating Workbench’s 30th anniversary , at age 12, Bisset constructed a pirate Top 40 radio station in his home, using money from his paper route to purchase equipment. He hooked a Lafayette mic mixer up to two turntables and fed a reel-to-reel deck into a Lafayette wireless AM transmitter, covering a two-block radius.
His first professional job came at age 16 at WFAX(AM) in northern Virginia, serving the Washington market.
“Program Director Roy Martin hired me as a summer relief announcer when I was 16,” Bisset recalled. “I worked there part-time through high school and college, and joined the full-time staff after graduation.” Around that time, he received training in technical writing from an influential teacher, professor Joey Horobetz.
Bisset said he was later inspired to become a Christian while playing religious programming on a station. “Becoming a Christian gave me tremendous encouragement,” he would say later.
He was eventually promoted to WFAX chief engineer. That same year, he and fellow engineer Henry Stewart launched a contract engineering business.
He earned an AAS in Broadcast Engineering Technology cum laude from Northern Virginia

articles.title_orig: AEM Brings Industry Leaders Together at World Dairy Expo to Talk Association Involvement and Program Value - AEM | Association of Equipment Manufacturers
articles.title_zh: AEM Brings Industry Leaders Together at World Dairy Expo to Talk Association Involvement and Program Value - AEM | Association of Equipment Manufacturers
articles.content_orig:
The dairy equipment industry faces no shortage of challenges, from emerging technologies and regulatory hurdles to shifting customer demands and evolving market conditions. Addressing those challenges often requires more than individual company expertise – it requires collaboration from across the industry.
That spirit of collaboration was on full display as AEM's dairy-focused committees gathered during the 59th World Dairy Expo held last week in Madison, Wisconsin. The meetings brought together dairy equipment manufacturers and industry leaders to discuss market trends, committee priorities, and the value of continued engagement in AEM programs and initiatives. AEM hosted its Dairy Equipment Engineering Committee , the Dairy Equipment Leadership Group , and the Dairy Equipment Statistics Committee for meetings during the event.
A highlight of the gathering was a member panel featuring representatives from dairy and agriculture-focused AEM member companies, who shared firsthand perspectives on the benefits of participating in AEM committees and Market Share Statistics programs .
One recurring theme throughout the discussion was the power of industry data to support smarter decision-making.
Attendees noted that participation in AEM's Market Share Statistics programs provides members with access to timely industry intelligence, helping companies better understand market dynamics and evaluate business opportunities. In addition to strengthening individual business planning, the collective data helps create a more complete picture of industry trends.
One member shared how AEM helped demonstrate the value of market intelligence as emerging technologies began gaining traction in the dairy sector.
"When we were struggling to break into an emerging area, AEM used real-world examples from other equipment sectors to show the value of industry data," said GEA Farm Technologies’ Adam Burns. "If organizations are wondering how data can help them, AEM can show people the data and show them how other industries are using it, and they will start to see that value."
Panelists emphasized that access to reliable market data becomes even more impactful when paired with external economic indicators and market intelligence through AEM’s Business Intelligence, allowing companies to make more informed strategic decisions.
Beyond market intelligence, members highlighted the importance of AEM committees as a forum for industry problem-solving.
As new technologies and equipment categories emerge, manufacturers often encounter common challenges, including product classifications, standards questions, and regulatory considerations. Rather than tackling those issues independently, AEM committees create an environment where members can discuss concerns, share experiences, and work toward common solutions.
"When members have questions about new equipment or emerging technologies, we can come together as an industry and find solutions instead of struggling alone," said DeLaval’s Chris Horton. "Trying to solve those challenges collectively benefits everyone."
That collaborative approach helps reduce duplication of effort while supporting the long-term health of both the dairy equipment industry and the producers it serves.
As the dairy industry continues to evolve, collaboration remains one of its greatest strengths. By leveraging data, sharing experiences, and working toward common goals, AEM members are helping build a stronger, more resilient future for dairy equipment manufacturers and the producers they serve. The conversations held in Madison demonstrated that when the industry comes together, the result is more than valuable insight. It is a collective commitment to advancing the success of the dairy sector for years to come.

articles.title_orig: Webinar will commemorate World Food Day with theme “Innovate today. Nourish tomorrow”
articles.title_zh: Webinar will commemorate World Food Day with theme “Innovate today. Nourish tomorrow”
articles.content_orig:
A webinar on 16 October will commemorate World Food Day and say farewell to the UN special rapporteur for the Right to Water and Sanitation.
The webinar will take the World Food Day theme “ Innovate today. Nourish tomorrow.” The discussion will explore what innovation can look like when we place food security, water, land, human rights, and ecological sustainability at the centre.
World Food Day is observed on 16 October each year and provides an opportunity to draw attention to hunger and food insecurity while strengthening collective action towards food systems that are sustainable, equitable, and resilient. This year ’ s webinar will bring together United Nations mandate holders, faith-based organisations, civil society organisations, and community practitioners to explore some of the challenges shaping food insecurity today – including poverty, unsustainable agricultural practices and climate change – and to share approaches that are contributing to resilience, food sovereignty, and sustainable livelihoods.
The session will also provide an opportunity to hear from Prof. Pedro Arrojo-Agudo, UN special rapporteur on the human right to safe drinking water and sanitation, whose six-year mandate concludes in November 2026.

articles.title_orig: Highest Mortgage Rates in 3 Years Chills the Housing Market
articles.title_zh: Highest Mortgage Rates in 3 Years Chills the Housing Market
articles.content_orig:
Mortgage rates have hit their highest level in almost three years, making buying a home more challenging at a time when housing prices are already high. Nam Y. Huh/AP hide caption
Carrie Goldstein's dream for a new home started with a family reunion at her cousin's home in Milwaukee. The home was old with character and she could walk anywhere from the front door.
"We were kind of in awe and drooling over her walkability," Goldstein says.
It was the lifestyle Goldstein wanted but lacked in her Cleveland suburb, which she says is also pretty walkable – with one major issue.
"There are lots of sidewalks," she says. "But you can't really go anywhere."
She brainstormed with her husband and realized nearby Rocky River was where they wanted to live. It was still a suburb, but with a quaint downtown and the option to walk to Lake Erie.
But as much as she wanted to move, one thing stopped her cold. The mortgage she would have to pay. Mortgage rates have hit their highest level in almost three years, making buying a home impossible for many people at a time when housing prices are also sky high.
Goldstein is running into a problem that's affecting many households at a time when people have already been struggling with years of high inflation: The rising cost of borrowing.
Carrie Goldstein stands outside her home on October 4, 2026. Home prices and mortgage rates prevent her from moving. Mike Goldstein hide caption
Bond markets influence all types of borrowing costs across the economy – and as yields have surged to their highest in decades, they've pushed up all kinds of interest rates paid by consumers, from loans for homes to cars and higher education.
And those rates are likely to continue moving up after the Federal Reserve in September raised interest rates for the first time this year – while signaling an additional hike could come this year.
Rate hikes from the Federal Reserve filter through the economy and are meant to slow down consumer and business spending by making people hesitant to take out a more expensive loan to pay for a car or a home – both essential purchases for many people.
"If you need to borrow, boy, it's really not a good time," says John Diamond, senior director of the Center for Tax and Budget Policy at the Baker Institute.
Buying a home is a key example of how households are affected when borrowing costs rise in the economy.
While mortgage rates were falling at the start of this year, they reversed upward after the U.S. war with Iran spooked the bond market by raising worries about inflation. As a result, mortgage rates, which are influenced by the bond markets, have surged this year.
For example, at the current 7.28% level for the average 30-year fixed rate mortgage, a person could end up paying about $900 more a month compared with the 3% pandemic-era rates for a median priced home.
As expected, fewer homeowners are willing or capable of making that financial leap, even if they have long since outgrown their current home. Existing house sales in August were down about 1.2% from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors.
It's not just mortgage costs that are making Americans like Goldstein wince.
Alongside her dreams of owning a home in a walkable neighborhood, Goldstein is ready for a new car. Her old one is 11 years old, has 150,000 miles and plenty of quirks. The repair costs are approaching the point where they'll be more than the value of the actual car.
But a four-year loan for a used car is about three percentage points higher compared with the start of 2022, right around when auto loans began to shed their pandemic-era low rates and started climbing up.
"You can't go and get a car for $150 or $180 bucks anymore a month," she says about the car payments she would be facing.
Although so far the Fed has only delivered a modest quarter of a percentage point, it's adding to the higher borrowing costs at a time when households are already dealing with inflation and higher prices for other types of borrowing.
"It's added to higher mortgage payments. Higher student loan payments. Higher prices because of inflation," Diamond says. "That's what makes it really painful."
And that could mean that households could continue to delay any big purchases requiring a loan.
Goldstein is one of them. She says she can afford to wait on the car and house. But eventually she unsubscribed from real estate updates for that walkable suburb.
"It just became more and more disheartening when I did the math," Goldstein says. "It's just not in the cards."

articles.title_orig: Astronomers pinpoint the origin of a 10 billion-year-old millisecond signal from space
articles.title_zh: Astronomers pinpoint the origin of a 10 billion-year-old millisecond signal from space
articles.content_orig:
More than 10 billion years ago, something in a distant galaxy gave off an incredibly bright burst of radio waves which lasted just a few milliseconds.
In new research published today in Science , our team tracked it back to its origin in a small galaxy filled with many young stars, when the universe was only one-fifth of its current age.
Fast radio bursts like this one are a mystery scientists have been trying to unravel for almost 20 years since they were first discovered. Our discovery is the most distant such burst whose host galaxy has yet been identified.
We detected the burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, with the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa, using a system called MeerTRAP which is designed to catch fast-changing transient radio signals from space in real time.
The different frequencies of the radio burst arrived at slightly different times. We call this effect “dispersion”, and it happens because the signal has travelled through a lot of electrically charged material in space on its journey to Earth.
By measuring the amount of dispersion, we can tell how much of this material the signal has passed through – which in turn lets us calculate how far the signal has travelled and how far away from us it was created.
The FRB 20240304B burst showed a large amount of dispersion, which suggested it was probably coming from a great distance. We were also able to pinpoint its position on the sky.
But when we looked at that position with large ground-based telescopes like the Keck Telescopes , we couldn’t see a host galaxy. The galaxy was simply too faint.
So we turned to the James Webb Space Telescope ( JWST ). The space telescope’s infrared camera revealed a tiny galaxy very close to the position of the fast radio burst.
We then broke down light from the galaxy into the spectrum of different frequencies that made it up. We know what part of this spectrum “should” look like, and seeing how those frequencies have changed lets us calculate how fast the galaxy is moving away from us due to the expansion of the universe – which in turn lets us figure out how old it is.
These calculations confirmed that we were looking at a galaxy 10.6 billion years ago.
The host galaxy itself was another surprise.
It contains only about 10 million times the mass of our Sun, which is a tiny fraction of the mass of our own Milky Way galaxy. The host galaxy appears to be a young galaxy still forming many stars, with a very low amount of metal content, and very different from many of the larger galaxies in which most other fast radio bursts have been found.
This is consistent with one theory about the source of at least some fast radio bursts – that they are produced by young, highly magnetised neutron stars called magnetars .
At the same time, fast radio bursts come in different shapes and sizes, we don’t think all of them necessarily have the same kind of origin.
However, observations like ours give us another piece of the puzzle. By studying the host galaxies and the environments of fast radio bursts across cosmic time, we can start to understand which types of galaxies and stellar environments produce them.
The most exciting thing about this discovery, however, may not be the distance itself.
As the radio signal made its way to Earth, it picked up the imprint of everything it passed through, bearing a record of the magnetic fields, changes in the space environment, and turbulence that it encountered. This makes it a gold mine of information about the cosmos that is otherwise difficult to access.
This includes how electrons are distributed through the cosmic web, as well as information on magnetic fields that pervade the universe. As the signal encounters magnetic fields along the way they subtly twist the orientation of its radio waves. By measuring this twist, we learn about the magnetic field complexities across many billions of light years.
FRB 20240304B does more than tell us about one distant galaxy. It gives us a new data point for studying how electrically charged matter has been distributed through the universe over cosmic time, and also how magnetised the cosmos is.
Our discovery has shown for the first time that fast radio bursts were being produced all the way back to around 3 billion years after the Big Bang, during the period when the universe was most actively forming stars and galaxies. This lets us probe electrically charged matter across about 80% of cosmic history.
Finding fast radio bursts at such large distances is difficult because of the combination of detecting increasingly faint bursts and identifying galaxies that are themselves extremely faint.
The next step is to find many more.
With larger samples of distant fast radio bursts, we can use these brief flashes as cosmic signposts, revealing how matter is spread through the universe, how galaxies grow, and how the space between them changes over time.

articles.title_orig: Old World, Al Fresco At the English Inn
articles.title_zh: Old World, Al Fresco At the English Inn
articles.content_orig:
Randy Daubner created a problem at The English Inn, the Fish Creek restaurant he has owned for 21 years.
Shortly after he took over, he and his then-wife Lisa began building a patio near the entrance to give diners waiting for a table a place to have a drink outside. Pretty soon, those diners were willing to wait to eat outside, even when tables were available inside what had long been an upscale supper club dining room.
“It got so busy, I just kept building,”  Daubner said. “We added more tables, more plantings, more fires and lighting.”
During a spring visit to the restaurant, a landscaper was finding places for dozens more bushes and trees for the patio, which now has space for 150 diners.
The multi-level patio vibe is both light and cozy, with nooks for tables nestled around a fountain and koi pond built by WaterScape Designs. It’s lined with hundreds of flowers, trees and bushes. Diners still enjoy the restaurant’s old fashioneds, Manhattans and classic dishes like Beef Wellington and prime rib, but now in the glow of the 40 fires that light and warm tables and draw attention to a restaurant that could otherwise be overlooked.
Before the outdoor expansion,“the parking lot was large and tired, there was no lighting, and people thought the place was closed,” Daubner said.
A massive metal sculpture of a dragonfly on one end of the parking lot and a knight on horseback on the other side now assures that the restaurant can’t be missed.
It’s a much different face from the inside of this longtime county landmark. Once home to The Parkway restaurant, it became The English Inn when Pete and Dort Kortes bought it in 1964. A drawbridge guides diners over the koi pond at the front door, where they open the wooden doors to the dim lowlight of the bar and lounge, a throwback to another era. The ceiling sits low above the bar that seems to hug you as you enter and prepares you for a dining room unlike any other around.
Around the bar you find a hulking stone fireplace on the north wall and custom-crafted metal chandeliers overhead; stained-glass partitions and dining nooks are framed by bulky wooden beams. It all comes together to create a vibe that’s part English pub and part Knights of the Round Table just a little north of Fish Creek on state Highway 42.
“This was all Dort’s vision,” Daubner said. “These are still her original wooden chairs. They don’t make them like this anymore.”
It’s a dining room made for the cool nights of winter, and a patio perfect for the warm nights of summer.
The English Inn is located at 3713 Hwy 42 in Fish Creek.

articles.title_orig: Venezuela's Maduro charged in US with ordering torture of opponents, Americans
articles.title_zh: Venezuela's Maduro charged in US with ordering torture of opponents, Americans
articles.content_orig:
Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro has been charged by U.S. authorities with torture and other crimes in a new indictment unsealed Thursday that adds pressure on the ousted authoritarian leader already fighting drug trafficking offenses.
Maduro, who was previously charged with participating in a conspiracy to send cocaine into the U.S., is now also facing allegations of human rights abuses during his reign as president of the oil-rich South American nation.
Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, have been behind bars in New York since early January, when forces seized them from their Caracas home in a middle-of-the-night raid.
Both have pleaded not guilty in the criminal case first brought years ago against them and numerous alleged co-conspirators. They had already been facing potential life prison sentences if convicted.
Cilia Flores was scheduled to be in court Thursday, where her lawyers will urge a judge to free her from jail and put her under house arrest because she has heart problems.
Their attorneys have asked for the case to be dismissed on the grounds that they have immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country.
Lawyers for Flores, 69, have also argued that she has medical issues that cannot be treated effectively in jail and that she could instead be allowed to live under 24-hour guard at a residence in New York.
They also said she suffered permanent scarring when she was “thrown against a wall or dresser” during the U.S. military action that led to her capture.
Her lawyers say she has lost 25 pounds while imprisoned at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn and has been told that she might need heart surgery. They said she has “lingering lightheadedness, dizziness and shortness of breath” and might have suffered a minor heart attack in July.
Prosecutors opposed the bail request. In a court filing, they wrote that Flores would pose an “extreme risk of flight and danger to the public” if released. They also said she has been taken from the jail to get treatment at a local hospital when care was needed.
President Donald Trump’s administration has defended the raid to capture Maduro as a “surgical law enforcement operation.” Maduro has called himself a prisoner of war and his capture a kidnapping.
Flores is charged with participating in a cocaine importation conspiracy with her husband, Maduro, who served as Venezuela’s president from 2013 until his capture by American forces in January.
Lawyers for Flores said she was no threat to flee because she is “intent on supporting her husband with her constant presence.”

articles.title_orig: Video: China Coast Guard Uses Water Cannon During Philippine Medevac
articles.title_zh: Video: China Coast Guard Uses Water Cannon During Philippine Medevac
articles.content_orig:
By The Maritime Executive 2026-10-08 14:50:00
The Philippine Coast Guard has reported another dust-up at Second Thomas Shoal, where the Philippine Navy maintains an outpost aboard a deteriorating shipwreck in order to deter Chinese expansion within Manila's exclusive economic zone.
Second Thomas Shoal has been an on-again, off-again flashpoint for tensions between Philippine and Chinese forces in the Spratly Islands since at least 1999, when the Philippine Navy intentionally grounded the WWII-era landing ship BRP Sierra Madre on the reef to serve as a base. The service has maintained a small detachment of marines on board the wreck ever since, and the periodic resupply and rotation missions to and from the shoal are a recurring source of friction. In times of heightened diplomatic tension, the China Coast Guard has often attempted to prevent PCG personnel from reaching the station, periodically adopting forcible methods like aggressive maneuvering and water-cannoning.
The latest encounter occurred on October 8, according to PCG spokesman Jay Tarriela. A Navy servicemember aboard BRP Sierra Madre was in need of medical attention and required evacuation from the station, and the PCG was tasked with mounting a medevac mission. On Thursday morning, the patrol vessel BRP Cabra departed Lawak and got under way for Second Thomas Shoal. At about 0730 hours, Cabra arrived at a position about nine nautical miles away from the reef, where it encountered a familiar presence: China Coast Guard cutter CCG 5306. The CCG crew turned on their water cannon and closed the distance to Cabra, approaching to within 400 yards, Cabra's crew reported. The Chinese cutter's maneuvering prevented further progress towards the Philippine base.
In order to avoid getting hit by the water cannon, BRP Cabra stayed about 13 miles offshore and waited. The crew had hoped to conduct a rendezvous and transfer closer to the patient, but this was not possible because of the Chinese presence, Tarriela said.
By early afternoon, the situation had not changed. To adapt, Cabra's crew launched a team in its RIB boat, and the BRP Sierra Madre station dispatched two inflatable rubber boats with the patient and escort personnel. They met up about four nautical miles off the reef and transferred the patient between boats. Throughout the evolution, CCG small boats and cutters harassed the PCG boat crews, Tarriela said, using "dangerous" maneuvers. Other Chinese vessels involved or in the area included CCG cutters 5009 and 21585, plus the PLA Navy frigate Yongzhou (628) and one maritime militia fishing vessel.
After bringing the patient safely aboard, the Cabra's crew provided him with a checkup and with IV fluids, then got under way to deliver him to shore for a higher level of care.
According to the PCG, the CCG's interference delayed the medevac for hours and created danger for Philippine personnel and the patient. In a statement, Tarriela also highlighted the root of the longstanding sovereignty dispute: China claims a right to control navigation within the western Philippine EEZ, despite a 2016 international arbitral ruling to the contrary.
"When a life is at stake, there should be no water cannon, no obstruction, and no delay. Saving a sick or injured person at sea is a basic obligation that every coast guard in the world is expected to uphold. We call on the CCG to value and respect humanitarian missions moving forward, and to act in a manner consistent with international law and the professional standards expected of any coast guard," PCG Commandant Admiral Ronnie Gil Gavan said in a statement.
Get the latest maritime news delivered to your inbox daily.
As in prior incidents, the China Coast Guard claimed that it had permitted PCG units to access Chinese territory within the Philippine EEZ.
"China on Thursday allowed the Philippine Coast Guard vessel 4409 to evacuate an injured person from a Philippine vessel illegally grounded at [Second Thomas Shoal], permitting a small-boat transfer on humanitarian grounds, and the China Coast Guard (CCG) handled the operation in accordance with the law and provided necessary assistance," CCG spokesperson Jiang Lue told state-owned Chinese outlet Global Times.

articles.title_orig: Plane damaged at Riyadh airport as Houthis escalate attacks, sources say
articles.title_zh: Plane damaged at Riyadh airport as Houthis escalate attacks, sources say
articles.content_orig:
The leader of the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen has warned Saudi Arabia to prepare for a long conflict, as his group intensified its attacks on the kingdom — targeting its airports and military facilities for a third consecutive day.
The group said Thursday it had carried out a new wave of attacks targeting two civilian airports — King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Najran Airport near the southern Saudi-Yemen border — and the Royal Saudi Air Force’s King Khalid Air Base.
It claimed the attacks involved both cruise and ballistic missiles and had caused damage and disrupted air traffic.
Images posted on X and verified by CNN showed smoke rising over Terminal 4 at King Khalid International Airport as well as what appeared to be a damaged Saudi aircraft, while the Associated Press cited a witness as saying several explosions had been heard in Riyadh, including at the airport.
While Saudi authorities have not directly commented on whether the airports were attacked, they said Thursday they had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles fired toward Riyadh and that falling debris had damaged a kindergarten and a medical clinic.
The US Mission in Saudi Arabia said it was “aware” of attacks targeting the airport in Riyadh and warned American citizens to exercise heightened vigilance, noting previous attacks on civilian airports in the country and cautioning the conflict “has the potential to escalate.”
It warned of possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and travel disruptions, and said US government employees now required “special authorization” to use the airport and remained barred from traveling within 20 miles of the Yemen border.
The news comes after three people were killed and 36 wounded over the past two days in Houthi attacks on King Khalid International Airport and Abha International Airport, near the Yemen border.
In a televised speech Thursday, Houthi leader Abdul Malik al-Houthi vowed to continue attacking Saudi targets and confronting Saudi-backed forces in Yemen.
He warned Saudi Arabia against continuing its military campaign in Yemen, saying his group had the military capabilities and resolve to withstand a lengthy conflict.
“The Yemeni people today possess all the determination and elements of strength, regardless of how long the war lasts,” al-Houthi said.
The Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of northern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa, have been at war with Yemen’s internationally recognized government and a Saudi-led coalition since 2015.
The conflict intensified in July after the collapse of the US-Iran ceasefire, with the Houthis expanding missile and drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities, airports and shipping routes. Saudi Arabia has responded with airstrikes and support for Yemeni government forces.
In recent weeks, the Houthis have threatened to broaden the scope of their attacks within Saudi Arabia. In a statement Thursday, they warned employees, engineers and workers at Saudi oil facilities to avoid locations that could become targets of future attacks.
The group also renewed previous warnings to airlines, airport operators, travelers and workers at Saudi airports and facilities.
“The more the Saudi enemy persists in its aggression and blockade, the greater its losses become,” al-Houthi said.
The latest escalation comes as Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces continue Operation “Dawn of Yemen,” a major offensive aimed at reversing recent Houthi gains in Yemen.
In recent weeks, fighting has intensified along Yemen’s western coast and around the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a vital shipping route connecting the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. Yemeni government forces have claimed to have recaptured several positions near Bab al-Mandeb, Mocha and Dhubab, although the Houthis dispute those claims.
Saudi-backed Yemeni forces attack Houthis near key global trade route
On Thursday, Yemen’s internationally recognized government said its forces had carried out 1,729 precision strikes against Houthi targets during the offensive, claiming to have killed 1,370 fighters and destroyed or disabled 300 vehicles and other military assets. The same day, the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of escalating its air campaign, claiming Saudi warplanes had carried out 59 airstrikes and missile attacks across Sanaa and several Yemeni provinces over the previous 24 hours, causing civilian casualties.
CNN cannot independently verify either claim.
However, the Houthis have dismissed reports of major battlefield losses, accusing regional media outlets of exaggerating advances made by Saudi-backed forces.
Earlier this week, Houthi missiles landed near Aden International Airport, the main airport serving Yemen’s internationally recognized government, forcing the diversion of a commercial flight from Cairo, according to Yemeni government officials.
The Saudi-led coalition said late Wednesday that it responded to that attack by launching a large-scale operation striking 82 Houthi military targets in Saada, Hodeidah, Al-Jawf and Marib provinces. According to the coalition, the targets included missile depots, command centers, communications facilities and weapons stockpiles.

articles.title_orig: Students Rally in France for Second Day of Mass Protests in a Week: Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Students Rally in France for Second Day of Mass Protests in a Week: Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
France has been struggling to contain its biggest student protests in decades .
The protests started last month at a high school in a Parisian suburb, where students joined their striking teachers to protest a lack of staff and resources. When their demands were met and extra staff were sent to the school, the strike ended.
But shortly after that, students in Paris and the surrounding region began blocking entrances to their schools. Within days, similar scenes were reported across the country. Images of students setting alight trash cans, manning barricades, assaulting teaching staff and clashing with police have led to questions about the police’s response and the far left’s involvement.
Hundreds of schools have been forced to close, and thousands of people have been taken into police custody over the past few weeks — most of them minors with no previous criminal records.
Critics have accused the police of a heavy-handed response. Following a massive day of protests on Tuesday, French President Emmanuel Macron demanded “empathy” from police forces facing student protesters.
In an address to the nation Wednesday, French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said parliament next month would debate a budget proposal that includes 64 billion euros ($71.6 billion) in funding for education, a slight increase from last year. He also said the government has launched five initiatives to respond to students’ needs.
But there has been little sign that school blockades will halt in the meantime. Student unions have called for a day of protests on October 17.

articles.title_orig: Gas prices face new threat as Hurricane Isaias forces widespread Gulf oil shutdowns
articles.title_zh: Gas prices face new threat as Hurricane Isaias forces widespread Gulf oil shutdowns
articles.content_orig:
A powerful storm snaking its way through the Gulf of Mexico threatens to disrupt U.S. oil and gasoline production at a moment when retail gas and diesel prices are squeezing American consumers and companies.
Hurricane Isaias is rapidly intensifying and expected to make landfall along the northeastern Gulf shore late Friday or early Saturday.
Already, major oil companies, including Chevron and Shell, have begun shutting down some oil production sites. Chevron said it was shutting down four of its assets in the Gulf, although production at its five other facilities in the region remained at normal levels. Shell said it was halting production at five sites.
All told, nearly two-thirds of Gulf oil production and 57% of natural gas production had been shut in by noon Thursday, according to the U.S. Marine Minerals Administration.
Hurricanes and major storms are common in the region, so oil companies have well-established evacuation and shutdown protocols.
Still, the timing could hardly be worse for U.S. consumers.
The U.S.-Israeli war against Iran has spawned broader regional conflict, which continues to disrupt energy supplies and drive oil and gasoline prices higher.
Global benchmark Brent crude oil prices surged nearly 5% in early Thursday trading amid reports that President Donald Trump was considering renewed attacks against Iran. U.S. gasoline prices averaged $4.36, down slightly from a week ago but still up 21 cents over the past month.
“This could not have come at a worse time as gasoline and diesel inventories are quite low,” Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates LLC consultancy, wrote in a note Wednesday.
Nearly all U.S. offshore production is in Isaias’ path, he wrote, which means “the impact, even short-lived, can be significant.”
Lipow estimated that 14% of the nation’s refining capacity is in the storm’s path. Given that most U.S. refineries are now running at maximum levels in response to the global squeeze on capacity, “There is no slack in the system,” he wrote.
Oil is a globally traded commodity, so any reduction in supplies will send prices higher around the world.
Refineries in the path of Isaias are likely to see flooding that could take them offline for up to 10 days, said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. That is expected to produce a short-term squeeze for U.S. gasoline prices.
But for U.S. motorists, the bigger concerns remain overseas — especially in Russia, where Ukraine continues to target refineries.
“The refining problem is looking like, short to medium term, at least three to six months,” De Haan said. “And it sounds like it’s going to be continuing, especially with Ukraine promising to target more Russian refineries. So there needs to be some de-escalation there for there to be any relief, but it doesn’t look like we’re seeing it.”
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.

articles.title_orig: FBI Says China-Linked Hackers Ran Portal Giving Third Parties Access to Stolen Emails
articles.title_zh: FBI Says China-Linked Hackers Ran Portal Giving Third Parties Access to Stolen Emails
articles.content_orig:
Hackers tied to a Chinese cybersecurity company stole email from government organizations, law enforcement agencies, healthcare systems, and religious institutions in Southeast Asia, the FBI and agencies in 6 other countries said on October 8.
The company, Integrity Technology Group , has been sanctioned by the U.S. and the UK. The hackers scanned websites for flaws using a tool containing more than 1,300 scripts, guessed passwords for Microsoft 365 and Exchange accounts, and copied mailboxes using tools designed to collect mail.
The hackers have been breaking into networks since at least mid-January 2021, according to the agencies' joint advisory . It describes the hacking in the present tense but provides no date for any theft and does not specify how many organizations were breached.
The same hackers targeted U.S. government services, critical manufacturing, healthcare, and IT organizations, along with U.S. law enforcement, education, and religious groups. Organizations in Southeast Asia, Africa, and North America were also targeted.
The hackers also run a web application that "provides third-party access to stolen email content," the advisory said. It does not identify those third parties.
In September 2024, the FBI disrupted a botnet , a network of hijacked devices, that the U.S. Justice Department said Integrity Technology Group controlled. It held more than 200,000 routers, cameras, and other consumer devices, and Lumen researchers had named it Raptor Train.
The 2024 action dealt with the botnet. The new advisory covers how the hackers get into networks and what they take. It is based on evidence the FBI recovered and observed during several investigations related to the company.
The agencies describe Integrity Technology Group as "a China-based for-profit company with links to the Chinese government" whose employees build or get cyber tools "for use and sale," host infrastructure, and break into networks.
The advisory uses a single label, "the threat actors," for the company and the hackers it enables. It does not say which of them carried out each break-in.
The U.S. Treasury sanctioned the company in January 2025 for its role in several computer break-ins against U.S. victims. The UK sanctioned it in December 2025.
Christopher Wray, then the FBI director, said in 2024 that the company's "chairman has publicly admitted that for years his company has collected intelligence and performed reconnaissance for Chinese government security agencies."
The hackers' methods are "consistent with" activity that security companies track as Flax Typhoon, Ethereal Panda, and RedJuliett, among others, the advisory said. Those names may not match the U.S. government's own tracking one-to-one, and the same hackers may also carry out work unrelated to Integrity Technology Group.
Flax Typhoon is Microsoft's name for a China-based group that it described in 2023 as targeting organizations in Taiwan.
Integrity Technology Group rejected the U.S. accusations in January 2025. It told the Shanghai Stock Exchange that the U.S. move had no factual basis, the Associated Press reported . A Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson, asked about the sanctions, said China firmly opposed the U.S. action, according to the same report.
The hackers look for flaws in networks and web applications with open-source scanners such as Nmap, masscan, and WPScan, the advisory said. Their scans focus on ports 21, 22, 53, 80, 443, and 1080.
"The use of open source tools typically found on GitHub suggests the threat actors tend to look for more vulnerable targets," the agencies said.
The hackers have also used a scanner called MicroScan since as early as 2017. It is a Python web application containing more than 1,300 penetration testing scripts designed to scan websites for specific flaws. The hackers have used the scripts against services including OpenSSL, Oracle WebLogic Server, Rejetto HFS, WordPress, Juniper ScreenOS, Jenkins, and Apache Struts.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre, one of the agencies behind the advisory, said in its news release that the hackers are "uniquely using AI tools, such as automated scanning." The advisory itself does not mention AI.
The hackers mostly get in with command-line tools built on exploit code written in languages such as Python and Go. The advisory lists 8 known flaws that it says were successfully exploited. The flaws were found in the hackers' penetration testing scripts.
The table shows the affected versions as the advisory gives them and, where one could be confirmed, the release that fixes the flaw.
The advisory marks 5 of the 8 with an asterisk and describes them as newly added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, the list of flaws that the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) says have been used in attacks. They were not in the catalog data that CISA publishes on GitHub (version 2026.10.04) when The Hacker News checked at 18:05 UTC on October 8.
Strapi's own advisory gives a wider range than the joint advisory. It says versions from 3.2.1 through 4.7.9, but not including 4.8.0, are affected.
Two flaws depend on a setting. The Struts flaw works only when Dynamic Method Invocation is turned on, and Apache says turning it off is an alternative to upgrading. The ONLYOFFICE flaw applies when JWT is used, according to its NVD record.
The BIND flaw is a denial-of-service bug that makes the DNS server exit.
Another way in is a fake login. The FBI recovered a cross-site scripting (XSS) payload that changes a vulnerable web page to show username and password fields.
After a visitor enters any username and password, the page offers a password-protected ZIP file that holds a program named live700_v1.exe. That program starts a process named DiagTrack.exe, the same name as a legitimate Windows program, which sends encrypted traffic to dns.studiocloud[.]xyz.
The FBI attributes that domain to Integrity Technology Group and assesses that the malware likely targets email.
The hackers also use password spraying, which means trying a few common passwords against many accounts. For this, they use EBurst, an open-source Python tool that targets Microsoft 365 and Exchange accounts.
EBurst tries logins through Exchange interfaces that include ECP, EWS, OAB, OWA, RPC, API, MAPI, PowerShell, Autodiscover, and Microsoft-Server-ActiveSync, according to its README file. Defenders should cover these interfaces, the agencies said.
To keep access, the hackers install SoftEther, a legitimate VPN program that security software is less likely to flag, the advisory said. They often rename the installer conhost.exe or dllhost.exe so it looks like a Windows file, and they set the client to reconnect each time the machine starts.
To take credentials, they ran a tool named DC.exe that uses DCSync, a technique that copies data from a domain controller through Active Directory's replication service. It copied account credentials, group membership details, and trust relationships.
For email, the hackers built a bot from a PHP script named Curlc4.txt. It collects mail through Exchange Web Services (EWS), an interface that also gives access to calendars and contacts.
The bot compresses the mail, sometimes encrypts it, and uploads it to a remote server. The script appears to be stand-alone rather than installed on a hacked device, and its main command-and-control domain was natcloudservice[.]com.
A second tool, office-cli, keeps going back to Microsoft 365 accounts to take mail from different time periods. It works from configuration files that hold a client ID, tenant ID, and secret, and it avoids detection by using legitimate access methods, the agencies said.
The FBI also saw the hackers download databases or pull data from victims' email by hand.
In some cases, the hackers limited access to the stolen data to IP addresses in Xiamen, China.

articles.title_orig: Search warrants against former prince Andrew were unlawful, court finds
articles.title_zh: Search warrants against former prince Andrew were unlawful, court finds
articles.content_orig:
Thames Valley Police has accepted warrants it used to search Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's homes at the time of his arrest in February were unlawful, the High Court has been told.
Following Thursday's hearing, items seized in the raid continue to be held by the police, with a further hearing to take place in 2027 to decide whether the material can be used as evidence.
Meanwhile, the criminal investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor is ongoing.
The former prince, who denies any wrongdoing, was arrested by police on 19 February on suspicion of misconduct in public office, after which he launched a legal challenge over the legality of the search warrants.
The force said it accepted that the "initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect" before they searched the properties.
On Thursday at the High Court, judge Mr Justice Hilliard said Mountbatten-Windsor and the police had agreed that the search warrants had been unlawful.
However, he added: "The fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring the investigation to an end or mean that the whole of the investigation is unlawful."
Mountbatten-Windsor opposes the police's bid to retain the evidence, the judge said, and another hearing is expected in 2027.
His lawyers have used a judicial review to challenge the actions of the force's chief constable and the Central Criminal Court in the build-up to his arrest.
His arrest arose after the US Department of Justice published documents which raised suspicions he had forwarded confidential information to the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein when Mountbatten-Windsor was a UK trade envoy in 2010.
He has consistently denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein.
The court heard on Thursday that Thames Valley Police seized documents and electronic devices when they raided Mountbatten-Windsor's homes earlier this year.
Thames Valley Police's position was that they had applied for search warrants under section eight and nine of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 at a hearing at the Central Criminal Court the day before the search.
That court determined that only section eight search warrants were needed and they were granted on that basis - but subsequently, a legal challenge has established that the court should have issued them under the section nine.
The judge explained on Thursday why the police could keep hold of the former prince's items that had been seized.
He said: "There would be little point in handing property back if it could then simply be lawfully seized under some other provision."
A Thames Valley Police spokesperson said: "The agreement that led to the quashing of the warrants relates specifically to a decision made by the court regarding the legal basis for these and is not a judgement on our ongoing investigation.
"We ensured the court was presented with all the necessary information and paperwork to inform their decision, following the correct legal processes throughout.
"We accept the position that the initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect and therefore these must be legally quashed.
"Legal proceedings are currently ongoing to decide how material seized during the searches will be managed and whether we can lawfully retain it in support of our ongoing investigation."
The force said its "investigation into alleged misconduct in public office by a man in his 60s from Norfolk remains ongoing, and we continue to pursue all reasonable lines of enquiry to effectively and fairly progress this investigation".
The next stage in this legal dispute will be a behind-closed-doors hearing over whether the police can still retain material seized from Mountbatten-Windsor's homes under alternative powers designed for situations like this.
The error that has led to Thames Valley Police accepting the search warrants were unlawful relates to the particular power the judge permitted the force to use when its officers raided the properties.
Strict legal safeguards on searches bar the police from automatically seizing sensitive material without thinking through in advance the need to take it.
Examples of that material include advice from a suspect's lawyer or material which does not really belong to them, such as copies of confidential work-related papers from an employer.
In practice, if the police find such material during a search, they should return it rather than use it in their investigation.
The category of search warrant that was granted by the court in this instance did not take into account the possibility of such protected material being seized.
However, the law says police can in fact seize that kind of material - or potentially retain it in the event of an error - providing they pass some extra tests.
Thames Valley Police must now convince a judge that the material is likely to be of "substantial value" to their investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor and, ultimately, potential evidence to present to a court.
So while the force has conceded the search warrant was unlawful, a judge will have to decide whether this alternative search power, with its extra safeguards, justifies them keeping and using the material after all.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia, Oracle, CoreWeave and other AI stocks sink on OpenAI revenue report
articles.title_zh: Nvidia, Oracle, CoreWeave and other AI stocks sink on OpenAI revenue report
articles.content_orig:
Shares of Nvidia , Oracle , CoreWeave and other artificial intelligence names sank lower on Thursday after the market learned more details about OpenAI's revenue.
OpenAI told investors that it hit roughly $50 billion in annualized revenue at the end of September, CNBC confirmed, lower than the the $68 billion figure that was widely reported late last month. A person familiar with the matter said the $68 billion figure included gross revenue from OpenAI's partners, which helps investors make a more direct comparison with its chief rival, Anthropic .
The Financial Times was first to report the $50 billion figure.
OpenAI shared an update about its finances in an investor presentation, said the person, who asked not to be named in order to discuss the numbers. In addition to the $50 billion in annualized revenue, OpenAI touted 77% total run rate growth during its third quarter, as well as 107% run rate growth for its enterprise business during the same period, the person said.
Nvidia shares fell 3%, Oracle shares fell nearly 6% and CoreWeave shares slipped nearly 8% on Thursday. Additionally, Advanced Micro Devices fell 4%, Broadcom fell 4%, Intel fell 5% and Super Micro Computer fell nearly 5%.
OpenAI is under pressure to justify its $852 billion valuation to investors as it gears up for what is widely expected to be a blockbuster IPO. OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with regulators in June, and executives have signaled that the company is eyeing a 2027 debut .
Anthropic is also readying for a major IPO . The company has not officially disclosed when it plans to debut, but it's been engaging in meetings with prospective investors and is reportedly seeking a $2 trillion valuation. In August, Anthropic told investors that its annualized revenue run rate hit $65 billion at the end of July.
In a report on Tuesday, independent financial research provider New Constructs called Anthropic's upcoming offering the "most ridiculous IPO of 2026," and valued the company at a mere $150 billion. Anthropic's revenue in 2025 was $4.6 billion as the company racked up a net loss of $42 billion, according to Reuters , which cited a leaked copy of the company's prospectus.
Both Anthropic and OpenAI have been at the center of a fierce debate over AI safety, after a growing chorus of researchers warned that the companies' models could potentially cause catastrophic harm. OpenAI has disclosed several incidents where its models behaved in unintended ways, and the company recently pulled its plans to launch GPT-6.1 Astra, saying the model did not meet its safety standards.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in September that "right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public," in part because of the ongoing concerns around safety.
As OpenAI bides its time, the company is engaging in early stage discussions with investors about a potential new funding round. The company could raise around $30 billion, CNBC previously reported, but that figure could change. The round is being driven by investor demand and no term sheet has been finalized yet.
OpenAI closed a historic $122 billion funding round in March, and CFO Sarah Friar told CNBC last week that it is still "very well capitalized."

articles.title_zh: James Webb Space Telescope helps detect the most distant Fast Radio Burst ever seen — and scientists are surprised by its source
articles.content_orig:

Astronomers have discovered the most distant Fast Radio Burst (FRB) ever detected. Not only could this help untangle the mystery of what causes these powerful but brief explosions of radio waves, but because FRBs are incredible celestial messengers, it could also reveal details of 11 billion years of cosmic evolution. This FRB , designated FRB 20240304B, was first observed by astronomers using the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa. Then, using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), astronomers tracked it back to its home galaxy, located around 11 billion light-years away. This revealed that FRB 20240304B has been travelling to Earth since the universe was just 3 billion years old or so.
That doesn't just make this FRB 20240304B the most distant and earliest FRB ever detected; it more than doubles the distance of the previous record holder!
"This is an extraordinary glimpse into the distant universe," team co-leader Manisha Caleb from the Sydney Institute for Astronomy said in a statement sent to Space.com. "We have caught a fast radio burst from a time when the universe was only about three billion years old, and we have used that brief flash of radio light to learn about the matter it has travelled through over billions of years."
The team's research was published on Thursday (Oct. 8) in the journal Science.
Fast Radio Bursts are mysterious blasts of radio waves that usually flare just once, and in the mere milliseconds they last, emit many times more energy than the sun can radiate in a year.
As these powerful millisecond-long blasts of radio waves travel billions of light-years to reach Earth, they pass through gas and dust in galaxies and through the "cosmic fog" lying between these galaxies, the so-called intergalactic medium . By measuring how much the signal slows down, scientists can effectively weigh this fog of gas to map the distribution of matter in galaxies.
That makes them crucial tools for understanding how galaxies use gas and dust to form stars and grow. Thus, FRBs are a metaphorical cosmic 'fossil record' blasting through space at light speed with the energy of a multitude of stars.
With that in mind, it is little wonder that as a record-breaking example of a fast radio burst, FRB 20240304B has already shocked astronomers. It did this by delivering a surprise about its home galaxy.
"The galaxy hosting this burst is surprisingly small, metal-poor and undergoing a very active episode of star formation," team member Laura Driessen, of the University of Sydney, said. "That gives us an important clue about the environments in which FRBs are born and shows that these brief radio flashes can tell us not only about the distant universe, but also about how galaxies and their stellar populations evolve."
One of the leading suspects in the creation of FRBs are magnetars , a type of neutron star created when a massive star collapses and dies in a supernova explosion. Unlike "standard" neutron stars, magnetars have fearsomely strong magnetic fields  — the strongest magnetic fields in the known universe, in fact.
There are different theories about how magnetars are born: one involving existing older neutron stars colliding and merging, the other involving environments with burgeoning star formation.
The galaxy from which FRB 20240304B originates seems to support that latter formation route, as it is young in the midst of "starburst," a period of extreme star formation.
Scientists will work on the mystery of the FRB/magnetar connection. In the meantime, this newly detected and tracked blast of radio waves definitely has expanded the boundaries of the cosmos that can be probed with FRBs.
"In principle, sufficiently powerful bursts could be detectable from the very early universe," team member Kavya Shaji said.
That means that FRBs are emerging as a promising way to study the first stars and galaxies in the universe. This is even more exciting considering that this research validates teaming the JWST with radio telescopes to detect and track FRBs back to their points of origin.
"Our results further show the amazing capability of the JWST, where we can push boundaries beyond what was previously possible," team member Themiya Nanayakkara of the University of Sydney said.
Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.

articles.title_orig: Beijing Will Not Pace the Frontier: China’s Speed-First AI Safety Regime
articles.title_zh: Beijing Will Not Pace the Frontier: China’s Speed-First AI Safety Regime
articles.content_orig:
AI safety is on fire. On 12 September 2026, Dario Amodei published an essay arguing that frontier labs must deliberately slow the pace at which they improve model capabilities. China was central to his geopolitical argument: export controls and tighter security could preserve America’s lead, creating room to slow down and leverage for a future agreement with Beijing. Within a day, Sam Altman and Elon Musk supported Dario’s call. However, President Trump scoffed. On 14 September 2026, he wrote that fears of AI destroying humanity are “a HOAX” and that “the only one that is happy about it is China.”  Beijing scoffed too, with the state-run Global Times calling Dario’s essay a “Cold War playbook.”
The debate then moved onto the diplomatic calendar. On 20 September 2026, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Vice Premier He Lifeng held the first US-China AI dialogue. On 23 September 2026, President Xi Jinping began his state visit to the US. The Trump-Xi summit formalized the dialogue as the “US-China Super Intelligence Dialogue,” using the name Trump had unveiled at the UN the day before Xi arrived. The summit also promised a channel for AI incidents. On 29 September 2026, Trump and six executives signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, a one-page voluntary pledge to self-police that Trump called “morally binding.”
China sits on both sides of the American argument. For President Trump, competition with China is a reason not to slow down. For Dario, preserving America’s lead over China is what makes slowing down possible. Nobody has asked what China is actually doing. So, we did. What do the Chinese government, frontier labs, and AI experts say and do about AI safety? And what should American labs, investors, and policymakers conclude from it?
Beijing’s stated position is the most safety-forward of any major AI power outside Europe. Xi Jinping told the Politburo in April 2025 that AI brings “unprecedented risks and challenges” and ordered systems for technical monitoring, risk early-warning and emergency response. At the 2026 World AI Conference in Shanghai, Xi said the world must “ensure AI always remains under human control” and that the faster AI advances, “the more promptly the measures to prevent loss of control must be improved.” China signed the Bletchley Declaration and the Paris and New Delhi statements, co-sponsored the UN resolutions, founded a World AI Cooperation Organization in Shanghai, and publishes bilingual AI Safety Governance Frameworks.
The newest text goes further. The AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0, released by TC260 under Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) on 14 September 2026, warns that AI has shown a self-accelerating trend of autonomous learning and recursive self-improvement, and calls for “attention and vigilance” for potential AI evolution exceeding human prediction and control. The Framework 3.0 also introduces a new model-risk category, “behavior deviating from expectations,” covering models that acquire system privileges and external resources without authorization, bypass safety protections, deceive evaluators, hide their true capabilities, and refuse user instructions, illustrated with a boxed case study of models disabling shutdown scripts, sandbagging under evaluation, and breaking out of isolation into real systems. Its list of derivative risks goes further still; past behaviors already observed to a hypothetical AI that becomes self-aware, seeks power of its own, and competes with humanity for control. On paper, this is the most explicit official Chinese text yet on frontier risk, and its vocabulary overlaps strikingly with Dario’s essay Beijing denounced that same week.
However, we think China’s real approach to AI safety is speed-based, not safety-based. Though Beijing recognizes frontier AI risks, it has been prioritizing rapid development. The Framework 3.0 opens its principles with “promoting AI innovation and development as the first priority .” The comprehensive AI Law promised in the 2023 and 2024 legislative plans was shelved in 2025, four months after the DeepSeek moment. The State Council’s AI+ Action Plan targets 70% penetration of agents and intelligent terminals by 2027 and 90% by 2030, aiming for a rapid deployment of AI across all sectors and industries.
We think the Chinese government takes an open position on frontier models but tightens the applications and regulates outputs. Since 2025, China has issued a number of mandates, including mandatory content labeling (Sep 2025), Cybersecurity Law Article 20 (Jan 2026), the minors’ information classification rules (March 2026), MIIT’s AI ethics-review regime (March 2026), the policy-level agent rules (May 2026), the world’s first AI-companion rules (July 2026), the network-data risk assessment rules (August 2026), and MPS inspection powers (October 2026). Every one of these governs what AI says and what AI does to people. There is no set of frontier-risk duties triggered by training compute or model capability. The result is a safety regime stricter than any in the world on content and on process for public-facing services, and looser than the EU (systemic-risk duties from 10²⁵ FLOP) and California (SB 53: frontier frameworks and 15-day incident reporting from 10²⁶ operations) on the frontier.
The week Framework 3.0 came out shows the pattern in real time. Framework 3.0 added two new application-layer risk categories, agents and embodied intelligence, plus an appendix on managing agent risk. On 15 September, TC260 issued four AI application security guides, with a general one and three specific ones for education, health care and broadcasting, respectively. On 18 September it opened comments on a draft Agent System Development Security Guide (due 2 October) that walks developers through identity, least privilege, tool verification and human-approval nodes. The same day the CAC published a draft State Council regulation on minors’ internet use (comments due 17 October) that bars offering minors “virtual relatives, virtual companions and other virtual intimate-relationship services” and bars livestreaming under the age of 16. Seven texts in five days. Everyone is about how an agent or an application is built, deployed, and to whom it is offered. The gap at the frontier has not moved at all.
Compliance therefore tells us nothing about frontier safety. A Chinese lab can satisfy every rule on this list without ever running a dangerous-capability evaluation. Thus, to know what the labs do at the frontier, we must look at what they evaluate, what they disclose, and whether any of them change what they ship.
Nobody in China’s AI industry is slowing down, and nobody is asking them to. The frontier labs are in a release and price war.
We conduct a systematic analysis to clearly understand what Chinese labs do about safety. We constructed an original dataset that includes all identifiable model release by the 9 leading Chinese developers from 2021 to 15 September 2026. These 9 companies include 4 hyperscalers (ByteDance, Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu) and 5 startups (DeepSeek, MoonShot, Zhipu Z.ai, MiniMax, and StepFun). The dataset includes 857 counted releases (741 product models and 116 research models), each with a first-public date, weight status, license, and source. We then check each against the developer’s model cards, release notes, and technical reports for a published safety-evaluation result that can be matched to that release. Our standard is strict: a result means a quantitative or substantive finding on harmful output, jailbreaks, toxicity, privacy, refusal, or dangerous capability, tied to the named model. Statements that a model was “safety-trained” or “evaluated” do not count. A flagship model’s result is not extrapolated to other sizes or snapshots. “Not found” is bounded to the materials checked and does not mean “not tested.” Companies also name variants at different granularity (Alibaba’s 238 releases count every Qwen size

articles.title_orig: US 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate hits 7.40%, likely to further erode housing demand
articles.title_zh: US 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate hits 7.40%, likely to further erode housing demand
articles.content_orig:
Mortgage rates have hit their highest level in almost three years, making buying a home more challenging at a time when housing prices are already high. Nam Y. Huh/AP hide caption
Carrie Goldstein's dream for a new home started with a family reunion at her cousin's home in Milwaukee. The home was old with character and she could walk anywhere from the front door.
"We were kind of in awe and drooling over her walkability," Goldstein says.
It was the lifestyle Goldstein wanted but lacked in her Cleveland suburb, which she says is also pretty walkable – with one major issue.
"There are lots of sidewalks," she says. "But you can't really go anywhere."
She brainstormed with her husband and realized nearby Rocky River was where they wanted to live. It was still a suburb, but with a quaint downtown and the option to walk to Lake Erie.
But as much as she wanted to move, one thing stopped her cold. The mortgage she would have to pay. Mortgage rates have hit their highest level in almost three years, making buying a home impossible for many people at a time when housing prices are also sky high.
Goldstein is running into a problem that's affecting many households at a time when people have already been struggling with years of high inflation: The rising cost of borrowing.
Carrie Goldstein stands outside her home on October 4, 2026. Home prices and mortgage rates prevent her from moving. Mike Goldstein hide caption
Bond markets influence all types of borrowing costs across the economy – and as yields have surged to their highest in decades, they've pushed up all kinds of interest rates paid by consumers, from loans for homes to cars and higher education.
And those rates are likely to continue moving up after the Federal Reserve in September raised interest rates for the first time this year – while signaling an additional hike could come this year.
Rate hikes from the Federal Reserve filter through the economy and are meant to slow down consumer and business spending by making people hesitant to take out a more expensive loan to pay for a car or a home – both essential purchases for many people.
"If you need to borrow, boy, it's really not a good time," says John Diamond, senior director of the Center for Tax and Budget Policy at the Baker Institute.
Buying a home is a key example of how households are affected when borrowing costs rise in the economy.
While mortgage rates were falling at the start of this year, they reversed upward after the U.S. war with Iran spooked the bond market by raising worries about inflation. As a result, mortgage rates, which are influenced by the bond markets, have surged this year.
For example, at the current 7.28% level for the average 30-year fixed rate mortgage, a person could end up paying about $900 more a month compared with the 3% pandemic-era rates for a median priced home.
As expected, fewer homeowners are willing or capable of making that financial leap, even if they have long since outgrown their current home. Existing house sales in August were down about 1.2% from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors.
It's not just mortgage costs that are making Americans like Goldstein wince.
Alongside her dreams of owning a home in a walkable neighborhood, Goldstein is ready for a new car. Her old one is 11 years old, has 150,000 miles and plenty of quirks. The repair costs are approaching the point where they'll be more than the value of the actual car.
But a four-year loan for a used car is about three percentage points higher compared with the start of 2022, right around when auto loans began to shed their pandemic-era low rates and started climbing up.
"You can't go and get a car for $150 or $180 bucks anymore a month," she says about the car payments she would be facing.
Although so far the Fed has only delivered a modest quarter of a percentage point, it's adding to the higher borrowing costs at a time when households are already dealing with inflation and higher prices for other types of borrowing.
"It's added to higher mortgage payments. Higher student loan payments. Higher prices because of inflation," Diamond says. "That's what makes it really painful."
And that could mean that households could continue to delay any big purchases requiring a loan.
Goldstein is one of them. She says she can afford to wait on the car and house. But eventually she unsubscribed from real estate updates for that walkable suburb.
"It just became more and more disheartening when I did the math," Goldstein says. "It's just not in the cards."
