articles.title_orig: Thousands to march in Madrid after death of evicted pensioner Maricarmen
articles.title_zh: Thousands to march in Madrid after death of evicted pensioner Maricarmen
articles.content_orig:
Rally to remember woman, 87, whose rent battle with investment firm triggered nationwide protests over housing crisis
Thousands of people are expected to march through the centre of Madrid on Thursday evening in memory of María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her flat in the capital a fortnight before her death triggered mass protests over Spain’s housing crisis .
The pensioner, whose flat had been bought by an investment firm that sought to increase her rent by 230%, had become the public face of the crisis before her death in hospital on Wednesday night.
Abascal’s eviction unleashed waves of demonstrations across Spain, led to the setting up of a protest camp in the centre of the capital, and prompted the socialist-led government to propose emergency measures to try to make the rental market more equitable. When those measures were voted down by rightwing and far-right parties last week, the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, announced a snap general election , to be held on 29 November.
Anger over the plight of the woman who had become known around the country as Maricarmen remained undimmed a few hours after her death. On the pavement across from the apartment building where she had lived for seven decades, a steady stream of people visited a small, steadily growing memorial. Some came to light candles or leave flowers, while others left handwritten messages such as, “You made history Maricarmen,” and “Thank you for changing Spain”. Sara, 41, who had come with her young son and a sign that read, “Maricarmen, we’ll fight for you”, said: “We’re here because I think Maricarmen’s death shows how institutions can kill a person by failing to care for them.”
For many, the site was a reminder of all that Maricarmen had gone through as she tried to stay in her home, fending off three eviction attempts before the investment firm succeeded in forcing her out. “When people are protected less than investors, that leads to these kinds of things happening,” Sara added. “This woman could have died – if she had died of natural causes – she could have died peacefully in her home.”
Jaime, 34, pointed to all that Maricarmen had come to represent, particularly in a country like Spain, where social rights are supposedly guaranteed. “She had become a symbol, albeit one she never wanted to be, of the fight for decent housing,” he said. “So I came here because I think it’s important to restore some of the respect that Spanish society took away from Maricarmen.”
Visitors included some of the housing campaigners who had helped Maricarmen fight off previous eviction attempts. “This is really hard to take,” said Miguel, 59, fighting back tears as he added a red rose to the memorial. “When money is more powerful than people’s lives, it’s unbelievable.”
He said he hoped Maricarmen’s death would mark a turning point in Spain. “At least now we’re talking about this and putting names to those who are being evicted,” he said. “Because until now, there were 44 people a day being forced out of their homes. To the people in power, those are just numbers – now at least we’ve started putting names to those going through this.”
The Madrid tenants’ union announced a commemorative march at 8pm on Wednesday from the camp in the Puerta del Sol square to Abascal’s flat.
“Farewell, Maricarmen!” the union said in a post on social media . “Tonight we’ll honour you with a march … to the place that was your home for 70 years, and where you just wanted to stay until the end.”
Abascal’s ordeal has made housing a key issue in the forthcoming election, with Sánchez’s government seeking to push a redrafted package of measures through the council that operates when parliament has been dissolved. Meanwhile, the rightwing and far-right parties that opposed the legislation in congress last week have accused the prime minister of failing to act to address the housing crisis over the course of his eight years in office.
Sánchez offered his condolences to Abascal’s family and friends on Wednesday night. “A hug also to everyone who’s feeling this loss today as their own,” he wrote on social media. “Rest in peace.”
after newsletter promotion
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party (PP), which voted against last week’s emergency measures, also offered his condolences.
“No campaigning, no political parties, no partisan ends, no more bricks in the wall,” he wrote on social media. “When a person dies, there should be nothing but respect.”
The following day, however, Feijóo accused the government of trying to “manipulate the emotions of the Spanish people” by focusing on one particular eviction when there had been countless others during Sánchez’s time in office.
PP politicians also joined forces with the far right on Thursday to veto attempts to hold a minute’s silence for Maricarmen in Madrid’s regional parliament and the country’s senate. In Madrid’s municipal council, meanwhile, a rightwing attempt to block a minute’s silence was thwarted by opposition parties.
Abascal’s death has prompted reflection on how she had been treated by politicians and the media. The far-right Vox party, which also voted down the new decrees, had falsely suggested that Maricarmen would have had a home had she been an immigrant from North Africa , while one commentator had opined that “Maricarmen was chosen during a casting call for people facing eviction” to become a leftwing saint.
At least two far-right figures, including one of Vox’s MEPs, sought to sow doubt over the cause of Abascal’s death, with one even suggesting an autopsy should be carried out to determine whether the government had been involved . Another wrote : “Maricarmen was probably already made to send in her postal vote before they did her in. I expect anything from this scum.”

articles.title_orig: Report alleges Ambassador Guilfoyle improperly asked a donor to pay her credit card bill. Rubio refuses to comment
articles.title_zh: Report alleges Ambassador Guilfoyle improperly asked a donor to pay her credit card bill. Rubio refuses to comment
articles.content_orig:
Eric Deters says US ambassador to Greece asked him to pay off American Express credit card bill in return for access
A Trump donor accused Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece and Trump family ally, of engaging in a “quid pro quo” by asking him to pay off her $100,000 debt in exchange for access to administration officials.
Eric Deters, a former congressional candidate and lawyer, told MS Now on Thursday that Guilfoyle had “ambushed” him last year with an offer to provide access to government officials if he paid her American Express credit card bill, before her US Senate confirmation hearing as ambassador to Greece.
“It absolutely was a quid pro quo,” Deters told the network in response to a Wall Street Journal report that she had pushed him for the money.
“Kimberly Guilfoyle is a grifter,” he added.
The Guardian has asked Guilfoyle’s lawyer for comment.
Jesse Binnall, a lawyer for Guilfoyle, told the Wall Street Journal that Guilfoyle disputed the authenticity of the messages, but that she was “owed a balance” for travel and speaking at events before her nomination. Deters told the Journal that he did not owe Guilfoyle any balance.
The report is the latest allegation about Guilfoyle’s conduct as a US official. Deters shared messages he and Guilfoyle exchanged in which the US ambassador to Greece promised him “ride or die” access to Trump administration officials if he wired American Express $100,000.
Asked about the report during a press conference in Athens on Wednesday, Marco Rubio , the US secretary of state, said he would not address the allegations. He reaffirmed his support for the US embassy in Greece adding, “ Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.” Asked again about the reports on Thursday, Rubio refused to comment.
The top Democrats on the House foreign affairs and Senate foreign relations committees have asked Rubio to open an investigation into Guilfoyle’s conduct as an ambassador.
A spokesperson for the Democratic staff of the Senate foreign relations committee confirmed to the Guardian that they were requesting further information and continuing to investigate.
JD Vance similarly expressed hesitation, similar to Rubio, on Thursday when asked to respond to a US ambassador offering access to government officials in exchange for money to pay off debts.
“With that hypothetical, Jen, obviously I don’t love that,” the vice-president replied. “But I don’t know exactly who you’re talking about. I don’t know the full details. What I find with these stories is you never want to comment in a purely abstract way because a lot of times the details really matter,” he added.
Concerns about Guilfoyle’s conduct were first raised in September when the Wall Street Journal reported she had used her position to invite Greek lobbyists to sit in on official diplomatic meetings and promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company.
Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the ranking Democrat on the Senate foreign relations committee, sent a letter to Rubio on Tuesday , asking him to look into the allegations against Guilfoyle.
“Such actions do not serve US credibility overseas and risk undermining US diplomacy,” Shaheen wrote. “In advance of your upcoming travel to Greece , I request an immediate review of Ambassador Guilfoyle’s actions and a clarification of what steps have and will be taken to avoid undue influence and even the appearance of a conflict of interest.”
Separately, Gregory Meeks, the ranking Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee, sent a letter to Rubio in September, requesting more information about Guilfoyle’s conduct, her relationship with the Greek construction and energy company and her relationship with the lobbyist.
“If these reports are accurate, Ambassador Guilfoyle is unfit to represent the United States abroad and should be removed from her position,” Meeks wrote.
Guilfoyle, 57, was once a member of the Trump family’s inner circle, having been engaged to Donald Trump Jr, the US president’s eldest son, for roughly three years. The couple ended their engagement in 2024, and shortly after taking office, Donald Trump nominated Guilfoyle to be ambassador to Greece.
But now further allegations accuse Guilfoyle of promising a Trump donor, Eric Deters, access to the Trump administration in exchange for a $100,000 payment to American Express.
Deters shared messages exchanged between himself and Guilfoyle with the Wall Street Journal in which she reportedly pleaded: “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today.”
Deters said Guilfoyle had promised him thatshe would “be your Trump ride or die, forever and ever” if he made the American Express balance. Deters said he never made the payment.
In other messages, Guilfoyle reportedly raised concerns about her communications with Deters becoming public and reprimanded him for not being discreet. “Eric, I really wish you would stop papering all these things. It’s really dangerous and not helpful to you or me while you could simply just call me on Signal,” she is said to have written in one message.
“What a nightmare, you’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship stop writing,” Guilfoyle reportedly wrote in another message.
A lawyer for Guilfoyle disputed the authenticity of messages Deters shared with the Wall Street Journal.
It is unclear whether Shaheen or Meeks will ask Rubio for further information about the latest report. The Guardian has asked Meeks and Shaheen for comment.

articles.title_orig: Google Cloud introduces Gemini agent for work as AI race heats up
articles.title_zh: Google Cloud introduces Gemini agent for work as AI race heats up
articles.content_orig:
Google on Thursday unveiled a new AI agent tailored for workplace tasks, positioning it to compete with other technology giants racing to offer their own virtual office assistants.
Called Gemini, the AI is a "universal agent" that can write and run code, create images and media and integrate with Google products like Gmail, Docs, Drive and Sheets, as well as third-party apps like Slack and Microsoft 365, Google said in its statement .
Thomas Kurian, the CEO of Google Cloud, shared the new product during a keynote address at Gemini at Work 2026 on Thursday, an annual event where Google showcases its suite of AI technology.
Google said the agent can seamlessly integrate into people's workflow, acting like a co-worker that can carry out tasks autonomously. Workers can delegate tasks to the agent, and it will return a finished product, Kurian said in the company's blog post.
"Gemini can function as your personal assistant or as a team member, where it works on behalf of a group of people, like a project manager within a team, or on behalf of a specific role in an organization, like an analyst in your finance department," he wrote.
To execute on certain tasks, Gemini can create its own "sub-agents," which Google described as "temporary, job-specific agents, each with their own identity," that can work together to accomplish goals over several days.
The AI agent, which runs in the Cloud, is designed to build memory and skills based on the tasks it's assigned and the questions users ask it.
"You never have to re-brief it or wonder which machine you told it to do something on," Kurian wrote in the blog post.
Gemini joins a growing field of AI agents marketed for personal and workplace use. In September, Meta introduced Muse , a personal AI assistant that has been downloaded millions of times. OpenAI followed suit late last month with the introduction of "Dots" , an "AI helper" available to ChatGPT users with Pro and Business Premium accounts.

articles.title_orig: ‘I just want to hold him’: USS Lincoln sailor to meet his 10-month-old son as ship docks
articles.title_zh: ‘I just want to hold him’: USS Lincoln sailor to meet his 10-month-old son as ship docks
articles.content_orig:
After more than 300 days at sea, the USS Abraham Lincoln is finally come back home to San Diego. NBC 7’s Dana Williams reports.
Among the thousands of family members awaiting to greet their loved ones as they step off the USS Abraham Lincoln will be 10-month-old Nathan, who is meeting his father for the first time.
Brent Ledbetter is an air traffic control center officer aboard the aircraft carrier. His son was born in November, about a week after Ledbetter reported to the ship, NBC News reported.
Stream San Diego News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC 7.
"I just want to hold him, play with him,” Ledbetter told NBC News. “He’s crawling around now, so I’m excited to chase him around the house and give him all the love that, that, you know — have been kind of withheld for the last 10 months. I’m so excited."
Ledbetter told NBC News his wife is also an air traffic control officer and had been assigned to the Lincoln. He replaced her on the ship shortly before she gave birth.
Among the roughly 5,000 sailors and Marines onboard the Lincoln, there are more than 50 babies waiting for a parent’s return on Thursday when the ship docks at Naval Air Station North Island.
What began as a Pacific deployment with a spring return soon shifted to a prolonged stay at sea as the carrier was diverted to Middle East to support the U.S. and Israel's war with Iran. Over the next several months, the crew would endure deployment extensions, supply shortages and deteriorating mental health.
Now, after nearly a year at sea, the beleaguered Lincoln is almost home and crewmembers who are parents will be among the first allowed off the ship.

articles.title_orig: Ex-prince Andrew search warrants quashed after police accept legal error
articles.title_zh: Ex-prince Andrew search warrants quashed after police accept legal error
articles.content_orig:
Thames Valley Police has accepted warrants it used to search Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's homes at the time of his arrest in February were unlawful, the High Court has been told.
Following Thursday's hearing, items seized in the raid continue to be held by the police, with a further hearing to take place in 2027 to decide whether the material can be used as evidence.
Meanwhile, the criminal investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor is ongoing.
The former prince, who denies any wrongdoing, was arrested by police on 19 February on suspicion of misconduct in public office, after which he launched a legal challenge over the legality of the search warrants.
The force said it accepted that the "initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect" before they searched the properties.
On Thursday at the High Court, judge Mr Justice Hilliard said Mountbatten-Windsor and the police had agreed that the search warrants had been unlawful.
However, he added: "The fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring the investigation to an end or mean that the whole of the investigation is unlawful."
Mountbatten-Windsor opposes the police's bid to retain the evidence, the judge said, and another hearing is expected in 2027.
His lawyers have used a judicial review to challenge the actions of the force's chief constable and the Central Criminal Court in the build-up to his arrest.
His arrest arose after the US Department of Justice published documents which raised suspicions he had forwarded confidential information to the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein when Mountbatten-Windsor was a UK trade envoy in 2010.
He has consistently denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein.
The court heard on Thursday that Thames Valley Police seized documents and electronic devices when they raided Mountbatten-Windsor's homes earlier this year.
Thames Valley Police's position was that they had applied for search warrants under section eight and nine of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 at a hearing at the Central Criminal Court the day before the search.
That court determined that only section eight search warrants were needed and they were granted on that basis - but subsequently, a legal challenge has established that the court should have issued them under the section nine.
The judge explained on Thursday why the police could keep hold of the former prince's items that had been seized.
He said: "There would be little point in handing property back if it could then simply be lawfully seized under some other provision."
A Thames Valley Police spokesperson said: "The agreement that led to the quashing of the warrants relates specifically to a decision made by the court regarding the legal basis for these and is not a judgement on our ongoing investigation.
"We ensured the court was presented with all the necessary information and paperwork to inform their decision, following the correct legal processes throughout.
"We accept the position that the initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect and therefore these must be legally quashed.
"Legal proceedings are currently ongoing to decide how material seized during the searches will be managed and whether we can lawfully retain it in support of our ongoing investigation."
The force said its "investigation into alleged misconduct in public office by a man in his 60s from Norfolk remains ongoing, and we continue to pursue all reasonable lines of enquiry to effectively and fairly progress this investigation".
The next stage in this legal dispute will be a behind-closed-doors hearing over whether the police can still retain material seized from Mountbatten-Windsor's homes under alternative powers designed for situations like this.
The error that has led to Thames Valley Police accepting the search warrants were unlawful relates to the particular power the judge permitted the force to use when its officers raided the properties.
Strict legal safeguards on searches bar the police from automatically seizing sensitive material without thinking through in advance the need to take it.
Examples of that material include advice from a suspect's lawyer or material which does not really belong to them, such as copies of confidential work-related papers from an employer.
In practice, if the police find such material during a search, they should return it rather than use it in their investigation.
The category of search warrant that was granted by the court in this instance did not take into account the possibility of such protected material being seized.
However, the law says police can in fact seize that kind of material - or potentially retain it in the event of an error - providing they pass some extra tests.
Thames Valley Police must now convince a judge that the material is likely to be of "substantial value" to their investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor and, ultimately, potential evidence to present to a court.
So while the force has conceded the search warrant was unlawful, a judge will have to decide whether this alternative search power, with its extra safeguards, justifies them keeping and using the material after all.

articles.title_orig: Amazon’s new Alexa Tablets are an iPad-inspired reboot, complete with the Play Store
articles.title_zh: Amazon’s new Alexa Tablets are an iPad-inspired reboot, complete with the Play Store
articles.content_orig:
Amazon has an all-new lineup of tablets ready to tempt you this holiday season, and for once, you might actually want to buy them. While the company has tried in previous years to make an upmarket play for relevancy in the tablet space, these new Alexa Tablets — RIP “Fire” — have the one thing everyone’s wanted for years: actual Play Store support.
Yes, a decade after ditching the “Kindle” branding in its tablet lineup, Amazon is ditching the Fire brand entirely for its new lineup of iPad competitors. That’s not me trying to write off its Android-powered rivals; rather, the sizes and designs all make for devices that, frankly, look like iPad knock-offs. Alexa Tablets come in three sizes: an 8-inch entry-level iPad Mini competitor, an 11-inch base iPad-esque slate, and a 12-inch “Pro” model that looks to be the most unique of the bunch. They’re all designed with aluminum bodies and, despite being much more expensive than the Fire tablets they’re replacing, still manage to undercut most of the market.
The 8.7-inch 60Hz Alexa Tablet 8 features 4GB of RAM, up to 128GB of storage, and comes in graphite, rosette, and teal, while the 90Hz 11-inch Alexa Tablet 11 features 8GB of RAM, up to 128GB of storage, and adds matcha and amethyst to the mix. Both run on a MediaTek 8189 8-core processor, a relatively recent chipset that appeared in a handful of seemingly-unreleased ChromeOS devices over the past year or so, before landing in these budget tablets. While I wouldn’t say there’s much to write home here about the specs — and again, the design is just absolutely a blatant copy of the iPad — it certainly sounds like a big upgrade over their predecessors.
And really, that comes down to the software. Despite Amazon’s current Android-less strategy on its Fire TV devices , the company seems to be doubling down on Android with its tablets. While it does have a unique launcher designed to push Alexa+, these things run proper Android, complete with the Play Store front and center on the device. YouTube is one of the highlighted apps on their store listings, and as someone who maintained Play Store sideloading guides at two different tech websites over the past decade, I can certainly say I never saw it coming. I have no idea how the actual software experience will feel day-to-day, but in terms of app support, it’s one problem that’s finally solved.
The star of the show, of course, is the 12-inch Alexa Tablet 12 Pro . This is, bar none, the most premium tablet Amazon has ever shipped, with a price that matches. It combines a 2.8K 3:2 120Hz display with quad speakers, 8GB of RAM, 128GB of storage, and a MediaTek Dimensity 8400 processor. That’s a real processor, and while I wouldn’t say it’s worthy of being called a flagship chipset, it’s undoubtedly the most powerful chip Amazon’s ever used. It’s a good sign when you’re using the same processor that a budget gaming-focused brand like Poco used just a year or two ago.
The 12-inch model also comes in an optional “nanomatte” version for an anti-glare experience, which also allows you to upgrade your RAM and storage to 16GB and 256GB, respectively. 16GB of RAM in an Amazon tablet — it’s a new day after all. And like its last attempt to go full-premium, the company does offer optional stylus and keyboard accessories for road warriors on a budget.
The Alexa Tablet 8 starts at $230 for the base 64GB model with lockscreen ads, or $250 without, while the Alexa Tablet 11 starts at $330 for its base model, or $350 for the ad-free version. Both feature a 128GB upgrade for $50 more. The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro starts at $500 for the base 128GB model; the nanomatte upgrade will run you $50 more. Meanwhile, that high-end 16/256 variant costs a whopping $680, and while that might sound pretty expensive on paper, it comes in well under Samsung’s latest 12-inch tablet for anyone who doesn’t need that level of processing power. Oh, and absolutely no ads on any of the 12 Pro models — the price you see is the price you pay, no upgrades necessary.

articles.title_orig: Psychedelic Paintings by Rafael Silveira Explore a World of ‘Visual Synonymies’
articles.title_zh: Psychedelic Paintings by Rafael Silveira Explore a World of ‘Visual Synonymies’
articles.content_orig:
Flowers for eyes, a horizon for a mouth… a popsicle for a holy relic? Rafael Silveira has long been interested in what he describes as “visual synonymies,” which he likens to “formal correspondences between seemingly unrelated things, moments in which one image unexpectedly recognizes itself in another.” The Brazilian artist’s surreal paintings replace facial features with landforms, flora, and fauna, sometimes hybridizing animals, figures, and other objects.
The works seen here were recently included in the artist’s solo exhibition Popsicledelic Trip at KP Projects Gallery in Los Angeles alongside a show by Silveira’s wife, the artist Flávia Itiberê . A series of vertical pieces with ornate, hand-carved wooden frames resemble the silhouette of popsicles, while figures hold giant versions of the frozen treats in a stylistic nod to religious art during the Renaissance .
The popsicle may seem like a quirky, even out-of-place reference within the context of these works, but for Silveira, the objects represent the broader idea that everything in the universe is connected. No matter how absurd it may seem at first glance—a man with a tree for a head or ice cream cones floating planet-like in a starry sky—the point is that they all really do exist simultaneously. Silveira juxtaposes objects and organisms in unlikely scenarios to challenge how we perceive the world around us and how even the same shape can have completely different associations.
One compositional form in particular, the tavola centinata , describes the shape of a canvas or relief with a squared base and rounded top. A feature commonly found in Gothic and early Renaissance paintings, it has the same silhouette as a classic popsicle. In a statement, Silveira says:
The connection is at once surprising and inevitable. One belongs to the sacred history of painting; the other to the realm of the ephemeral, the popular, the sweet, the melting. Bringing them together creates a bridge between devotional form and unstable matter, between permanence and disappearance, between the spiritual weight of the altarpiece and the fragile delight of something destined to dissolve.

articles.title_orig: Odyssey Launches Odyssey-3, Its Most Powerful Foundation World Model Built to Power AI Across the Physical World
articles.title_zh: Odyssey Launches Odyssey-3, Its Most Powerful Foundation World Model Built to Power AI Across the Physical World
articles.content_orig:
Odyssey Launches Odyssey-3, Its Most Powerful Foundation World Model Built to Power AI Across the Physical World
New model demonstrates a shared understanding of the world across robots, humanoids, vehicles, drones, AI agents, and video games
Odyssey , an AI research company pioneering foundation world models, today announced Odyssey-3, its most powerful world model to date. The new model represents a significant advance toward general-purpose intelligence that can understand, predict, and interact with both physical and virtual environments.
This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261008756684/en/
Caption: Odyssey’s latest world model powering Flexion’s robot. Credit: Odyssey
World models learn from vast examples of the world evolving to predict and simulate what happens next, including how actions affect outcomes. Odyssey-3 gives intelligent systems a general understanding of how the world works before they are taught a specific task. The model has shown the ability to control robots and humanoids, drive vehicles, pilot drones, generate environments for training AI agents, and play video games. The new model has already been adopted by companies including Flexion, a leader in humanoid autonomy.
Trained on a vast dataset of visual observations of the world, Odyssey-3 builds on world models the company has been developing over the past three years. It has learned representations of physics, dynamics, cause and effect, and human behavior that can be applied across physical and virtual systems.
Using this pretrained foundation, Odyssey-3 enables physical agents: intelligent systems that can apply a shared understanding of the world across different machines, environments, and tasks. Rather than learning every new task entirely from scratch, these systems can draw on a broader model of how the world works and adapt that knowledge to new situations with relatively little additional experience.
“Odyssey-3 is a big step toward a single intelligence that can understand and operate in the world around us,” said Oliver Cameron, co-founder and CEO of Odyssey . “World models give physical agents a foundation of knowledge they can carry from one machine, environment, or task to another. We believe that the ability to learn broadly and then adapt with relatively little experience is the path toward increasingly general physical intelligence.”
The company has demonstrated Odyssey-3 across six domains:
Odyssey-3 is designed as a foundation that can span these domains rather than a model optimized for a single machine or application. By learning common representations of how environments behave and how actions change them, Odyssey is working toward world models that can transfer knowledge across increasingly diverse physical and virtual systems.
Odyssey is an AI lab pioneering general world models: causal, multimodal systems that learn to predict and interact with the world over long horizons. This foundational technology promises to revolutionize robotics, science, healthcare, education, gaming, defense, and beyond.
Odyssey’s founders previously pioneered one of the most complex applications of physical AI: self-driving cars. They’ve since brought together a world-class research team from DeepMind, Tesla, Waymo, Meta, Apple, and Wayve, whose members have contributed to language models, video models, world models and autonomous systems, including DeepMind Gemini, DeepMind Veo, Wayve GAIA and Tesla FSD.

articles.title_orig: World Sight Day: Restoring sight where cataract surgery is scarce
articles.title_zh: World Sight Day: Restoring sight where cataract surgery is scarce
articles.content_orig:
Lloyd Williams, MD, PhD, discusses rising cataract blindness and low-cost surgery in conflict zones for World Sight Day.
Cataract remains a leading cause of vision impairment and blindness worldwide. At least 2.2 billion people have a near or distance vision impairment, and in at least 1 billion of those cases, the impairment could have been prevented or has yet to be addressed, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Cataract accounts for 94 million of those cases, and 1 in 2 people who need cataract surgery do not have access to it.¹
World Sight Day is an annual day of awareness held on the second Thursday of October and coordinated by the International Agency for the Prevention of Blindness (IAPB). This year, it falls on October 8. The 2026 #LoveYourEyes campaign centers on personal stories, lived experiences, and community action ahead of the first Global Summit for Eye Health on November 2 in Antigua and Barbuda.²
To mark the occasion, Lloyd Williams, MD, PhD , director of Duke Global Ophthalmology at Duke Eye Center in Durham, North Carolina, spoke with Ophthalmology Times about why cataract blindness continues to rise and how teams deliver high-quality surgery in low-resource settings. Williams received the American Academy of Ophthalmology's 2025 Outstanding Humanitarian Service Award for expanding access to cataract and corneal surgery in underserved regions.
Williams attributed the increase to aging populations in regions where ophthalmic care has not expanded, compounded by conflict and poverty that make many areas harder to reach. He cited a recent cataract camp in South Sudan.
"We literally had to negotiate a ceasefire in order to do cataract surgery," Williams told Ophthalmology Times .
Williams highlighted several organizations working to expand access to eye care. Readers can donate or get involved through the following: • Duke Global Ophthalmology: Give to Duke GO .³ • Cure Blindness Project: Donate ; ophthalmologists and practices can also join its Global Partners Program.⁴ • IAPB: Individuals can become a Love Your Eyes Visionary , and organizations can apply for membership .⁵ • CBM (Christian Blind Mission): Donate .⁶ • Sightsavers: Donate or fundraise through Sightsavers USA.⁷
On a recent trip to Abyei, surgery cost approximately $70 per case using manual small incision cataract surgery (MSICS), which requires a microscope as the only electrical equipment. In skilled hands, Williams said, MSICS achieves results roughly equivalent to those in the US. A $700,000 donation this year is expected to fund approximately 9000 surgeries, a volume he said would not be possible with phacoemulsification or laser-based approaches.
"I strongly believe that we're not providing somebody substandard care," Williams said.
Williams also addressed studies linking cataract surgery to lower rates of dementia diagnosis, which cannot yet establish cause and effect. He recalled veterans whose anxiety and depression appeared to improve after surgery during his residency, and he said he discusses the cognitive benefits of sight with families of older patients. Reflecting on his own vision problem as a resident, he described sight as "something that you could lose just like your arm."

articles.title_orig: New GETI publication explores future of Christian unity
articles.title_zh: New GETI publication explores future of Christian unity
articles.content_orig:
A new publication from the World Council of Churches (WCC) Commission on Ecumenical Education and Formation (EEF) brings together the voices and theological reflections of young ecumenists from around the world who attended the 2025 edition of the WCC Global Ecumenical Theological Institute (GETI). It brings fresh inputs to the pressing question for the churches today: Where now for visible unity?
From left: Rev. Prof. Dr Meehyun Chung, moderator of the WCC Commission on Ecumenical Education and Formation; Prof. Dr Ani Ghazaryan Drissi, WCC programme executive for Ecumenical Theological Education and coordinator of GETI 2025; Rev. Dr Nathan Digby, GETI 2025 facilitator and member of the WCC Commission on Ecumenical Education and Formation; during the launch event of the GETI 2025 book on 8 October.
“ GETI 2025: Voices and Visions of Transformative Unity,” edited by Prof. Dr Ani Ghazaryan Drissi and Rev. Prof. Teddy Chalwe Sakupapa, emerges from the WCC ’ s 4th GETI, held in the context of the Sixth World Conference on Faith and Order in Wadi El Natrun, Egypt. The publication, launched on 8 October, during the biannual meeting of the EEF Commission, comes at a significant moment.
“ The fruits of ecumenical dialogue must take root in the lives of our churches,” said Ghazaryan. “ The GETI 2025 message brought this bold challenge to the Sixth World Conference on Faith and Order and the wider ecumenical movement: let the unity we confess become the life we share.”
This publication carries that call forward, she added, through voices and visions rooted in different churches, cultures, and lived realities. “ Their theological reflections invite us to ask how the fruits of ecumenical dialogue can shape our communities, deepen our relationships, and renew our common witness,” said Ghazaryan. “ They call us to listen more deeply, confront exclusion, and share responsibility for the future of our churches.”
Bossey students who took part of GETI 2025 shared their testimonies during the launch event.
The volume presents a global and contextually grounded exploration of Christian unity. Its contributors reflect on reception, Nicaea, pilgrimage, trust and companionship, while also addressing colonial wounds, trauma, migration, ethnic violence, Palestine, digital ecumenism, and ecological crisis.
Rather than treating unity as an abstract theological ideal, the book emphasizes unity as something that must be embodied through relationships, truth-telling, healing, solidarity, and public witness. Its concluding message describes young ecumenists as contributors to the present and future of the ecumenical movement.
GETI 2025 facilitator and EEF commissioner Rev. Dr Nathan Digby explained that a central goal of the WCC ’ s Ecumenical Theological Education work is to provide opportunities for emerging ecumenical leaders to be formed in ecumenism and to ensure that their voices are heard, encouraged, and shared with the wider church.
“ The publication of GETI 2025: Voices and Visions for Transformative Unity gives concrete expression to this commitment,” he said. “ As part of their theological formation, students participating in GETI 2025 developed academic papers exploring the theme of visible Christian unity in relation to their own theological interests, contexts, and experiences.”
This volume recognizes and celebrates their intellectual and theological work while creating a platform through which their perspectives can contribute to broader conversations about the future of Christian unity, added Digby.
“ By bringing these emerging voices together in one publication, GETI 2025: Voices and Visions for Transformative Unity not only documents an important dimension of the GETI experience but also invests in the next generation of ecumenical thinkers and leaders, whose insights and visions are essential for shaping a more transformative and visible unity among Christians.”
Published by WCC Publications, the book offers churches, theological institutions, students, and ecumenical partners a rich resource for reflection and conversation on the future of Christian unity.
The session also included the presentation of the GETI Visual Report and a short video featuring voices and moments of GETI 2025.
The EEF Commission is meeting at the WCC Ecumenical Institute at Bossey 4-9 October.

articles.title_orig: Iran strikes tankers outside Hormuz in signs of expanding campaign
articles.title_zh: Iran strikes tankers outside Hormuz in signs of expanding campaign
articles.content_orig:
Iran's armed forces struck two commercial tankers outside the Strait of Hormuz within 24 hours this week, in what appeared to be a deliberate expansion of attacks beyond the strait, as Iranian officials issued a fresh wave of warnings against the United States.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said several projectiles hit the oil and chemical tanker Acers, flagged in Antigua and Barbuda, 51 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal in Qatar on Wednesday. Casualties were reported.
Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard identified the vessel and said it was heading toward the Strait of Hormuz.
It was the first attack in that area in more than six months.
In a separate incident on Thursday, Vanguard reported a fire on a tanker some 40 kilometres off Fujairah in the Gulf of Oman, which it identified as likely the Marshall Islands-flagged Dhalgout.
The UKMTO had not recorded the incident, and the cause of the fire was not immediately clear. NASA's FIRMS fire-detection system confirmed the blaze, and US military aircraft — including two KC-46 tankers, a KC-135, a P-8A maritime patrol aircraft and several helicopters — were over the area at the time.
Iran and media affiliated with the IRGC did not officially claim responsibility for either attack. IRGC-affiliated outlets implicitly suggested that Tehran had "extended the scope of its operations against commercial vessels that violate Iranian laws and regulations in the Strait of Hormuz to waters beyond the strait."
Both incidents fall outside the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of global oil and gas shipments normally pass. The strait has been effectively closed since the war began in late February, after Iran and the US imposed concurrent naval blockades.
"The distance between you and us is determined by our missiles," Acting Defence Minister Majid Ebn ol-Reza posted on X on Thursday.
"Yesterday the Gulf of Oman, today the Indian Ocean and tomorrow the Bay of Pigs. If you make a mistake, you will see a new set of dividing lines.," ol-Reza added in an apparent reference to a failed, US-backed military landing on the southwestern coast of Cuba from April 1961 aimed at overthrowing the communist government of Fidel Castro.
Yahya Rahim Safavi, a senior military adviser to Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, had earlier warned that if the US or Israel attacked Iran again, Tehran could extend the war "as far as the Indian Ocean or other places," adding that Iranian forces had prepared contingency plans for worst-case scenarios.
Ebn ol-Reza was appointed acting minister after Aziz Nasirzadeh, Iran's then defence minister, was killed on 28 February — the first day of the war — alongside several other military commanders. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has nominated Mehrdad Akhlaqi as a permanent replacement, and parliament is due to hold a confidence vote on 18 October.
Iran's army spokesman said separately that its forces were ready to carry out pre-emptive operations, if necessary, to prevent what he described as "any aggression or attack by the enemy."
At a midterm election campaign rally in Nebraska, US President Donald Trump defended the decision to go to war with Iran. "This is a small price to pay for keeping the world and our country safe. They can destroy a city. Let them destroy it. Let them destroy Los Angeles, let them destroy San Diego," he said.
At a separate rally in Texas on Wednesday night, Trump walked back those remarks after criticism. "We protect our own cities. We will not allow such a thing to happen," he said.
US President Donald Trump defended the launch of war against Iran at a midterm election campaign rally in Nebraska, stating that "this is a small price to pay for keeping the world and our country safe."
"They can destroy a city. Let them destroy it. Let them destroy Los Angeles, let them destroy San Diego," Trump said.
However, in another speech in Texas on Wednesday night Trump responded to criticism of his controversial remarks two days earlier about a possible Iranian attack on Los Angeles and San Diego.
"We protect our own cities. We will not allow such a thing to happen," he said.

articles.title_orig: A Rare Image of Mars at Dawn Reveals the Beauty of Its Ancient Cliffs
articles.title_zh: A Rare Image of Mars at Dawn Reveals the Beauty of Its Ancient Cliffs
articles.content_orig:
The captivating shapes of wind-carved crags called yardangs are revealed in this zoomed-in crop of a broader panorama captured by NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover on Aug. 11, 2026. Scientists are eager to learn more about how the yardang layer formed.
Sunlight illuminates wind-carved cliffs in a dramatic new image.
A newly released panorama captured by NASA’s Curiosity rover offers the most detailed view yet of distant, wind-carved Martian cliffs, highlighting features the mission’s scientists have long been waiting to see up close. The scene was snapped at 8:30 a.m. local Mars time, showing striking blue hues in the foreground as bright morning light illuminates crags known as yardangs on the horizon.
The panorama was captured by Curiosity’s Mastcam on Aug. 11, the 4,982nd Martian day, or sol, of the mission, and comprises six individual images that were stitched together after being sent to Earth. Unlike most of Curiosity’s Mastcam images, this one was processed without white balancing, preserving the early morning appearance.
The six shots that make up this panorama, captured by NASA’s Curiosity on Aug. 11, were stitched together after being sent back to Earth. Unlike most images from the rover’s Mastcam, this one was processed without the usual white balancing — an artistic choice that preserves the early morning appearance.
The yardang layer extends roughly 10 miles (16 kilometers) across the northwestern reaches of Mount Sharp, a 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain that Curiosity has been ascending since 2014. In fact, the rover recently passed another milestone in its ascent, reaching 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) of elevation — the most ever climbed on Mars. As it draws ever-closer to the yardangs, mission scientists expect to get even more amazing imagery — and, they hope, answers to how these cliffs were created.
Mount Sharp is made up of layers, each recording a distinct period of Mars’ history. By studying them, scientists have been able to learn more about lakes and streams that covered this part of the Red Planet billions of years ago. Eventually, the water dried up and left salty minerals behind. After new material stopped settling on the mountain, some of it may have been stripped away by wind, giving rise to the yardangs.
This artist’s concept shows Mount Sharp, the 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain that NASA’s Curiosity has been ascending since 2014. The location of the yardang layer, which the rover recently captured from a distance, is indicated by an ellipse annotation on the mountain’s northwestern shoulder.
NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover captured this view looking back at the floor of Gale Crater on Sept. 5, 2026. Just nine days prior, the rover had marked 1 kilometer of elevation gain above the crater floor since beginning its ascent of Mount Sharp in 2014.
“The yardang layer looks out of place. It’s the wrong color, the layers tilt at an odd angle, and it almost appears plastered on,” said Ashwin Vasavada, Curiosity project scientist of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “But that’s what makes it exciting to reach. No one is sure exactly what created this layer, but one idea is it may be ash deposited by ancient volcanic eruptions.”
Curiosity is in the second year of its fifth extended mission, which started with an exploration of the spiderweb-like boxwork ridges . The rover will spend most of the next year or so driving through layers enriched with sulfates and carbonates, both signs of ancient drying on the surface. Sometime in 2027, scientists hope to reach the base of the yardangs, where Curiosity will be able to use its robotic arm to collect one-of-a-kind data on these mysterious features.
From Mars to the Milky Way — never miss a discovery! Delivered straight to your inbox.
Curiosity was built by NASA JPL, which is managed by Caltech in Pasadena, California. NASA JPL leads the mission on behalf of the agency’s Science Mission Directorate in Washington as part of its Mars Exploration Program portfolio. Malin Space Science Systems in San Diego built and operates Mastcam.

articles.title_orig: Amoris laetitia: Pastoral experiences in Asia and challenges of digital world
articles.title_zh: Amoris laetitia: Pastoral experiences in Asia and challenges of digital world
articles.content_orig:
Families today are âa challenging mosaic of diverse realities, marked by joys, hopes, struggles and wounds. The family is not only a place to which the Church brings the Gospel. It is also a place from which the Gospel comes alive â from one generation to another, from one family to another, and from families to society.â
Cardinal Filipe Neri Ferrão, Metropolitan Archbishop of Goa and Daman, opened his address with this reflection at the start of the second day of Pope Leo XIVâs meeting with the heads of the Eastern Churches and the presidents of the Bishopsâ Conferences, ten years after Amoris laetitia .
The Indian Cardinal addressed the theme âFamilies today: reality, beauty and challenges. Discerning the signs of the times through the experience of families and the Churchâs pastoral commitment today.â
He invited participants in the meeting, conducted in a synodal style, to ask themselves in their discernment: âWhat is the Holy Spirit asking the Church to change?â
This concerned ânot only in what we do for the families, but in how we understand, accompany and empower them as protagonists of the Gospel and as enduring loci of Godâs revelation.â
Drawing on his experience as a pastor in Asia, particularly in India, Cardinal Neri Ferrão acknowledged that families had changed in their identity, nature, and composition, with smaller households, new forms of cohabitation, and interreligious marriages.
Families were increasingly on the move, and many faced economic insecurity, poverty, unemployment, and uncertainty about the future.
âChristian families in many parts of India and Asia,â the Cardinal stressed, âmust also live amid growing religious polarisation and hostility, making the public expression and transmission of faith increasingly difficult.â
Yet, these families also offered the Church beauty through their care for children, the elderly, the sick, and vulnerable people. Even amid poverty and uncertainty, the Cardinal explained, âour families continue to create positive spaces for joy and hope.â
Following the publication of Amoris laetitia , he recalled, the Churches in India and across Asia âlistened first to families,â and that listening âshaped how we walk with them. We now see marriage preparation as the start of a lifelong journey, offer spiritual renewal and counselling to couples and children, and keep forming families and lay leaders over time.â
He stressed that pastoral ministry needed to move âfrom mission to families to mission among families.â Families were not simply recipients of assistance but, in his words, âthe Church's partners in mission.â
Cardinal Neri Ferrão concluded by recounting the experience of a priest who had begun family ministry in his parish not with a program, but by visiting a family experiencing underlying difficulties in communication between the parents and between them and their children. It had begun with âa conversation and a willingness to listen.â
The second speaker, Vincenzo Rosito, Professor of the History and Culture of Family Institutions at the Pontifical Lateran University and Vice Dean of the Pontifical John Paul II Theological Institute for Marriage and Family Sciences, summed up his address with questions to guide participantsâ synodal discernment.
He began with an invitation inspired by Pope Leo XIVâs reflections in the encyclical Magnifica humanitas : âLet each of us be mindful of the relationships we build within our own families and within the Church.â
Professor Rosito stressed that âfamily practices, in fact, help us to understand how churches and families learn from one another. Both the Church and the family, in fact, learn through the practices of their daily lives.â
He then offered a question for participants to consider as a father, mother, theologian, or pastor: âAm I able to recognise and share with others at least one new thing that I have learnt to do, or to do differently, in recent years of my family or pastoral life?â
Changes in family life, Prof. Rosito explained, âare not problemsâ but âhuman activities.â Recalling Amoris laetitia , he presented them as an opportunity, as concrete processes âin which individuals and families act, react, learn and develop new resources.â
âConsider, for example,â the political philosopher continued, âhow the use of new digital technologies is transforming the daily habits of families and the way children are brought up.â
The family and the Church, Prof. Rosito continued, âlearn together through change.â He drew on the Gospel image of Jesus, Joseph, and Maryâs flight into Egypt.
He noted that today, âdrawing on the experiences of refugee and migrant families, some Christian communities are re-establishing themselves as ârefuge churchesââ for those arriving in a new land or making a long journey.
He also addressed the tragedy of violence shared by many families: âThe insecurity stemming from social and political violence is a worrying reality that many Churches must deal with today, in their daily lives.â Such insecurity, he warned, could âeven devour family bonds and church relationships themselves.â
Josephâs dream was also part of the experience of this flight.
âTo dream, to imagine new forms for the Church,â Prof. Rosito concluded, âalso means renewing what we already do. To imagine the Church means being willing to learn from one another, whilst we are transformed together, as churches and as families.â
His final question for discernment was therefore: âWhat do we need, amidst the light and shadow of today, to learn and imagine new ways of being a family and new ways of being the Church?â

articles.title_orig: Amazon launches first Android tablets, raising prices and incorporating Alexa
articles.title_zh: Amazon launches first Android tablets, raising prices and incorporating Alexa
articles.content_orig:
Amazon on Thursday debuted a set of new, pricier Alexa tablets and said it's ditching its budget-friendly Fire lineup, marking a significant shift in the e-commerce juggernaut's devices strategy.
The company unveiled 8-inch, 11-inch and 12-inch models, which start at $230 and run up to $550. All devices are available for preorder on Thursday and will begin shipping Oct. 14.
Amazon has historically sold its devices at or near the cost of manufacturing them, partly to undercut competitors with extremely cheap prices, but also with the goal of promoting its other products and services. It's hoped that for every $80 Echo smart speaker it sells, users will purchase movies, audiobook subscriptions or items from its sprawling webstore, which tend to have higher margins.
The company has recently taken steps to make more money from its devices business under CEO Andy Jassy , who succeeded founder Jeff Bezos in 2021. Last year, it introduced pricier versions of its Echo smart speakers and began charging non-Prime members a subscription for Alexa+ , the souped-up version of its digital assistant.
The $550 Alexa Tablet 12 Pro costs more than double the price of the $155 Fire HD 10, Amazon's base model, and puts it more in line with Apple 's iPad, which runs from $449 to $1,199.
The launch comes as Amazon and other device makers are grappling with a historic surge in memory prices . Amazon in August boosted prices on Echos, Kindles, Fire TVs and other hardware, citing the memory crunch. And earlier this year, Apple raised its prices on MacBooks and iPads, while Nintendo hiked the price of its Switch 2 console.
Amazon denied that rising memory costs played a role in its decision to charge more for the Alexa tablet. But Panos Panay, the company's devices boss, acknowledged that the shortage made it "quite tricky" to build a premium tablet at a reasonable price without making any "trade-offs."
"I think the team did a good job designing without making that trade," Panay told CNBC in an interview. "They gave you the full craftsmanship of a product, but are able to keep it at that price point."
The company said the Alexa tablet's improved speed and performance, artificial intelligence features, and upgraded design warrant a higher price tag and put the devices on par with "the best tablets on the market."
Amazon added a sleeker, sturdier aluminum backing, higher resolution display and faster processors. On the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, the highest-end model, it incorporated "Nanomatte" display technology that was developed in partnership with Corning to "dramatically reduce screen glare."
One of the most notable upgrades is that all of the devices run Google 's Android operating system, a major departure from earlier models, which relied on a custom Android version dubbed Fire OS and used Amazon's own app store, limiting the number of apps that were available.
It's also the first time Amazon has attached a set of devices to the Alexa brand, the company's automated assistant first launched in 2014 via the Echo smart speaker. Alexa is front and center in the new tablets, via a "dynamic tab" on the home screen that offers recommendations and lets users quickly pick up where they left off reading or watching a TV show. Users can say "Alexa" or tap the "Ask Alexa" button to ask questions.
The company also introduced a new feature called "On-Screen Intelligence," where users can ask Alexa to look at what's on their screen and make suggestions or take actions.
In a demo, Panay showed how users could watch a TikTok clip of someone cooking on a grill and ask Alexa to shop for a burger press used in the video. Users can also pull up a game schedule and add every date to their calendar, Amazon said.
"She'll do the homework, and if things work out, she's going to bring up a shopping list where I can just hit buy now," Panay said.
Amazon said it will continue to support the Fire lineup for four years after the final shipment and consumers can continue using their devices as they do today, but it is no longer manufacturing new units. The Fire lineup includes a 10-inch and 8-inch model as well as two versions targeted for kids.

articles.title_orig: Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro hands-on: Taking aim at the iPad Pro for less than half the price
articles.title_zh: Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro hands-on: Taking aim at the iPad Pro for less than half the price
articles.content_orig:
It's a promising tablet that starts at about $500.
When it comes to tablets, only a few names are left standing: iPads , Galaxy Tabs , Surface and Fire . Amazon's Fire tablets have acquired a bit of a cult following, thanks mostly to the value they deliver for their relatively low prices. So it's a bit of a risky move for the company to announce today that it's completely replacing that line with a new family of Alexa tablets. The good news is, you'll still find the new 8-inch and 11-inch models fairly comparable to the Fire HD 8 and Fire HD 10. And the (probably) better news? The new Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro looks set to take on the iPad Pro.
The 12-inch device starts at $499, with a more premium variant going up to $549. At that price, the latter version comes with 16GB of RAM and a texturized screen that the company calls a "nanomatte" display. It's powered by a 4-nanometer 8-core processor by MediaTek (specifically, the Dimensity 8400) and has some powerhouse display specs. It can refresh at up to 120Hz, has a 3:2 aspect ratio and a pixel density of 280ppi. It also has four speakers onboard with Dolby Atmos support for a surround sound-like experience, along with a promised 16-hour battery life. And as its new name suggests, Alexa is deeply integrated into the tablet's interface. I'll get into how all that felt in person in a bit.
I was able to speak with Panos Panay, the company's head of devices, Alexa and Leo this week, along with a couple of reporters. Acknowledging the Fire tablet's popularity, Panay said millions of units have been sold, as "they're fairly inexpensive and different."
The Alexa tablets, he added, are the result of 2.5 years of work. He said it was rebuilt from the ground up to offer "the most premium experience we possibly could" at "an affordable price point."
Panay said Amazon had three areas of focus when designing the Alexa tablets: All the apps users want (via, for the first time, the Google Play Store) and "Alexa intertwined throughout the entire OS." The third one, which actually was the first one he mentioned, seems to be a mix of the redesign and hardware.
Panay then went on to say that his philosophy whenever building a product is "What's the one thing?" This one thing is slightly different from those three things we mentioned earlier. It's the one thing that, according to Panay, should not be compromised on, no matter what. And for the Alexa tablet, "the one thing on this product was we were going to go reinvent the screen. No matter what."
My confusion over all those numbers aside, the nanomatte display on the Alexa tablet is certainly unique. That is — on a gadget made by Amazon. When Panay first brought the device into view, before he even mentioned the display, I already noticed its texture. But my immediate reaction was that it's very reminiscent of the nano texture Apple brought to the iPad Pro line starting with the M4 generation in 2024. More recently, I've seen a similar treatment on the iPhone Duo's internal display.
It's not a bad thing that the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro's nanomatte screen reminds me of Apple's. Both options are striking in person and effectively reduce glare. When I used a video camera to record the non-nanomatte and nanomatte tablets side by side, it was clear the untreated model was more reflective of overhead lights at various angles. I did find it impacted brightness and readability ever so slightly in direct sunlight, though.
The thing that differentiates Amazon from Apple in this case though, is Kindle mode. "We challenged the team, because of the nanomatte display and what we could do with it and how it feels when you put a pen on it," Panay said. "Shouldn't this be a Kindle? Shouldn't it be a Kindle Scribe?"
As the story goes, the team delivered. Kindle Mode is available across the entire Amazon Alexa tablet lineup, and it's basically a focused fullscreen reading environment that mutes notifications and reduces blue light. It also extends battery life to allow for 20 hours of reading. You can customize what contacts or apps can break through when you're in this mode, and for now it appears the only app that works with Kindle mode is, well, the Kindle app.
Since Kindle Mode only kicks in when you launch the Kindle app, there's not a lot of setup you have to do. There's also a pleasant animation when you enter and exit the app that has colors fade in and out, serving as a visual indicator of which mode you're in.
You can tweak the software to default to one of three color schemes in this view: Ink Paper, Color Paper and Standard. The first is a grayscale rendering, the second is a muted effect similar to newspaper comics and the third is somewhat like the glossy pages of a magazine. On the nanomatte model I tried, the effects were even more appealing. In that Color Paper option, something about the textured screen added a visual grit that scratched a nostalgic itch somewhere deep in the recesses of my almost-40-year-old brain.
With its page-turn animations and fullscreen two-page layout, it's pretty easy to imagine Kindle mode on any other tablet, like the iPad Pro with nano-texture glass I've mentioned a few times. And sure, it feels like you can simply buy a Kindle for the privilege of reading on a gadget that won't bother you with alerts. Even Panay conceded "You could argue that I'm challenging my own Kindle business by creating an Alexa tablet that does incredible Kindle work."
"But I think it's rad for the customer," he said. I guess if you're a person who mostly wants a tablet that can sometimes double as a pretty effective distraction-free Kindle, then the Alexa tablet could be right for you.
You can also use the company's new Pro Pen with these tablets, which will cost an extra $90. It felt quite similar to the Kindle Scribe's stylus in my brief experience doodling with it, but I need more time to fully evaluate it.
One of the most noteworthy additions to the Alexa tablets is the Google Play Store. Whereas the previous Fire tablets ran the company's FireOS and could only install apps via its included App store, the new versions allow you to easily access the entire ecosystem of Android apps. Because you're getting them via the Play Store, you'll also benefit from the vetting and security policies of Google's system.
As for the Alexa tablets' interface, there's a mostly familiar skeleton here that is based on Android. On top of it are some Alexa+ integrations, like a box in the top right corner of the home page that Amazon is calling the "Dynamic Tab." Unlike the Dynamic Island in Apple's products, this isn't an area that expands and contracts depending on the activities running in the background. It's just a 3-inch-wide box that's almost 2 inches tall and stays that size no matter what you're doing. In it are suggestions by Alexa+ based on your recent activity, whether that be the city you're visiting, the last show you watched on Prime Video or a book you're reading.
On the bottom right is a little rectangular cutout that houses the Alexa+ input bar with the A-shaped logo, the words "Ask Alexa" and a microphone button to start a voice chat. This is fairly straightforward – just tap the bar or microphone and start typing or saying what you need. A window will pop up to show your request and the assistant's responses to you.
More interesting, however, is the systemwide gesture of dragging in from the bottom right. No matter what app you're on, when you drag in from the bottom right, Alexa+ will detect what's on your screen. A glowing blue halo appears along the screen's edges to indicate it's looking at your tablet, and then a window pops up to show you a handful of suggestions about what Alexa thinks you want to ask. You can either choose from one of the options or just initiate a conversation.

articles.title_orig: Italy approves elections overhaul as opposition accuse Meloni of 'scam' law
articles.title_zh: Italy approves elections overhaul as opposition accuse Meloni of 'scam' law
articles.content_orig:
Italy's parliament has approved fiercely contested changes to the country's electoral system championed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni ahead of elections due next year.
Lawmakers voted 227 to 164 in favour of moving to a fully proportional system, which Meloni has argued will boost the chance of clear winners and more stable government.
Opposition parties say her right-wing coalition has designed the proposals to improve its chance of retaining power and, in a heated debate on Thursday, accused it of pushing through the "fraudulent" reform to flout democracy.
Meloni had warned she could resign and trigger an early election if the plans were rejected, with the secret ballot seen as a test of her authority.
Meloni's coalition has overseen a rare period of political stability for Italy since her election in 2022, and last month her government became the country's longest-running since World War Two.
The voting reform will see the country move away from its current hybrid voting system, in which about a third of members are chosen through a first-past-the-post vote and the rest through proportional representation.
Parties proposing to form a coalition will be required to put forward their joint candidate for prime minister, and their political programme, before any general election.
A party or coalition which emerges with the largest share of the votes - provided this exceeds 42% - will be awarded 105 additional seats in parliament (70 in the lower house and 35 in the senate), which could turn a narrow victory into a more comfortable majority.
Centre-left members held up signs with slogans including "No to the scam" and "fraudulent law" during a debate ahead of the vote, and accused the government of forcing through the new voting rules.
"Go ahead and change the electoral law, we will win in any case under any voting system," said Democratic Party (PD) leader Elly Schlein.
Five Star leader and former Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte told AFP news agency that the move was "a mess, a convoluted scheme, devised solely to find a formula to gain an advantage in the upcoming elections".
The proposals have also exposed tensions within the ranks of Meloni's coalition, too, with the Brothers of Italy (FdI) party and its allies, the far-right League and centre-right Forza Italia.
Analysts had predicted that Thursday's final vote was unlikely to fail - particularly given the number of lawmakers who would risk losing their eligibility for a parliamentary pension if their term was ended early as a result of the threatened snap election.
"To those who hoped to see the centre-right divided," Meloni wrote on social media after the vote, "today we respond with facts: we are united, cohesive, and determined to carry forward the commitments made to citizens."
She added: "We are introducing rules designed to promote the stability and parliamentary coherence of any government, regardless of its political colour."
Meloni's term officially comes to an end in October 2027, although she could bring elections forward to the spring.

articles.title_orig: South Korea to recall its ambassador to Ukraine over North Korean POW dispute
articles.title_zh: South Korea to recall its ambassador to Ukraine over North Korean POW dispute
articles.content_orig:
FILE - Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at United Nations headquarters, on Sept. 23, 2026. Seth Wenig/AP hide caption
SEOUL, South Korea — South Korea said Thursday it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, stepping up its protest against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's recent revelation of a supposedly secret transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.
The South Korean announcement came days after its President Lee Jae Myung threatened to take unspecified punitive steps if Ukraine refuses to apologize over the revelation.
South Korea's Foreign Ministry didn't say when the ambassador, Park Hee-chang, will be brought back home. A ministry statement said that South Korea will continue consultations with Ukraine, adding it hopes the dispute between the two countries would be resolved smoothly.
South Korea and Ukraine became embroiled in a diplomatic row after Zelenskyy spoke about the transfer of the North Korean soldiers during his U.N. speech on Sept. 23. South Korea has accused Ukraine of violating a nondisclosure agreement on their transfer in mid-September, but Kyiv has denied agreeing to such a deal.
The soldiers were among thousands of North Korean troops deployed to support Russia's war against Ukraine. Since their capture in early 2025, the soldiers had expressed their desires to resettle in South Korea, because they could face persecution if repatriated home. South Korea had said it would accept them, because it legally regards the North as part of its territory and has a policy of accepting and financially supporting North Korean defectors.
South Korean officials said the non-disclosure agreement was made because they were concerned about the safety of the North Korean soldiers and their relatives in the North. But many experts say South Korea's liberal government likely also worries the disclosure of their arrival may hurt its efforts to improve ties with North Korea.
North Korea's state media hasn't commented on the soldiers' transfer. But the North previously reacted with fury to major defections of its citizens, accusing South Korea of kidnapping them. North Korea has shunned any talks with South Korea and the U.S. and focused on bolstering its nuclear program since 2019.
It's unclear what other steps South Korea would take. Experts say maintaining good relations with Ukraine is in South Korean national interests because Kyiv could provide Seoul with intelligence about North Korea's expanding cooperation with Russia and its battlefield experiences. They say cooperation with Ukraine is important for South Korea's partnerships with many Western countries supporting Ukraine over the war.
Observers say Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer of the North Korean POWs to expose the danger of North Korea's military support to Russia as a way to win more international assistance.
South Korea has provided $445 million in humanitarian assistance to Ukraine since 2022. In July, Lee pledged $100 million in aid to Ukraine in a meeting with Zelenskyy,

articles.title_orig: Tanker hit by multiple projectiles in Gulf off Qatar, maritime agency says
articles.title_zh: Tanker hit by multiple projectiles in Gulf off Qatar, maritime agency says
articles.content_orig:
A tanker has been struck by "multiple projectiles" north of Qatar in the Gulf, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency.
The incident - a rare attack deep inside the Gulf - happened 51 nautical miles (94km) from Madinat al-Shamal with casualties reported, the UKMTO said.
Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard identified the vessel as the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged oil and chemical tanker Acers. On Saturday it was reported as sailing towards the Strait of Hormuz waterway, which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman.
Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the region since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February.
At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 93 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization (IMO).
The IMO said the last incident that resulted in casualties was on 9 September, when two sailors were killed in an attack on the Panama-flagged tanker El Gaia in the Strait of Hormuz, just north of Oman's Musandam peninsula.
This is also the first reported attack on a ship this far west of the Strait of Hormuz since that same day, according to Martin Kelly, head of advisory at EOS Risk Group.
Also on Thursday, Vanguard amended an earlier report that had said there was a fire on board another tanker in the Gulf of Oman, about 40km east of Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates.
The company clarified that there were no indications a fire occurred on the vessel, which it had identified as the Marshall Islands-flagged Dhalkut.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Tehran's missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.
To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
Over the past two weeks, crude exports through the waterway have averaged 12 million barrels per day (bpd), which is around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler.

articles.content_orig:

At a Google Cloud event on Thursday, the company announced it’s bringing its Gemini AI into the agentic age, with the launch of a unified agent that can not only answer questions but also get things done on the user’s behalf, all from a single interface.
The move comes as AI tools have been moving beyond being just conversational experiences to those that can take ownership of assigned tasks, generate code, schedule meetings, book appointments and travel, and more. It also follows the rise of consumer-facing agents like Meta’s Muse and those that operate over messaging, like Instinct and others, as well as the recent debut of ChatGPT’s Dots.
The company still has a good shot at achieving scale for its agentic efforts: as Google CEO Sundar Pichai pointed out at the event’s start, Gemini today has over 1 billion monthly active users. He also noted that nearly 90% of Fortune 100 businesses now use Gemini Enterprise at work.
Given Gemini’s adoption in the corporate world, Google will initially focus on bringing the agent to businesses before later rolling it out to consumers.
According to Pichai, this will allow the company to solve the “harder problems around security, scale, and performance,” which come with launching powerful agents such as these.
Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, explained that the new agent can be given “objectives, not just instructions.” That means it’s able to plan the work, use custom skills and tools, and connect to businesses’ internal systems to accomplish its goals.
By default, the AI will pick the best model to complete the task, but users can also take over to choose a model — including those from third parties, starting with Anthropic’s Claude models. Google said that it will expand the model picker to include open source models and other private models in the future.
The request can include attachments, like files, folders, or other projects designed for specific workstreams, like those that combine files and skills. The agent can connect to the business’s data and systems, like Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack, Jira, Confluence, Git, BigQuery, Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, and others.
It can also connect and work securely with any Model Context Protocol (MCP) server inside or outside the company’s network.
Users can keep track of what Gemini is doing from a “tasks inbox” interface, where they can see Gemini’s thinking process, delegation of tasks to subagents, loading of special skills, code, and progress.
Notably, the AI will have its own Workspace account, as if it’s just another coworker. That means it has its own email address and its own context, Google said. It knows who at the company is on what team, their time zones, who needs to approve items, what’s on people’s calendars, and more. Users can call the agent by tagging it, emailing it, sharing with it, or adding it to a group chat. As it takes action, it writes an audit trail attributed to the agent, instead of a person.
The agent will be accessible from iOS and Android mobile devices, Windows and Mac desktops, the command line interface, Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, ServiceNow, and Slack.
The agent’s early testers included sportswear brand On, Shopify, and PayPal, and noted that Gemini Enterprise customers include large businesses like BNP Paribas, Bradesco, Merck, Orange Spain, Santee Cooper, SOMPO, Ulta Beauty, and Wesfarmers.
Google said new flexible spending options, including multi-model orchestration, smart routing, and real-time spend caps, will help businesses keep their enterprise AI costs under better control.
